title: Transformative Innovation Policy Africa Exploratory Hub
description:
This project will enable three countries in sub-Saharan Africa to undertake research and inform policymaking in science, technology, and innovation (STI) in their respective countries. These short pilot projects will map out the current state of STI with a lens of “transformative change” that has been successfully applied by the Transformative Innovation Policy Consortium (TIPC) in recent years in high and upper-middle-income countries. 

The TIPC is a group of policymakers and funding agencies working together to give substance to a new framing for STI policy that aims to contribute to addressing global societal challenges, as encapsulated in the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals. These include climate change, inequality, employment, and pathways to economic growth and development. 

Case studies will be developed by in-country researchers using the TIPC methodology to help identify specific recommendations for STI policy. The three selected countries will also have an opportunity to engage in the global conversation around innovation policy with the entire consortium, and to explore opportunities for continued participation beyond the pilot phase. This project will directly benefit the work of the Science Granting Councils Initiative in providing new research and policymaking avenues for STI in sub-Saharan Africa.

The project will build on TIPC’s successes in the past two years in reconceptualizing innovation for sustainable development, and in exploring new ways for research funders around the world to have a greater impact in this area. The TIPC approach includes policy experimentation, capacity-building, and research, which all inform local implementation projects and sustain a global research network. This network in turn aims to fundamentally change how we approach science and innovation policies, from their inception to their evaluation. | Ce projet permettra à trois pays en Afrique subsaharienne d’entreprendre des recherches et d’éclairer les responsables de l’élaboration des politiques dans le domaine des sciences, de la technologie et de l’innovation (STI) dans leurs pays respectifs. Ces projets pilotes de courte durée mettront en évidence l’état actuel des STI avec en tête l’idée d’opérer des changements en profondeur, point de vue qui a été adopté avec succès par le Transformative Innovation Policy Consortium (TIPC) au cours des dernières années dans les pays à revenu intermédiaire, tranche supérieure et les pays à revenu élevé. 

Ce consortium regroupe des décideurs politiques et des organismes de financement qui, ensemble, donnent corps à l’élaboration d’une nouvelle politique de STI visant à contribuer à résoudre les problèmes sociétaux mondiaux, tels qu’ils sont définis dans les objectifs de développement durable des Nations Unies. Parmi ces objectifs, on retrouve les changements climatiques, les inégalités, l’emploi et la marche à suivre vers la croissance économique et le développement. 

Des études de cas seront réalisées par les chercheurs locaux à l’aide de la méthodologie du TIPC pour aider à formuler des recommandations précises pour la politique de STI. Les trois pays retenus auront également l’occasion de prendre part à une conversation mondiale autour du volet innovation de la politique avec l’ensemble du consortium et d’envisager la poursuite de leur participation après la phase pilote. Ce projet fera directement avancer les travaux de l’Initiative des conseils subventionnaires de la recherche scientifique en proposant de nouvelles pistes de recherche et de développement de politiques dans le domaine des STI en Afrique subsaharienne.

Le projet s’appuiera sur les réussites du TIPC obtenues ces deux dernières années pour reconceptualiser l’innovation aux fins du développement durable et aider les bailleurs de fonds du monde entier à explorer de nouvelles façons de gagner en efficacité dans ce domaine. L’approche du TIPC inclut l’expérimentation des politiques, le renforcement des capacités et la recherche, qui favoriseront la réalisation de projets à l’échelle locale et le maintien d’un réseau de recherche mondial. En retour, ce réseau cherche à modifier de manière fondamentale notre approche des politiques sur la science et l’innovation, de leur conception à leur évaluation.

title: Maralal Diocese Integrated Livelihoods and Peace Building Programme
description:
The Catholic Diocese of Maralal covers the administrative County of Samburu, an area of 21,000 Sq.km with three livelihood  zones of Pastoral in lowland areas, (80% of the total population), Agro-pastoral in highland areas, Urban and sub-urban areas. Samburu county is a remote and marginalized from mainstream development and lacks basic infrastructure, for example, roads, communication infrastructure and water facilities. Water facilities are inadequately developed and spatially far apart. Livestock markets are generally few in remote areas, hence over-supplied with livestock for sale, resulting in very low prices for livestock. Extension services for livestock production are lacking,  Livestock diseases are prevalent with frequent outbreaks, of foot and mouth disease, contagious caprine preneumonia (CCPP), east coast fever (ECF) and infestation of parasites.

The County is classified as arid and semi-arid and is affected by frequent droughts which have become more severe in recent years due to climate change. These droughts have devastating effects on Pastoralist's livelihoods (livestock) and food security as they cause livestock losses, and subsequent food insecurity.  Cattle are particularly badly affected by drought compared to small livestock as natural resources like pasture and water deteriorate during droughts. As a result, the communities are periodically dependant on food aid. The problem is made worse by communities’ reliance on a single source of livelihood (livestock), as they lack alternative sources of income mainly due to high rates of illiteracy and unemployment. Lack of alternative sources of livelihoods forces communities to turn to charcoal burning as a coping mechanism, which in itself leads to environmental degradation. Further, local breeds of livestock produce low yields of milk and have small body size and they are often unattractive in the competitive markets.

Samburu County is also affected by inter-community conflict mainly resulting from cattle raids and struggle over access to natural resources like pasture and water for livestock during drought. However, there are  other  factors  to conflict,  political  instigation on ethnic  grounds,  inadequate participation and representation of social, economic and political minorities in development initiatives, events and forums. Influx of small arms and light weapons due to civil strife in the neighbouring countries of Ethiopia, Somalia, Sudan and Northern Uganda, porous borders and Inadequate legal and institutional framework to deal with conflicts internally.

It is important to note that the above factors interact in such a way that behind any conflict, there are other underlying, unresolved or related issues, which would need to be understood before amicable solutions can be reached. The conflicts in the region have, therefore, handicapped the livelihoods of the communities subjecting them to endemic poverty.

This is cycle 3 Integrated livelihoods and peace project for three years 2012 -2014. The  project  seeks to enhance house hold food security through increased incomes, seeks to enhance communities  capacities  for  peace  and  conflict  transformation.  The project has   livelihoods and peace building activities that are complementary.

The target areas are Wamba, Maralal and Baragoi zones. The 14 Parishes of the Diocese provide structures at the grassroots level through which spiritual as well as development activities of communities are implemented. The project will utilise a combination of activities including a baseline survey, capacity building of farmers on modern farming technology, introduction of drought resistant crops, and income generation activities. To support harmonious co-existence the project will support local justice and peace structures on early warning signs, empower the community to participate and engage in development activities that include resident associations, governance and training forums, and media advocacy amongst others. The  project  will  seek  to  have  coordinated  interventions  by  peace  actors  for  sustainability and  bigger  impact.

The total budget  for  project this will be  80,000 per  year  for three  years.  Whereas peace building activities will target the larger population, the project will reach a total of 805 households: 225 (organized into 10 groups) with IGAs, 430 with crop farming, 100 households with Dairy Goats and 50 with bucks for cross breeding.

title: Peace Building, Reconciliation and Resettlement Response to Post Election Violence in Kenya.
description:
Kisii district is one of the twelve districts, situated in Nyanza Province in the Western Part of Kenya. The district is mostly hilly and lies on a highland equatorial climate and as such receives rain almost throughout the year. Kisii district is one of the most densely populated in Kenya with around 50 % of the population below the age of 20. Due to its high population density, land is put to maximum agricultural use with plots becoming ever smaller as it is subdivided within families. A result of this is that a large population of Kisii community members migrated to neighbouring districts in order to be able to support their families. 

The Kisii community was greatly affected by ethnic tensions and violence during the last post election violence which resulted in a country wide displacement of 250,000 people and an estimated 1,200 killed many of whom were from the Kisii community.    

The post election humanitarian situation within Kisii came about when Kisii community members were forcefully evicted from the Rift Valley by the Kalenjin community from business/ work or land they had possessed in Rift Valley making them resort to return to their ancestral home district. Many people from the Kisii community currently feel unable to return to the areas they have fled from due to fear of fresh attacks and are opting to remain in their ancestral home district in Kisii. 

This has posed a problem because host families often have limited resources on their own and are already overcrowded and their financial resources overstretched.

This project proposes to provide livelihood support to vulnerable returnee families who show the capacity to potentially re-establish their livelihoods which were lost during the post election violence. 

This project does not use funds from CAFOD, as it is funded by the Irish government through Trocaire and part of a Post Election Violence consortia between CAFOD and Trocaire.

title: Diocese of Isiolo a Pilot Project on Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR)
description:
The Catholic Diocese of Isiolo covers two administrative districts of Isiolo and Garbatulla. The two districts are located in the Arid and Semi-arid (ASAL) areas in Northern Kenya. These areas are prone to drought on a cyclical basis. Analysis over the past two to three decades highlights the greater prevalence of drought in these areas, reduced recovery periods and increasing intensity. The main livelihoods of people living in the ASAL areas are largely dependent on consistent climatic conditions, particularly a reliable and predictable pattern of rainfall, with adequate recovery periods between droughts and floods. According to the Kenya Food Security Steering Group’s (KFSSG) Assessment Report, 2008, “reduced recovery periods between droughts are breaking down their existing coping strategies and increasing dependency on external humanitarian interventions”. Further, conflicts over scarce resources resulting from the harsh climatic conditions continue to dog these ASAL areas.  Rains are supposed to fall twice a year; the long rains fall between March to May and the short rains in October - December.  These rains have been unreliable and inadequate over the years. 

According to the KFSSG’s Long Rains Assessment Report, 2008, a significant and growing proportion of the population in Northern Kenya suffers chronic and acute food insecurity. The population is not able to meet their minimum food requirements during the drought periods. The poor performance of the long rains season was compounded by a complex combination of other food security factors within the livelihoods including the spread of the highly virulent Peste de Petits Ruminants (PPR) livestock disease which has a mortality rate of 50-80 percent, heightened food and non-food prices, rising conflict; below normal short rains seasons and reduced resilience caused by cumulative effects of consecutive years of eroded coping strategies caused by drought, floods and conflict.   The report indicated that food security has been declining in the Northern areas and in the significant areas of the agro pastoral and marginal agricultural clusters. The long rains was characterised by early cessation and most areas reported less than 50 percent of normal rainfall. The poor rains resulted in livestock and pastoralists having to trek distances of up to 10 Kilometres in search of water and pasture as the drought conditions set in earlier than usual. Furthermore, livestock disease outbreak resulted in movement quarantines and closure of markets, thus limiting trade. Moreover, food prices rose up to 50-80 percent higher than normal, while crop yields declined by up to 80 percent in agro pastoral areas in Isiolo District. Conflicts over limited resources including water points and pasture is causing displacement and negating livestock production prospects.

According to the Arid Lands Resource Management Project (ALRMP) Early Warning System bulletins and an assessment carried out by the District Steering Group (DSG) in July 2008 the poor rainfall has resulted to pasture depletion, poor harvest and deterioration of the livestock body conditions. This has further led to reduced earnings from livestock sales and increased food insecurity. 

According to the Kenya Food Security Update, January 2009, the situation is worsening as a result of the failure of December short rains. The report shows food security has deteriorated to critical levels and the livestock body conditions are rapidly deteriorating due to inadequate pasture, browse and water. Currently, the food commodity prices are more than 120 percent above long-term averages across the region and on an upward trend. The report predicts that the resulting migration of livestock towards limited water resources is likely to exacerbate conflicts and predispose livestock disease, leading to livestock productivity loss and, in some instances, increased mortality. In a nutshell, a succession of failed seasons in substantial areas in Northern Kenya, the PPR and other livestock diseases, conflicts in the pastoral areas, the unprecedented rise in food and non-food prices, crop failure, and substantial gaps in non-food interventions have combined to predict acute food insecurity while heightening chronic food insecurity across the arid and semi-arid areas in Northern Kenya.

The communities’ in ability to predict, prepare for and mitigate the effects of disasters, acute water shortage for human and livestock use during prolonged droughts and unsustainable natural resource management practices are major problems that the proposed project is going to tackle. Due to the cyclical occurrence of disasters, it has been difficult to realize long term sustainable development in the target area. To build resilience of the local communities to the adverse impact of recurrent droughts and other disasters, CAFOD plans to support the Development Office of the Diocese of Isiolo to implement a two year DRR project whose overarching goal is "reduced impact of disasters on the lives and livelihoods of vulnerable communities in the Diocese of Isiolo". The main focus for the two-year DRR Project is to empower the vulnerable pastoralists and agro-pastoralists communities to effectively prepare, mitigate and manage the adverse effects of disasters. This will be achieved by implementing a number of carefully selected activities including undertaking a baseline survey, contingency planning and disaster preparedness trainings, development  and implementation of community-managed disaster preparedness plans, development and rehabilitation of water points, developing community early warning systems and advocacy on DRR and climate change. 

The project is intended to strengthen the establishment of sustainable livelihoods that are geared towards reduction of vulnerabilities of communities to hazardous effects. The proposed DRR Pilot phase will be an intermediate recovery, mitigation and preparedness phase in the Diocese of Isiolo after a three months’ humanitarian project being supported by CAFOD. The project is also indented to strengthen the existing integrated Sustainable Livelihoods and Peacebuilding projects already being supported by CAFOD in the diocese. The peacebuilding component will be a crucial component in addressing resource conflicts. The proposed project will therefore not be a stand alone project but will be systematically integrated with the existing CAFOD supported projects in the Diocese. In this way, the project offers a good opportunity for addressing disaster issues in an holistic manner. This holistic approach is believed will result in increased impact in reducing community vulnerability to recurrent disasters. 

The project plans to target 8,380 beneficiaries from the most vulnerable drought-prone communities of Korbessa, Kina, Badana and Oldonyiro with plans of scaling up the project activities in other vulnerable communities living in Merti Center, Kisile, and Modogashe in the subsequent project cycles based on availability of funds. These areas were selected based on need and vulnerability to droughts and other climatic shocks.

title: Diocese of Marsabit a Pilot Project in Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR)

The poor pursue unsustainable resource management practices such as overgrazing which weighs heavily on the fragile environment. 

According to the Kenya Food Security Update, January 2009, the situation is worsening as a result of the failure of the December short rains. The report shows food security has deteriorated to critical levels and the livestock body conditions are rapidly deteriorating due to inadequate pasture, browse and water. Currently, the food commodity prices are more than 120 percent above long-term averages across the region and on an upward trend. The report predicts that the resulting migration of livestock towards limited water resources is likely to exacerbate conflict and predispose livestock disease, leading to livestock productivity loss and, in some instances, increased mortality. The communities’ in ability to predict, prepare for and mitigate the effects of disasters, acute water shortage for human and livestock use during prolonged droughts and unsustainable natural resources management practices are major problems that the proposed project is going to tackle. Due to the cyclical occurrence of disasters, it has been difficult to realize long term sustainable development in the target area.  To address these problems, CAFOD plans to support the Diocese of Marsabit to embark on a capacity building exercise of the target local communities to predict, prepare for and mitigate the effects of disasters through community managed processes by implementing a two-year pilot phase of Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) Project whose overarching goal is, “increased resilience of vulnerable communities in the Diocese of Marsabit in the light of recurrent climatic shocks and disasters”. This will be achieved by implementing a number of carefully selected activities including undertaking a baseline survey, contingency planning and disaster preparedness trainings, development and implementation of community-managed disaster preparedness plans and development and rehabilitation of water points, development of early warning systems and advocacy on DRR and climate change. This project plans to target 3,000 beneficiaries from the most vulnerable drought-prone communities living in the Locations of Kargi, Hurri Hills, Dirib Gombo and Sololo. 

The proposed DRR Pilot phase will be an intermediate recovery, mitigation and preparedness phase in the Diocese of Marsabit after a three months’ humanitarian project being supported by CAFOD. The project is also indented to strengthen the existing integrated Sustainable Livelihoods and Peacebuilding project already being supported by CAFOD in the diocese. The peacebuilding component will be a crucial component in addressing resource-based conflicts in the target areas. The proposed project will therefore not be a stand alone project but will be systematically integrated with the existing CAFOD supported projects in the Diocese. In this way, the project offers a good opportunity for addressing disaster issues in an holistic manner. This holistic approach is believed will result in increased impact in reducing community vulnerability to recurrent disasters.

title: Conflict resolution in Isiolo
description:
The aim of the envisaged project is to contribute towards peaceful co-existence among the communities and its environs through community capacity building on conflict resolution and management.  Over the years Isiolo has experienced many forms of conflict the year. From the years 1996 – 2002 Isiolo experienced serious forms of conflicts that prompted many actors to intervene with varying degree of success. Since the year 2002 up to 2009 Isiolo experienced a period of peace probably due to the change in the political climate. 

Given the Catholic Church position of non partisan, non political and being voice of the voiceless it is better placed to intervene and foster peace in the affected area. The church realizes that issues of peace can not be handled single – handedly. It is in this spirit that the diocese envisages to work with other likeminded people and institutions in this endeavor. The diocese of Isiolo and partners are ideally suited to support this initiative because of their interest in development, human rights and promotion of human dignity and peaceful society.

The project's two main aims include, to promote peaceful and harmonious co-existence among the Isiolo communities and the neighbors; and to enhance communities capacities on peace and conflict transformation.

title: Kyatune Sustainable Livelihoods and Disaster Risk Reduction Project
description:
The Kyatune Sustainable Livelihoods and Disaster Risk Reduction Project is a pilot phase intended to serve the community living in Kyatune Location in Kitui District. The project targets 2,000 most poor and vulnerable drought-prone individuals in the location.

The overarching goal of the proposed project is ‘to improve resilience of most poor vulnerable drought-prone communities of Kyatune through creation of economic community based assets to mitigate the effects of drought and climate change’

The project aims at achieving four major closely interrelated outcomes. Firstly; improved capacity for the local communities residing in Kyatune to prepare and mitigate against the effects of droughts and other natural calamities by 2012 through training local leaders on DRR, drought contingency planning, awareness creation on DRR and climate change, formation of Early Warning Groups and preparation and dissemination of early warning information, establishment of tree nurseries and planting of ecologically friendly trees. Secondly, Increased availability, access and management of water for domestic, agricultural and livestock production through out the dry season by 2012 through construction and protection of water structures through voucher for work system, formation and training of Water User Associations on water management and DRR, awareness creation on hygiene and sanitation and construction of ar-baloo toilet slabs for the most poor and vulnerable households. Thirdly; increased food production through better farming technologies such as community demonstration farms, green houses at household level, drip/watering irrigation instead of relying on rain-fed agriculture, support for horticultural crops, vegetable and fruit tree growing, preparation and application of compost manure, training on conservation agriculture, establishment of producer marketing groups, awareness creation on drought tolerant crops and establishment of seed banks. Finally; the project also aims at achieving increased household incomes through improved market access for sale of farm produce. This outcome will be achieved through supporting most affected households with ghalla goats and bucks, training Community Animal Health Assistants (paravets) on animal husbandry, increasing farmers’ access to market information through establishment of market information centres and boards and supporting farmers to establish market linkages. Further, energy saving technologies will be incorporated in the training sessions. 

The project will utilize the existing Diocesan Church structures especially the Parishes to reach out to the intended beneficiaries. The project will also collect and analyze gender-specific information on the participation of women and other vulnerable groups. The project will take into consideration the interests of women, children, youth and poor men as well as the voices of the community leaders and other individuals and community based groups in ensuring that human rights upheld.

title: Towards the Realisation of Climate Change Bill in Kenya
description:
The Kenya Climate Change Working Group (KCCWG) plans to organise a key stakeholders' workshop and two sets of meetings whose overarching goal is to develop and achieve a climate change bill in Kenya. 

The proposed project 'Towards Realization of the Climate Change Bill in Kenya' is aimed at achieving three key outcomes. First; a parliamentarians and KCCWG Climate Change Bill Team Set Up. Secondly; a revised edition of the climate change bill produced and Finally; a specific roadmap to achieve the Climate Change Bill is drawn and implemented.

To realise these outcomes, the KCCWG plans to undertake the following activities: -
1. To form a Parliamentarian and KCCWG Team that will be involved in organising a stakeholders' workshop on Climate Change and organising Task Force Meetings. 
2. To engage a KCCWG technical persons to provide specific inputs to the current draft bill on climate change.
3. To Produce relevant Information Education and Communication (IEC) materials for creating awareness on the climate change bill.
4. Organise One meeting between KCCWG Technical Persons and the Bill Drafters

title: Climate Change Advocacy in Kenya
description:
Climate change poses immense challenges to the lives and livelihoods of many people in Kenya. For instance through recurrent droughts, drying of water sources, erratic rainfall, flash floods and landslides and the spread of diseases like Malaria. 
Therefore this project aims to create a people free from the vulnerabilities of climate change, and empowered by the improvements to their livelihoods. 

The project seeks to achieve this through 4 closely interlinked outcomes which include; a positive policy and legislative framework being in place, strengthened participation of Kenyans in the climate change debates at the local, national and international level; vulnerability of poor communities to climate change in Kenya being reduced.

The proposed project will be implemented by the Kenya Climate Change Working Group (KCCWG) through working in close collaboration with the Parliamentary Committee on Renewable Energy and Climate Change (PANERECC), and actively engaging the Kenya Populace in climate change issues. The project is closely linked to ongoing CAFOD work on Sustainable Livelihoods and Disaster Risk Reduction and Climate Change Adaptation.

title: Community Climate Change Adaptation and Resilient Project
description:
The Catholic Diocese of Maralal covers three administrative districts of Samburu Central, Samburu East and Samburu North, a total of 21,000KM2. It serves a population of 223,947 people. The area covered is arid and has been adversely affected by recurrent droughts leading to increasing levels of drought losses. To reduce the impact of recurrent droughts on target communities over the coming years, the Diocese of Maralal plans to implement a second phase of Disaster Risk Reduction Project titled, 'Community Climate Change Adaptation and Resilient Initiative". 

The proposed project is meant to address the main problem of the target communities' ability to predict, prepare for and mitigate the effects of the disasters. Due to the cyclical occurrences of drought related disasters, it has been difficult to realize long-term sustainable development in the target areas. This has been exacerbated by the fact that the community’s traditional ways of predicting, preparing for and mitigating the effects of disasters have been over ridden by modern methods as well as poor access to government services.

The Community Climate Change Adaptation and Resilient Project Goal is to enhance target communities' resilience to hazards in Samburu North and Samburu Central to predict, prepare for, mitigate and develop positive coping mechanisms to the effects of drought by 2014. The project has six closely interrelated outcomes including: improved community and partner capacity to effectively engage in DRR and climate change work; improved awareness on climate change and environmental protection; improved access to potable water for human, livestock and agricultural use; improved hygiene and sanitation for target communities; and improved accessibility of target communities through construction of rural access roads.

The proposed project will be implemented in two divisions of Lorroki and Baragoi and will target a total of 6,500 beneficiaries. In Lorroki the project will be implemented in Longewani, Amaiya, Logorate, Lolmolong and Malaso while in Baragoi the project will be implemented in Logetei and Ngilai.

title: Muvitha Kathemboni Watershed Management project
description:
The project target area is Kitui County/ Diocese which is situated in South Eastern Kenya and borders Embu and Tharaka to the North, Makueni and Machakos to the west, Tana River district to the East and Taita Taveta to the South. The Catholic Diocese of Kitui covers an approximated arid and semi-arid area of 30,142 Km² out of which 6,903 Km² is occupied by Tsavo East National Park. It has a population of around 1.09 million people. 
The Catholic Diocese of Kitui is currently within 16 Government administrative districts. The region is situated within the vast arid and semi-arid lands of Kenya characterized by harsh climatic conditions and resultant frequent and prolonged drought events.
Due to limited rainfall received in the district, water resources are scarce and are composed of seasonal rivers that form during rainy seasons and immediately dry up after the rains. Although a major water source, the Athi and Tana Rivers are the only perennial rivers found within Diocese limits and flow along the border with Machakos to the West and Tharaka to the North. Several water pans and dams also supply water and are supplemented byGround water sources (boreholes, wells and springs) that are found in hilly areas. However, the ground water supplies are also insufficient since some have low yields and others high salinity. Although the water facilities are many, most are poorly maintained and unreliable and dry up during dry seasons leaving households without adequate supplies for domestic and livestock use. Poor rainfall has led to inadequate recharge of water sources leading to an ever shrinking reserve for an increasing population.
Nearly 90% of households in the region do not have access to clean water points and those who do, trek an average of 5 Kms to get to the nearest water sources. 
The climate of the district is arid and semi-arid with very erratic and unreliable rainfall. Most of the areas are generally hot and dry leading to high rate of evaporation. Deforestation has increased risk of disasters, a situation the diocese is at presently where the recurrence of droughts and other disasters has been increasing in frequency. 
The implementation of this project is intended to improve food security, enhance livelihoods and increase access to clean water to 628 households within Muvitha/Kathemboni/Syomuunyu areas of Yatta District. This translates to 1592 males and 1718 females making a total population of 3310 individuals who are set to benefit from the project. 375 boys and 615 girls within the schools in this area shall also benefit from this project.   More funds will be solicited for the project in order to go beyond the two years so that the whole catchment area can be reached.  This will bring the total population reached to 8275 individuals (1659 households), 3981 men and 4294 women.  The implementation of this - project is meant to offer lessons which would later be utilized in the initiation of similar interventions within the diocese. Water scarcity in the project area affects women more than men since it is they who have the responsibility of providing it. This project is intended to lessen the burden for the women who will now have more time to work in their farms and take care of their families. Children who often miss school to assist their parents in the search for water may now have the opportunity to attend school without interruptions. Enhanced hygiene and sanitation practices adoption is expected to lead to reduction in cases of water borne diseases, hence improved health for the community. 
Adoption of good environmental management practices is expected to increase productivity and improve conservation leading to sustainable utilization of  current resources. In the long term it is anticipated that these practices will go a long way in sensitizing the community about the dangers of over-exploitation of the natural resources. Regeneration is not automatic but a responsibility of the communities concerned to put in place measures to ensure that resources used are always done bearing in mind that measures to regenerate the same are adopted. This is expected to be done through the empowerment and capacity building of the, Natural Resource Management Committees (NRMC). The committees will be responsible for management of the water facilities and they will also act as the drivers for the conservation practices. This is one sure way of ensuring sustainability in that the community themselves would be driving their own change in ways that they understand and address problems that are clear to them.

title: Improving Access to Water and Sanitation in Bangladesh Informal Settlement in Mombasa
description:
This proposed project will address poor water access, hygiene and environmental sanitation in urban informal settlements. The poor in the these settlements have continued to bear the brunt of the burden brought about by poor investment in the water sector and diminishing fresh water availability in the country due to a myriad of factors including climate change. The WHO/UNICEF JMP report (2012)  indicates that by 2010, 59% of the population in Kenya had access to an improved water source. However this comprised 52% in rural areas and 82% in urban. While in urban areas 82% of the population has access to an improved water source, only 45% has source piped into the premise and 37% sources water out of the premise. With regard to sanitation, the report shows that 32% of the population in rural Kenya used improved sanitation facilities while 21% used unimproved ones or didn’t have one. In urban areas, 32 % had access to ‘improved’ sanitation facilities and 48% shared. Furthermore, according to a World Bank report on water and sanitation(2012) , Kenya loses Sh27 billion each year due to poor sanitation, and 21 million Kenyans, more than half the population, use unsanitary or shared latrines while 5.6 million others have no latrines at all and are forced to defecate in the open. According to the Ministry of Public Health and Sanitation, the sanitation coverage for urban areas is 68% and for rural areas is 28% and about 50% of water borne illnesses is related to poor sanitation and hygiene.
On the other hand, Kenya is rapidly urbanizing and the proportion of the population in urban areas is expected to reach 50%  by 2030 although according to the GOK census, 2009, about 33%(12.5 m) of the population dwell in urban areas.  According to the UNDP indicator data base, 55% of the urban population live in informal settlements. Most of the urban areas, especially the smaller towns do not have well equipped infrastructure to support the growing population. Much as the statistics look good for urban areas, water supply is unequally distributed in the low income areas (slums and peri-urban settlements) per capita water coverage is very low and the demand far outstrips the supply. Due to lack of connectivity, many of the slums have survived with illegal connections on the outskirts of the settlements. Often the quality of these illegal connections is poor and prone to leakages hence contamination. Furthermore, this water ends up in the hands of private vendors who sell it exorbitantly (up to 20 ($0.23) shillings/20 litres of water). This is more than three or more times the tariff that is charged by the water companies.  
The options for solid waste disposal in Kenya are very limited, and many people resort to burning or dumping their rubbish in open areas or drains. Poor people have even more limited options as they cannot afford to use private collection agencies which have come in to supplement the overwhelmed city councils.  Many of the residents without latrines in the slums use “flying toilets” as a mode of faecal matter disposal.  This combined with reckless disposal of other forms of household waste results in clogged drains, littered and hazardous environment that exacerbates spread of diseases
Inadequate water coupled with poor sanitation has been responsible for the prevalence of water-borne or sanitation-related diseases that make up the majority of the morbidity rates in these areas. The most common instances of disease in include respiratory system infections and diarrhoea and intestinal worms.
Therefore the proposed project aims to improve water and sanitation accessibility in Bangladesh informal settlement located in Mombasa. The proposed program adopts a multi-dimensional approach which has the following aspects:  increased access to improved water supply through installation of water points providing portable water; improved sanitation through implementation of waterborne toilets; adoption of hygienic practices through hygiene promotion activities; environmental sanitation promotion through solid waste  management, particularly by recycling waste and; capacity building which will entail developing sustainable community project management structures. Delivery of this program will involve active participation of beneficiaries (Bangladesh community) in all stages of project cycle, selected beneficiaries representatives will also be taken through a need driven capacity building process to enhance program results. title: Climate Resilient Agriculture: transforming the livelihoods  poor women, men and children in Samburu
description:
This is a three year project to be implemented, to achieve improved food and livelihoods security for poor women, men and children from hazard-prone and/or marginalised rural communities in Samburu Central and Samburu East sub counties in Diocese of Maralal, Kenya.

Women, men and children living in remote and hazard-prone rural areas in Samburu- Kenya rely on smallholder agriculture and livestock to provide their main source of food or income. Poverty is widespread, many face food insecurity, and livelihoods are highly dependent on climatic conditions. 
The most recent research has found that there is high probability that climate change will exacerbate the vulnerability of agricultural systems particularly in regions of Africa (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2014 5th Report).  Smallholder farmers are vital in supplying food to the local population. However, growing competition over scarce resources, limited technical support and inadequate policies have contributed to environmental degradation, low productivity and an unfavourable environment for local economic development. Poor smallholder food producers lack the capacity, technical skills and financial resources to adapt to changing climatic conditions, which renders them more vulnerable to food insecurity and inhibits their active participation in local markets (CAFOD, Setting the post-2015 development compass, 2013).

This project aims to increase the productivity and resilience of agricultural systems; consolidate engagement in markets and diversify income generation; strengthen adaptation to climate change; and increase the ability of local, small scale food producers to access services and influence development practices.

The proposed project fits with the CAFOD East Africa Regional Strategy in that it is an integrated project. In the current strategy integration is the main focus. Additionally, the project focuses on food security that include accessibility, availability, stability and affordability while integrating key components on disaster risk reduction, climate change adaptation and governance which are core components of the East Africa strategy.  
Poor Women, men and children living in remote and hazard-prone rural areas in Kitui, Marsabit and Maralal - Kenya rely on smallholder agriculture to provide their main source of food or income. Despite macro-economic growth in Kenya communities are unable to maintain a basic standard of living. Poverty is widespread (MDG1), many face food insecurity, and livelihoods are highly dependent on climatic conditions. The most recent research has found that there is high probability that climate change will exacerbate the vulnerability of agricultural systems particularly in regions of Africa, (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, 2014 5th Report,  in Kenya, prolonged periods of drought are common (National Climate Change Response Strategy, 2010). 
CAFOD has significant experience of working in Kitui, Marsabit and Maralal in these areas there exist clear constrains that hinder people from realising a sustainable livelihood exemplifying the need for the proposed action. title: Research and advocacy project - Promoting pro-poor, climate compatible energy for poverty reduction
description:
The overall aim of this project is to promote informed, inclusive and integrated local and national discussion of the economic, environmental and social cost-benefit analysis of different energy pathways for sustainable economic development and poverty reduction in Kenya. In particular, the aim is to frame this discussion from an “energy for national development” rather than – or rather than solely – a “climate protection” perspective in order to get greater political traction.

The project comes at a critical time for influencing the implementation and financing of Kenya’s national energy and climate change policies . Kenya’s 2030 economic vision is for a 10% increase in GDP from 2012 onwards with energy as one of the key sectors for reform. In terms of its development needs, the Kenyan population is growing at a high rate, which has led to increase in demand for resources such as energy, food, and infrastructure – in the case of energy access, population growth is outstripping electrification. 67% of Kenyan citizens live in rural areas. Up to 90% of people living in these areas lack access to electricity, and rely on crude and unsustainable forms of energy supply such as traditional bio-mass.
This project also reflects a crucial moment for local development in Kitui County, where CAFOD’s strategic partner Caritas Kitui works. Planned open-cast, lignite coal extraction in the Mui Basin, Kitui County starting in 2016 could have potentially devastating economic, social, and environmental impacts on local communities, including on their food and water security and their land rights. Again, there is a huge information and analysis gap among local communities, and other stakeholders, including County and National government, and Catholic Bishops on the implications of the coal investments for sustainable economic development and poverty reduction in Kitui. It is vital that a baseline study be carried out before any coal investment-related activities begin.

title: ISIOLO INTEGRATED FOOD SECURITY PROJECT PHASE II
description:
This project will directly target 240 pastoral and agro-pastoral households with a total population 1200 individuals (480 males and 720 females) in Isiolo County. The beneficiaries comprise rural pastoralists and agro-pastoralists drawn from 4 locations namely Kinna, Merti, Oldonyiro and Leparua. These areas are targeted primarily because of its high vulnerability to socio-economic crises manifested by livelihood and food insecurity, environmental degradation and malnutrition. In the past, it has noted that beneficiaries of such interventions end up sharing the inputs with other under privileged families with the context of the traditional social support mechanism, thereby increasing the number of direct and indirect beneficiaries. In this arrangement, this project is anticipated to reach up to 1,800 people. The target group includes highly vulnerable members including the disabled, elderly people, women headed households and people living with HIV/AIDS. The beneficiaries will be selected through an inclusive community-based targeting approach using vulnerability criteria. The following will be considered during the identification of the beneficiaries:
•	Access to social support networks- Priority will be given to households with no external social support.
•	Female headed households
•	Number of members in a household
•	Households caring for a disabled person
•	Households supporting elderly and/or infirm persons
•	Young orphan-headed households caring for siblings
•	Vulnerability to climate change 

The targeting was arrived through needs assessment carried out involving community opinion leaders, government officers, religious leaders, nongovernmental organizations and community members. A needs assessment was carried out and it informed on the different needs for men women boys and girls on the following; conflict, livelihoods, health and nutrition, water, disaster risk reduction and governance status in the County. After analysis, the needs lying in the people of Isiolo County were prioritized as: food security, health and nutrition, environment conservation and water. 
Based on the analysis done, the project will focus its resources at women, children and youth.  The rationale behind this is that women are the ones who are affected most and are vulnerable to shocks. Further, there will be an emphasis to identify female and child headed households, being groups in society that are often unattended to by communities. The youth have been targeted to support in establishment of livelihoods for future generations who have not been fully engaged in economic activities such as farming and trade in the region.  The youth are also intended to provide linkages to markets due to their agile nature.

title: Integrated Food Security project Phase 2
description:
Farmers in Kitui County rely on small scale agriculture for food and income. Despite macro-economic growth within the Country, communities are unable to maintain a basic standard of living and many households face food insecurity. Majority of population relies on rain-fed agriculture which is highly vulnerable to the effects of climate change resulting to low crop and livestock production. There is limited access to farm inputs, inadequate capacities on appropriate dry land farming and inadequate market system development. The combined effects of climate change and rapid population growth are increasing food insecurity, environmental degradation, and poverty levels in the county. Already scarce resources such as arable farmland must be subdivided among more people, resulting in over-exploitation and low productivity. The population below the Poverty Line in Kitui County is at 60% which is way below the national rate of 45% with Human Development and Gender Inequality index at 0.45% compared to the national index of 0.49%.
This project aims to build farmers capacity on good agricultural practices and market access for collective marketing.

description:

This project will contribute to Kenya Uganda Resilience programme; 
Outcome 3: Degraded landscapes are restored and provide a stream of ecosystems services;
 Outcome 4: Women and youth influence change through voice, action, and civil society engagement and

title: NIHR CLEAN-Air(Africa) Unit “Clean modern energy for all”. Benefitting health, society, environment and climate in sub-Saharan Africa to achieve the 2030 Sustainable Development Goals.
description: Globally 3.8 billion people rely on polluting fuels (e.g. wood, charcoal, kerosene) for cooking. Household air pollution (HAP) from burning these fuels caused 2.3 million premature deaths in 2019 (more than HIV/AIDS, malaria and tuberculosis). With 695,000 premature deaths and 38 million Disability-Adjusted-Life-Years (DALYs) in 2019, Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) bears a disproportionate fraction (30%) of the global HAP-related disease burden. The NIHR CLEAN-Air(Africa) Unit will accelerate the understanding of HAP-related disease burden through a unique set of studies that will (i) strengthen national health systems for community health prevention of HAP-related disease and (ii) provide evidence-based recommendations for population transition to clean household and institutional energy. The Unit will leverage the expertise of community health workers (CHWs), an overlooked frontline health promotion workforce, via implementation of a national Ministry of Health (MoH) led training of CHWs in HAP, health and prevention. This will include (i) development of curricula/ job aids in Cameroon, Rwanda and Uganda, (ii) creation of a digital platform for CHW training and health surveillance to maximise reach of training and (iii) effective rollout of training in Kenya to 140,000 CHWs. To inform national strategies to achieve UN Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7 (ensuring universal access to clean, modern household energy by 2030) and address the associated negative health, gender, and climate impacts of reliance on polluting cooking fuels, the Unit will collaborate with several international organisations (e.g. WHO, World Food Programme) to investigate innovations that have potential for rapid scale in SSA. We will run 5 randomised controlled trials to test technological (pay-as-you-cook LPG smart meters and pressure cookers), nutritional (pre-cooked, vitamin enhanced beans) and behavioural (cooking classes) innovations for addressing barriers to adoption and exclusive use of clean cooking fuel for households (n=620) and schools (3,600 pupils) in East Africa. A focus on institutional cooking in schools is particularly novel, with a high degree of HAP exposure to school cooks and pupils offering high value for money in terms of population-level reductions in polluting fuel use. An in-depth mixed-methods evaluation (n=400) will be conducted of a successful social entrepreneur company in Kenya providing LPG access to rural women (20,000 current users) to understand their ability to facilitate microfinance for clean cooking. Through Africa's first Air Pollution Centre of Excellence at KEMRI, we will use state-of-the-art air monitoring equipment to elucidate relationships between exposure to HAP and respiratory disease (spirometry study; n=500) and cardiovascular health (heart rate variability study using wearable technology; n=100) in Cameroon. The Unit will also quantify hidden burdens related to gender inequity (time poverty from fetching firewood) and burns/ scalds (establishment of clinical/ primary care surveillance). Research activities will begin by Year 2 after Unit launch and start of the capacity building program in Year 1. The Unit's academic trainee programme will run from Years 1-4. Our dissemination foci on (i) population awareness raising and (ii) rapid knowledge translation of research evidence to policy will be enabled through close engagement with ministerial stakeholders steering national energy strategy.

title: Joint programme Support to low carbon climate resilient development for poverty reduction in Kenya
description: The Government of Kenya recognizes the importance of climate change (CC) impacts on Kenya’s development and risks towards achieving Vision 2030 as highlighted in the National Climate Change Response Strategy 2010. It is a cross-cutting issue that affects all sectors and segments of Kenya’s urban and rural populations. The National Climate Change Action Plan 2013-2017 (NCCAP) stipulates the need to mainstream CC adaptation and mitigation measures in national and county planning and budgeting processes and in all sectors of the economy as a means to further Kenya’s people-centered development strategy. The NCCAP background briefings and studies clearly identify the needs of Government, private sector and the CSOs to successfully implement the NCCAP and result in meaningful change towards a low carbon, resilient development pathway for the benefit of Kenyans. This consolidated UN Proposal will contribute to this end. The UN programme consists of six outputs which will contribute towards achieving the intended outcome and objectives. The primary beneficiaries of the project will be members of the Kenya population; particularly those who are most strongly impacted by increasing climate variability as a result of long-term climate change.

title: Youth Employment for Sustainable Development
description: The project intended to empower selected young women and men to participate in addressing the teething socio-economic challenges in their communities through providing them with marketable skills, decent jobs and business opportunities. The Project will link broader employment, economic and social policies to targeted interventions aimed at overcoming the specific disadvantages faced by young people in entering and remaining in the labour market. It is based on the ILO’s Global Employment Agenda (GEA) that lays out a comprehensive framework to address youth employment through an integrated and inclusive approach. By including the ILO Green Jobs Initiative approach as part of the Decent Work Country Programmes (DWCP), the Project will also help to fill the knowledge gaps and contribute to policy formulation aiming at minimizing the costs and manage the effects of future climate change. The Project will address both labour demand and supply, creating employment opportunities for youth as well as strengthening their employability by providing them technical and business skills training as well as advice on establishing and sustaining business. The demand-side will be addressed through linkages with broader Government strategies for employment such as Kazi kwa vijana (KKV) and Roads 2000 Programme. The key requirements for a successful implementation of such project include strong commitment from policy makers, efficient project management and supervisory capacity, vibrant private sector participation and strong community ownership. It also calls for building adequate training capability that caters for personnel at all levels of authority. There is further a need to mainstream crosscutting social and environmental issues in the regular programmes of roads agencies in order to conform to international and national laws, norms and good practices (particularly with respect to upholding human rights, gender equality, fair working conditions, HIV & AIDS prevention and protection, child right and environmental protection). The project will therefore assist local partners to build planning and implementation capacity infrastructure development programmes as well as strengthening training institutions in the Ministry of Roads thereby creating a vibrant employment intensive programme that is responsive to the social-economic needs of the country. The proposed project will run for twelve months from January 2012. Following on the foregoing, the proposed project will have the following four areas of focus: i) Development of youth owned SMEs ii) Strengthening training capacity of KTC through mainstreaming models for cobblestone and Do-nou technologies iii) Capacity building for implementing agencies iv) Strengthening programme/project Monitoring and evaluation These will be informed by ILO experiences in the country and elsewhere as well as interventions that have worked, such as the use of ILO entrepreneurship training packages and other tools related to EIIP. These interventions are in line with the Kenya’s Decent Work Country Programme priorities particularly employment creation, youth development, and expansion of social protection. The desired long term impact of the project is also framed along ILO/AU/IGAD Employment for Peace, Stability and Development Strategy, which calls for a holistic approach to employment as key to poverty alleviation.

title:
Enhancing Partnerships for Industry-led Vocational Training
and education in Water for Agriculture (ePIVOT - Water)
description:
OKP-ICP-KEN-104675 | The proposed project must contribute to the following ++long-term impacts++:

1. Promote agricultural growth;
2. Create ecologically sustainable food systems;
3. Water efficiency in agriculture increased (i.e. water-smart agriculture); and
4. Water is used sustainably and equitably, ensuring the needs of all sectors and the environment.

 Summary of the project proposal . Horticulture is the fastest growing sub-sector in Kenya. It is expected to contribute the most towards the envisioned poverty reduction, and overall food security. Irregular rainfall patterns causing persistent droughts and excessive rainfall floods are creating difficult challenges for the agricultural sector. Solutions to tackle these challenges are often not incorporated in the agricultural and horticulture curricula, creating a lack in capacity on water- and climate smart horticulture. This project aims to improve the horticulture sector by improving the curriculum on water- and climate smart practices, increasing teachers’ capacity, creating more access to practical training facilities and strengthening knowledge and communication links between educational institutions and the public and private sector. It will also align the labour market demand with the educational offerings, increasing the output of skilled students. This project aims to close the knowledge and skill gaps in relation to water- and climate smart horticulture, strengthening the capacity of the TVCs through a strong collaboration between the education institutions and the private sector, strengthening linkages among the various actors enable practical learning and innovation through linking the horticulture and water sector.

title: Clean Water & Sanitation for Kenyan Primary School
description: In 2011, the Horn of Africa experienced one of the most severe droughts in over 60 years. KRA works with communities throughout Kenya to provide technologies that will increase their resiliency to the effects of climate change and drought. Matuiku Primary School has no running water and substandard sanitation facilities. By providing a rainwater storage tank, farm pond with drip irrigation, improved latrines, and capacity building this project will improve the health and education of 137 pupils.

title: F.a: Empowering Partners to Respond to Environmental and Climate Change
description:
The purpose of the Project is to increase the capacity of the partner on environmental conservation and food security so as to improve the livelihood of ten Communities in Kenya. The Project seeks to address the destabilized livelihoods of the communities 
due to environmental and climatic change as a result of harmful human action. The Full Gospel Churches of Kenya is the Fida Partner in Kenya. The Church has a membership of 1.2 Million members and is administratively organized in 12 regions and 83 district
s in throughout the Country. The target communities live in the most difficult places in arid and semi-arid lands which have harsh climatic conditions caused by increased global warming. Deforestation through human activities has also contributed to the re
duction of forest cover in Kenya in a great way. The Communities in these areas have encountered great challenges in their lives due inadequate food and water. The project will focus in the areas of food security, environment protection through alternative
 livelihood strategies and formation of Children Clubs for their participation purposes. The will sensitizing the communities on their rights to the basic needs and encourage them to increases environmental conservation. The communities will be empowered b
y providing them with adequate knowledge on how to respond to the impacts of climate change and increased food production. The communities will be trained on modern skills for establishment of tree nurseries and water harvesting which allows a network of p
artners to be engaged. The project intends to continue intensifying interventions in the former pilot areas and add 4 new areas. The empowerment process will include establishment of tree/fruit nurseries, environmental management training, Farming in God's
 Way, soil erosion control, poultry keeping, bee keeping, improving livestock breeding and production of energy saving Jikos to reduce deforestation. Through the partner, the well-being of the communities in arid and semi-arid areas of Kenya will have impr
oved in the way of increased food security and forest cover. Members of the community will continually access enough and nutritious food adequate for their lives and realize healthy living. Farmers have practiced agro-forestry which has increased forest co
ver as they grow their food.

title: Establishing Climate Resilient Water Supply System and Strengthening Water Security in Turkana West, Kenya
description: The Core Issue: Establishing a Climate-Resilient Water Supply for Local Communities In the Turkana region, the decline of groundwater, a crucial water source, is attributed to climate change. This decrease in water availability poses a significant threat to the health and livelihood of the residents, who are unable to meet even the minimum humanitarian standard of 15L of water per day due to extreme scarcity. Core Objective: Building Climate-Resilient Water Supply and Enhancing Water Security The primary goal is to create a climate-resilient water supply environment for local communities in Turkana, promoting water security. Key measures include increasing underground water storage and recharge, improving access to safe drinking water, and empowering local residents and governments to ensure sustainable water use for future generations. | Building climate resilient water supply system and strengthening water security in Turkana West Kenya수자원(지하수) 회복력 강화, 연중 내내 이용 가능한 식수시설 확보, 기후변화를 고려한 지역사회 수자원관리 역량 강화

title: Africa Biogas Partnership Program
description:
Aim
To develop and support a sustainable market sector for household biogas digesters in the target countries.

Where
Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda

Why
Worldwide, more than two and a half billion people lack clean and safe cooking fuel. They rely on traditional sources such as wood, agricultural residues, dried manure and charcoal. The indoor pollution from these fuels kills nearly two million people a year and makes many more sick. Unsustainable collection of these traditional fuels is further exhausting natural resources, damaging the environment and contributing to climate change.

How
Biogas digesters have many benefits and fit nicely into farming systems that include livestock. ABPP's main strategies are to develop the supply and demand side of the market, provide supporting services such as training and credit provision, and create a supporting institutional environment for the use and promotion of biogas.

Results so far
The results of Phase 2 so far include the installation of 60,000 biogas digesters, more than 300,000 ha of land organically fertilized (with 20-30 per cent crop production increase), the creation of 90 biogas construction enterprises and 4,200 jobs, as well as the involvement of 45 credit providers who give loans to customers who want to buy a biogas digester. On average, 38,000 women save 2.5 hours daily by no longer collecting firewood or scrubbing soot from pots.

Period and budget
2014-2019 (Phase 2), €88 million (including €60 million household contribution and €3 million carbon revenues)

Partners
Netherlands Ministry of Foreign Affairs (donor), Energising Development, 5 national implementing partners and their country's governments

title: e Right coffee: Development of sustainable, inclusive and  innovative coffee value chain
description: The initiative takes place within SDG 2 and aims at promoting a sustainable model for agriculture in the coffee  value chain in Kenya. The project objective is to increase the average income of 9460 male producers and 2720  female producers and of 4 cooperatives involved in the wet processing of the coffee. Production of coffee has always been a sector of great importance in Kenya and in 2017 was at the fifth place  among the agricultural products exported with 190 million dollars, equal to 6,5% of the total value of exports in  the Country. The value chain faces different challenges related to complex and interconnected factors. These challenges,  together with inadequate policies, brought to a significant reduction in the quantity and quality of the coffee  produced, as well as to excessive costs for the farmers which negatively impact their income. The main  challenges identified are: 1) inadequate skills of the producers; 2) presence of an aggressive disease called  Coffee Berry Disease (CBD) caused by a pathogenic fungus; 3) use of obsolete techniques and equipment; 4) lack  of a traceability system of the produce within the value chain; 5) limited access to the market; 6) exclusion of  youth and women in the production and 7) absence of a formal Kenyan coffee brand. From 2000, there has  been a rapid and progressive decrease that, in the last years, brought the production at 45000 tons a year  against the 120-130000 tons reached in the 90s. The partners CELIM, IPSIA, Caritas Nairobi, Dedan Kimathi University of Tecnhnology, Kenya Coffee Platform and  Association of Women in Coffee Industry combined their expertise to develop a project strategy that promotes  a sustainable, inclusive and innovative supply chain model to address the challenges mentioned above. Particularly, the project proposes an holistic intervention on three different levels: R.1: the coffee local producers increase the efficiency, sustainability and quality of the production by enhancing  their technical skills on the cultivation of the plants and soil fertility (A.1.1); by adopting climate smart  production methods to control diseases (pest management), to increase productivity and to enhance the quality  of coffee plants (A.1.2) and by developing eco-friendly practices in order to improve the quality of coffee  berries, such as beekeeping (A.1.3). R.2: local cooperatives, involved in the wet processing, introduce good practices of governance and reduce their  environmental impact by adopting modern and environmentally friendly techniques (A.2.1); by strengthening  the management skills of the board of directors (A.2.2) and by introducing good practices for the traceability of  the product (A.2.3). R.3: The cooperatives improve their ability to take advantage of the opportunities offered by the local market  through the promotion of local consumption and the diversification of the products of the value chain, by  creating new products from the organic waste of the wet process (A.3.1), through the capacity building of youth  and women in the sectors of selection and transformation of the coffee (A.3.2), through the start-up of small  roasting centres at cooperative level (A.3.3) and through the creation of local coffee brands for the  enhancement of cupping profile (A.3.4) The methodology proposed by the project “Right coffee: development of a sustainable, inclusive and  innovative coffee value chain” will have a mid and long-term impact by increasing producers’ income by 51%  and cooperatives’ income by 20%, and by contributing to increase the land dedicated to sustainable agriculture  in Embu and Kiambu by 35% | L’iniziativa si colloca all’interno dell’SDG 2 e mira a promuovere un modello di agricoltura sostenibile per la  filiera del caffè in Kenya. L’obiettivo del progetto è quello di incrementare il reddito di 9.460 produttori e 2.720  produttrici e di 4 cooperative coinvolte nel processo di trasformazione a umido del prodotto. La produzione di caffè è infatti da sempre un settore agricolo di grande importanza per il Kenya e occupa (al  2017) il quinto posto in valore fra i prodotti agricoli esportati, con circa 190 milioni di dollari pari al 6,5% del  valore totale delle esportazioni agricole. La filiera affronta però diverse sfide legate a complessi e interconnessi  fattori lungo l’intera catena del valore che, uniti all’attuazione di politiche e forme di regolamentazione non  idonee, hanno portato a una drastica riduzione della quantità e qualità di caffè prodotto, e a oneri eccessivi per i  produttori con conseguente impatto negativo sul reddito. Le principali problematiche individuate sono: 1) scarsa  formazione dei produttori; 2) aggressività della cosiddetta “Coffee Berry Disease” (CBD) dovuta a un fungo  patogeno; 3) utilizzo di tecniche e macchinari obsoleti; ) assenza di un sistema di tracciabilità del prodotto lungo  la filiera 4) limitato accesso al mercato locale 5) l’esclusione di giovani e donne dalla filiera produttiva e 6 )  assenza di una caratterizzazione formale del caffè keniota. A partire dai primi anni 2000 si è verificato quindi un  rapido e progressivo decremento che, negli ultimi anni, ha visto la produzione stabilizzarsi intorno alle 45.000  tonnellate annue contro le 120 - 130.000 raggiunte negli anni Novanta. I partner di progetto CELIM, IPSIA, Caritas Nairobi, Dedan Kimathi University of Tecnhnology, la Kenya Coffee  Platform e la Association of Women in Coffee Industry hanno unito le proprie competenze per elaborare una  strategia progettuale che promuova uno modello di filiera sostenibile, inclusivo e innovativo in risposta alle sfide  evidenziate. Nello specifico il progetto i propone di intervenire sinergicamente su tre differenti livelli: R.1: I produttori e le produttrici locali di caffè migliorano l’efficienza, la sostenibilità e la qualità della  produzione migliorando le proprie conoscenze sulle tecniche di coltivazione delle piante, trattamento e resa dei  suoli (A1.1); adottando di tecniche per una produzione “climate smart” per il controllo delle malattie,  l’aumento della produttività e il miglioramento della qualità delle piante di caffè (A.1.2) e sviluppando pratiche  eco- friendly per il miglioramento della qualità del chicco di caffè, come l’apicoltura (A.1.3). R.2: Le cooperative locali , operanti nei processi di prima trasformazione del caffè, introducono buone pratiche  di governance e riducono il proprio impatto ambientale adottando tecniche di lavorazione moderne ed  ecocompatibili (A.2.1); rinforzando le capacità manageriali dei direttivi delle cooperative (A.2.2) e introducendo  buone pratiche di tracciabilità del prodotto (A.2.3) R.3: Le cooperative migliorano la propria capacità di sfruttare le opportunità offerte dal mercato locale,  incentivando il consumo locale di caffè e diversificando i prodotti della filiera, creando nuovi prodotti derivanti  dalla scarto organico delle lavorazione a umido (A.3.1), migliorando la competenze di giovani e donne nella  selezione e trasformazione del caffè (A.3.2) avviando piccole torrefazioni locali a livello di cooperative (A.3.3) e  creando brand di caffè locale per la valorizzazione del profilo di tazza (A.3.4) La metodologia proposta dal progetto “Caffè Corretto: sviluppo di una filiera del caffè sostenibile, inclusiva e  innovativa” avrà un impatto sul medio e lungo termine aumentando del 51% il reddito dei produttori e delle  produttrici , del 20% le entrate delle cooperative, contribuendo ad aumentare del 35% la quota di terre  destinate a un’agricoltura sostenibile nelle contee di Kiambu ed Embu.

title: Contribution to the strengthening of the devolution process in Kenya - Capacity development for better management and mobilization of own resources.
description: The Joint Programme “Consolidating gains and deepening devolution in Kenya” will be implemented by UNDP, UNICEF and UN Women, focusing on the 17 poorest counties of Kenya. The Italian Cooperation will contribute to the basket fund supporting the Programme with an instalment of 400.000 Euro. The Programme’s goals are embedded in the UNDAF which was signed with the Government of Kenya in June 2018. In particular it will contribute to the achievement of the Outcomes related to improved service delivery, social protection and resilience to climate change, with a particular focus on gender equality and vulnerable children. The approach is based on strengthening the capacity of local governments to better manage and mobilize resources (through PFM) and thus improve service delivery. Furthermore, technical assistance from Italian experts will be provided, in order to deepen bilateral cooperation on the issues of DRM and fiscal decentralization. | Il programma si pone come scopo di raggiungere i seguenti 3 obiettivi, indicati dall'UNDAF 2018-2022 (quadro di riferimento per la cooperazione tra le Nazioni Unite e il Governo del Kenya)

title: Farming the future. Sustainable value chains in agriculture for ASAL (arid and semi-arid lands) in Kenya.
description: Through an holistic approach originating from Permaculture Principles, the project aims at increasing agricultural production and profitability of business activities for 11 target groups (770 direct beneficiaries), improving in this way the economic conditions of the agro-pastoral groups of Laikipia North, and encouraging the resilience of the communities in the arid and semi-arid areas of Laikipia County.The main actions concern the training and supply of equipment for agriculture, access to water for four communities, support to supply chains suitable for dry climates (honey, aloe, opuntia) and strengthening the tourism sector. All actions are anchored on environmentally friendly methods and principles to have a positive impact in mitigating desertification and encourage the protection of local natural resources. The transformation of opuntia stricta, in particular, is a suitable methodology to contain the propagation of this intrusive plant species, which diffusion in the area represents a threat to the community, causing injuries to people, as well to both domestic and wild animals. Due to ulcerations caused by the spines when animals feed on it, Opuntia stricta cause the death of Maasai population's livestock which is the main economic activity hence, raising the poverty levels of the already poor indigenous communities in Laikipia. | Attraverso un approccio olistico derivante dai principi della permacultura, il progetto mira a incrementare la produzione agricola e la redditività delle iniziative imprenditoriali di 11 gruppi target (770 beneficiari diretti), migliorando quindi le condizioni economiche dei gruppi agropastorali di Laikipia North, e favorendo in tal modo la resilienza delle comunità nelle zone aride e semiaride della contea di Laikipia. Le azioni principali riguardano la formazione e dotazione di equipaggiamenti per l'agricoltura, l'accesso idrico per quattro villaggi, il supporto a filiere di trasformazione adatte ai climi aridi (miele, aloe, opuntia), il potenziamento del settore turistico. Tutte le azioni privilegiano metodologie ecocompatibili e hanno una ricaduta positiva nella lotta alla desertificazione e nella tutela delle risorse del territorio. La trasformazione dell'opuntia stricta, in particolare, risulta una metodologia adatta al contenimento della proliferazione di tale specie infestante, la cui diffusione nell'area costituisce una minaccia per le mandrie delle popolazioni pastorali masai.
