description: Contract related to: Planned contract - direct award elections  - This Action is funded by the Civil Society Organisations (CSO) Thematic Programme 2021-2027, under the Multiannual Action Plan 2025-2027. The Action intents to contribute to Specific-Objective 1.3: Support CSOs as actors of good governance and development in partner countries and to the achievement of the related result 1.3: CSO ability to engage as actors of good governance and development at country level is improved.The Action rolls out the EU support to country-level CSO initiatives aimed at implementing priorities reflected in the NDICI-Global Europe, Annex III CSO Thematic Programme and the subsequent Multiannual Indicative Programme (MIP) for the same. In line with the policy of geographisation, a majority of funds under the CSO MAAP 2025-2027, amounting to around ¿ 428.2 million, are allocated under the Action to support civil society in partner countries in Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia and the Pacific, Americas and the Caribbean, and in Neighbourhood countries and Russia . As a result, for the whole 2021-27 period, the country allocations will represent 90 % of Priority I (excluding DEAR and Support Measures).Activities funded under the Action will support a broad range of civil society actors including and prioritising, but not limited to, women and youth organisations. In the framework of the Country Roadmaps for EU and Member States engagement with civil society (so called, Civil Society Roadmaps), all initiatives under the Action will aim at contributing to strengthening civil society partner¿s institutional and operational capacity through a comprehensive approach;  enabling and ensuring their participation; and on improving the environment in which they operate. Particular attention will be paid to CSOs¿ capacities to benefit from the digital transformation.This Action is aligned with the 2012 Communication on "The roots of democracy and sustainable development: Europe's engagement with Civil Society in external relations" as well as the DAC Recommendation on Enabling Civil Society in Development Co-operation and Humanitarian Assistance.  It will contribute to all EU priority areas, such as Good Governance, gender equality, climate, environment and energy or sustainable jobs and growth. The main sector for funding initiatives will accordingly be Government & Civil Society. It will also contribute to meeting EU¿s commitment to preserve and broaden an enabling space for an active, organised, transparent and strengthened civil society, in accordance with the Samoa Agreement with African, Caribbean and Pacific States.Support to, and dialogue with, CSOs should also take place in the context of the 360° approach of the Global Gateway¿s Strategy , where green and clean investment in hard infrastructure goes together, among others, with compliance with social, environmental and governance standards, in order to ensure that the initiatives reach local communities, mitigate risks and strengthen sustainability.  The Action will strongly complement and reinforce country and regional programmes, particularly Global Gateway flagships, through support for CSOs working in EU priority areas, and through its focus on improving the environment in which CSOs operate. This will enable them to participate in an informed way in dialogue with the EU and national and local actors, representing and voicing the concerns of people, including those in vulnerable and marginalized situations, and contribute to combating inequalities and boost inclusivity in our partner countries. The Action will furthermore strengthen CSOs ability to implement and analyse initiatives funded under the country and regional programmes thereby contributing to their successful implementation.

title: FARM: Strengthening investment for adoption of alternatives and sustainable management of agrochemicals and agriplastics in Africa and Latin America through pilots in Kenya and Uruguay
description: Reduce the use and prevalence of harmful agrochemicals by supporting farmers to access finance, innovative practices, and markets required to incentivize sustainable practices. | Note: Disbursement data provided is cumulative and covers disbursement made by the project Agency. | As outlined in the global environmental problem section, pesticide and plastic emissions and residues have a negative impact on soil quality, populations of natural predators etc.  This has an impact on seed germination, plant growth and animal health. These negative consequences of pesticides and plastics reduce the productivity and resilience of the farming system to existing pests and the growing impact of climate change. A robust ecosystem is more resilient to climate change due to higher levels of biodiversity.[1] Farmers are already increasing the number of times they spray per cropping cycle and the concentration of active ingredient applied because of growing resistance in the pests and the loss of natural predators.  Replacing HHPs with less toxic and more selective pesticides and non-chemical options will allow natural predators to thrive which combined with other integrated pest management practices will reduce the impact of pests on yields. Reducing micro and macro plastic pollution that could contaminate soils before it becomes a problem will allow farmers in Uruguay and Kenya to avoid the problems of reduced germination and plant growth that are starting to be seen in Asia.     The project environmental results will also directly benefit health. Reducing the exposure of farmers and their families to HHPs will reduce the incidence of accidental poisoning and the subsequent loss of labor and the cost of treatment for farming families. Reducing residues of HHPs on food produce will reduce the incidence of accidental poisoning amongst consumers, whilst there is no statistic on this problem available in Uruguay or Kenya this is due to lack of data on this issue, as academic studies in both countries have found pesticide residues that exceed accepted residue levels. HHPs have been associated with suicides in rural communities in Asia and banning HHPs has been correlated to reductions in the number of suicides (see baseline).  Whilst research in this issue has not been carried out in Kenya and Uruguay, there is a probability that HHPs contribute to the number of suicides in these countries.     Finally, alternative pest and crop management approaches can bring economic benefits for farmers. Pesticides and agricultural plastics are expensive inputs for farmers, and the disposal of hazardous waste is another expense that needs to be borne either by manufacturers, importers, or farmers.  At the farm level, reducing the number of pesticides and plastics used is potentially a way to improve margins on crops, providing yields can be maintained, whilst removing the possibility of accidental poisoning reduced the associated health care costs. At the national level, reducing the use of HHPs reduced the risk of accidental poisoning for both farmers and consumers and the cost imposed on the public health system. Elimination of HHPs also eliminates the risk that export crops are rejected by importing countries that have strict phytosanitary requirements and robust testing regimes. title: Scaling-up pathways of last mile climate information services for community resilience in Uganda and Kenya
description:
Crop yields in Africa have fallen over the years, leading to a decline in per capita food production. There is a global consensus that unless urgent action is taken, this situation will be aggravated by climate variability and change. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, Africa should adapt to climate change because adaptation will guarantee benefits now and in future. However, adaptation is information-intensive, and farmers in Africa lack access to climate information in user-friendly formats and within an acceptable lead time to enable them to make informed decisions to minimize losses and maximize the opportunities presented by climate variability and change.

A climate information generation and dissemination tool that was developed and piloted by an IDRC-funded project in Uganda can help bridge this gap. The tool leverages the use of mobile phones and traditional technologies such as community loudspeakers and FM radio transmissions. It has enabled more than 200,000 farmers (49% women), to reduce crop losses and damage by 50-65%. The challenge now is to scale up the model to the rest of Uganda and across Africa.
This project, implemented in Uganda and Kenya, aims to support the scale up of the model. Like other parts of the continent, these two countries have low crop yields. Particularly in Kenya, cereal yields rarely exceed 1.5 tons per hectare, less than half of those realized in other parts of the world. Thus, approximately 30% of Kenya’s population is chronically hungry and more than 40% live in abject poverty. Similarly, Uganda has a cereal yield of only 2 tons per hectare. 

It is anticipated that the project will enhance agricultural productivity and incomes when climate information is used and adaptive actions taken by farming households. It will produce skilled manpower expected to implement, manage, and sustain the scaled-up climate information services. Furthermore, the project will produce a rich body of knowledge and propose the policy framework and institutional arrangements required to realize impact at scale, which can inform similar scaling initiatives in the region and beyond. With the knowledge generated, the project has the potential to inform climate policy review in Kenya and climate legislation being drafted in Uganda. | Le rendement des cultures en Afrique a chuté au fil des ans, entraînant une baisse de la production alimentaire par habitant. Partout dans le monde, on s’accorde à penser que si aucune mesure d’urgence n’est prise, cette situation s’aggravera en raison de la variabilité et du changement du climat. Selon le Groupe d’experts intergouvernemental sur l’évolution du climat, l’Afrique devrait s’adapter aux changements climatiques parce que cela aura des répercussions positives à court et long termes. Cependant, le processus d’adaptation dépend fortement de la circulation de l’information, et les exploitants agricoles en Afrique ont difficilement accès à des renseignements sur le climat qui leur permettraient de prendre des décisions éclairées pour réduire au minimum les pertes et tirer le meilleur profit des possibilités offertes par le changement et la variabilité du climat.

Pour remédier à cette situation, on pourrait s’appuyer sur l’outil de production et de diffusion des renseignements climatiques mis au point dans le cadre d’un projet financé par le CRDI en Ouganda. Cet outil tire parti de l’utilisation des téléphones mobiles et des technologies traditionnelles, telles que les haut-parleurs communautaires et la radio FM. Cela a permis à plus de 200 000 fermiers (49 % de femmes) de réduire de 50 à 65 % les dommages et les pertes de récolte. Le défi qui se pose à présent consiste à étendre le modèle au reste de l’Ouganda et partout en Afrique.

Ce projet, mis en place en Ouganda et au Kenya, a pour objectif de soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle du modèle. Comme dans le reste du continent, ces deux pays ont vu leurs rendements agricoles baisser. 

Le projet devrait améliorer la productivité et les revenus agricoles, une fois que les renseignements sur le climat seront utilisés et que des mesures d’adaptation seront prises par les ménages vivant de l’agriculture. Cela permettra de disposer de travailleurs qualifiés capables de mettre en place, de gérer et de soutenir des services d’information sur le climat à grande échelle. Avec les connaissances qu’il générera, le projet pourrait servir de base à l’examen des politiques liées au climat au Kenya et à la préparation d’une législation sur le climat en Ouganda.

title: Blended finance, impact businesses and investing with a gender lens: Fostering collaboration and developing a forward-looking agenda
description:
Blended finance (using official development assistance to leverage private capital for sustainable development) is gaining traction as part of an innovative finance mechanism for achieving the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Although momentum is building, movement towards a new financing model is slow in developing countries, and the effects and possibilities are not well understood.  

Canada recently launched a series of innovative finance initiatives. In January 2018, the Development Finance Institute Canada (FinDev) started operations to deliver innovative financial solutions to inclusive businesses with the potential to create jobs, empower women, and mitigate climate change. In August 2019, Canada launched the International Assistance Innovation Program, which aims to promote sustainable development impacts through its investments. Both finance mechanisms put gender at their core. The recently launched Canada’s Equality Fund includes a gender lens impact investing strategy to leverage finance as a tool to scale and transform systems for gender equality.

IDRC is supporting action-research to strengthen the ecosystem for purpose-driven business and impact investing with a gender lens, including through the development or refinement of impact management and measurement tools. This work brings researchers and business networks together to generate robust evidence on the impact of business and investment to meet the SDGs. This project will undertake four main activities to explore how IDRC can collaborate with Canada’s efforts on gender lens innovative finance. These activities include commissioning a scoping paper to map research gaps; facilitating a workshop that brings relevant IDRC-funded projects together with Canadian institutions working on innovative finance; supporting outreach and engagement through three high-level events that showcase Canadian approaches to innovative finance with a gender lens; and developing a joint action plan to inform a programming strategy for IDRC. | Le financement mixte (c’est-à-dire l’utilisation de l’aide publique au développement pour mobiliser des capitaux privés pour le développement durable) gagne des adeptes dans le cadre d’un mécanisme financier innovant visant à atteindre les objectifs de développement durable des Nations Unies. Bien qu’une dynamique soit en train de se dégager, l’évolution vers un nouveau modèle de financement est lente dans les pays en développement, et les effets et les possibilités ne sont pas bien compris. 

Le Canada a récemment lancé une série d’initiatives financières innovantes. En janvier 2018, l’Institut de financement du développement Canada (FinDev) a commencé à proposer des solutions financières innovantes aux entreprises inclusives ayant le potentiel de créer des emplois, de contribuer à l’autonomisation des femmes et d’atténuer les changements climatiques. En août 2019, le Canada a lancé le Programme d’innovation en aide internationale, qui consiste à stimuler le développement durable et à générer des retombées grâce à ses investissements. Le genre est une question fondamentale pour les deux mécanismes de financement. Le Fonds pour l’égalité du Canada, qui a récemment été créé, comprend une stratégie d’investissement axée sur la sexospécificité pour utiliser le financement comme un outil pour la mise à l’échelle et la transformation des systèmes pour l’égalité des genres.

Le CRDI soutient la recherche-action visant à renforcer l’écosystème pour les entreprises axées sur des objectifs précis et des investissements à impact qui tiennent compte de la sexospécificité, notamment grâce à la conception et au perfectionnement d’outils de gestion et de mesure des impacts. On rassemble pour cela des chercheurs et des réseaux d’entreprises afin d’obtenir des preuves solides sur l’impact que les entreprises et les investissements ont sur la réalisation des ODD. Dans la cadre de ce projet, on mènera quatre grandes activités pour déterminer comment le CRDI peut collaborer avec le Canada au financement novateur dans une optique de genre. Les activités en question sont les suivantes : commander un document de cadrage pour cartographier les lacunes en matière de recherche, animer un atelier réunissant les responsables de projets pertinents financés par le CRDI et des institutions canadiennes travaillent sur l’innovation dans le domaine de la finance, soutenir la sensibilisation et l’engagement par l’intermédiaire de trois événements de haut niveau, et élaborer un plan d’action conjoint pour orienter la stratégie de programmation du CRDI.

title: Strengthening Capacity of Government of Kenya and Resilience of Vulnerable Border Communities to Enhance Peace and Security along Kenya-Somalia border.
description: The project aims to contribute to durable solutions for the migrant and host communities in Mandera, Wajir, Garissa and Lamu Counties of Kenya that border Somalia, affected by negative impacts of the displacement triggered by the civil war in Somalia and climate hazards in the region, and to promote peace and security along Kenya-Somalia border. The project will fulfil the objective by achieving two outcomes of enhancing community resilience and social cohesion and strengthening the capacity of the Government of Kenya (GoK) at borders.The initial phase of the project will include livelihood and psychosocial support to at-risk youth and returnees and sensitization of the County Governments and community leaders on community policing and reintegration and rehabilitation in order to strengthen their socio-economic inclusion and resilience. The second part will focus on enhancing capacity of the GoK authorities and border officials to better counter transnational threats and respond to health needs specific to vulnerable migrants crossing borders. It will also offer benefits of enhanced trust between communities and border authorities to promote peace in border communities.

title: SDGP Kenya: Developing a low-carbon coffee value-chain
description: This value-chain intervention will develop and invest in: a. Low-Carbon specialtycoffee by upgrading and lowering the carbon footprint of farmers  washing stationsand dry-mill  b. Sustainable intensification practises leading to food security resilience and higher income of smallholder farmers located around Mt. Kenya  c.local value-addition and job-creation for women and youth in Mt. Kenya region bysetting up local production-facilities of bio-compost  d. local value-addition and jobcreationfor women and youth by roasting and packaging at origin.Moyee Coffee will invest in developing a low-carbon specialty coffee  roasted and packaged in Kenya  providing a market linkage for smallholder farmers. Agriterra will select and support high-potential Primary Cooperatives (PC’s) to produce this sustainable coffee and support the PCs in governance  financial management and women and youth participation. Furthermore  Agriterra will train the extension officers and lead-farmers on low-carbon farming practices and setting up bio-compost producing facilities at PC’s.The Fairchain Foundation will provide its FC Tech programs  which include solutions such as digital farm-management and training programs  traceability and transactions marketplaces using blockchain technology. Blockchain-technology will be used to connect all stakeholders in the supply-chain and enable value-transfers from consumers to impact-projects (i.e. tree-planting  healthcare  womenempowering  education etc.) thus directly benefiting local livelihood. Blockchain will also be used to report on the actual reduction of carbon for each stakeholder due to project-interventions  thus giving measurable and verifiable proof of impact which is backing the claim of low-carbon coffee. Strategies for climate-smart and low-carbon agricultural practices such as intercropping  to ensure food security  will be provided by KALRO (Coffee Research Institute)  and implemented by partners and beneficiary PCs and farmers.MCCMCU  the only farmer-led and farmer-owned coffee mill in Kenya  will provide local value-addition of the low-carbon specialty coffee  set up an organic demo farm and nursery for intercropping trees to support the project. | Developing a low-carbon Coffee Value-Chain in Kenya | Kenya’s rich endowment of volcanic soils  altitude  rainfall and temperatures enables the country to produce high-quality arabica coffee that is rated among the best in the world. The sector contributes to the livelihoods of over 700 000 smallholder growers and 5 million beneficiaries  as well as providing substantial foreign exchange earnings.Yet  Kenya’s coffee sector is facing unprecedented challenges which have dramatically affected the production levels. Key among them:a. Exceptionally long payment periods for coffee farmers (over 6 months)b. Low global coffee prices; expected to remain low for years to come.c. Lack of direct access to the international market.d. focus and dependency on cash-cropsBased on FairChain’s experience running a smallholder program  and doing extensive research  we came to the conclusion that current programs will not lead to a living income for a majority of small farmers. The higher prices that impact-driven coffee brands like Moyee (+20%) can absorb  plus the income increase from yield and quality improvement programs are insufficient to push incomes to living-income levels.The farmer training approach places 7 200 farmers on a Living Income Roadmap  in order for all coffee producing households - each with different starting points in terms of land size  household income  motivation and agricultural and business skills - to benefit from the targeted interventions.Involving farmers in creating a low-carbon coffee  focusing on gender equality  and giving them access to markets  will bring many families to a living income.Moyee coffee will pay a 20% higher price  and directly ‘at the gate’ for cherry instead of after 6 months for clean coffee at the auction. The farmer will receive a higher  set price and save on the cost of credit  credit that many farmers have to take to bridge the 6 month payment period.The farmers will be included in a training program led by Agriterra  on good agriculture and climate-smart practices  soil-fertility and bio-composting practices and intercropping strategies. Locally tested and proved climate-smart agricultural practices will be provided by KALRO’s Coffee Research Institute.Fairchain Foundation will provide digital farm-management software  with data feeding the training program  for optimizing yields and increasing foodsecurity in a climate-smart approach. This approach is used to continuously monitor farm sizes  numbers  age and ‘categories’ of trees (cash/food)  other variables affecting production  and to create individual farm development plans  based on yield and income increase predictions  used to motivate farmers to adopt the new practices.Primary Cooperatives will receive support from Agriterra in the areas of governance  financial management and women and youth participation.Local value-adding investments will be made in washing station modernization  roasting and packaging facility and storage. State-of-the-art equipment will be installed to replace fossil-fuel-based energy sources (i.e. bio-compost production  biogas installation  husk-briquettes  solar).A traceability system using blockchain technologies  will be implemented  to make the farmers visible in the chain  up to the Western consumers  and to prove the value distribution by registering all transactions in the chain. This system will build a trustworthy and bankable value chain  improving access to markets and finance.

title: Farmers-Focused Transformation Kenya
description: In 2021, Agriterra entered into a ten-year (2021-2030) strategic partnership with the Directorate-General for International Cooperation (DGIS) of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the Netherlands, officially titled “New Decade for Cooperative Agribusiness Development”. In this new programme – by Agriterra called Farmer-Focused Transformation (FFT) – Agriterra concentrates on its core business of strengthening farmers’ organisations and cooperatives and increasing access to finance by (organised) smallholder farmers. Agriterra's core business aligns with the DGIS objectives of ensuring Dutch knowledge and expertise worldwide to achieve the SDGs and to take advantage of new business opportunities, since the Netherlands can make a difference in agriculture for developing countries thanks to the outstanding Dutch position in this sector.As such, Agriterra strives for interventions with long-term perspectives that contribute to the development of a modern, vital agricultural sector which is both economically viable and socially just. This can only be achieved through concrete intermediate results in terms of job creation, mobilizing finance and increasing productivity.Agriterra’s services will maintain a focus on strengthening farmers organisations via three-tracks: farmer-led business, sustainable services and farmer lobby and advocacy. While implementing these three trajectories, Agriterra mainstreams the cross-cutting issues of: gender, youth, and climate.At the beginning of the FFT programme, FFT operations were carried out in 19 countries. From 2022 onwards, the FFT programme focuses exclusively on 12 countries spread through 4 regions (West-Africa, East-Africa, Great Lakes and South-East Asia). The 12 focus countries for FFT include: Ivory Coast, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Ethiopia, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, DR Congo, Uganda, Philippines, Indonesia & Vietnam. | The FFT programme focuses on generating evidence-based outcomes for Farmer Organisations via quantifiable KPIs that require systematic tracking and reporting. The overall evidence-based goals envisioned for FFT in its first five years (2021-2025) are:• Goal 1: Support one million farmers through 320 farmers’ organisations. • Goal 2: 50 million euro mobilised because of lobby and advocacy proposals. • Goal 3: 60 million euro mobilised with 70 FOs linked to financial institutions. • Goal 4: 30 new farmer-led enterprises that improve farmers’ access to markets and Agri services. • Goal 5: 10,000 direct jobs supported. • Goal 6: 30,000 people trained (9,000 women and 4,500 youth), with 50 female leadership training courses, 30 youth councils and 20 women’s councils. | Farmer Organisations and CooperativesMember Farmers

title: Acting Now Kenya
description: Africa is currently facing severe food insecurity, with low agricultural productivity being one of the root causes. Factors such as limited access to quality inputs, inadequate extension services, lack of finance, and post-harvest handling issues contribute to low agricultural productivity. Food insecurity is exacerbated by economic, political and demographic shocks, including the war in Ukraine, which has caused rising food and energy prices and lower yields in 2022. Climate change further intensifies food insecurity, with extreme weather events such as droughts and floods impacting crop and livestock production and access to markets. Conflict and insecurity are also major drivers of acute food security issues, leading to population displacement and disrupted livelihoods, depriving people of income sources. Action is needed to relieve acute food insecurity, whilst at the same time structurally transforming food systems. Farmers’ Organisations and its member farmers play a critical role in obtaining this, as they contribute not only to food production, but also to sustained economic growth and climate change mitigation. The Acting Now for Food Security and Resilient Food Systems programme, with funding from the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs (specifically IGG), builds upon its existing strategic partnership with DDE by reinforcing and expanding its efforts on food security, contributing to a more measurable impact on SGD 2 (Zero Hunger). It contributes to improved food and nutrition security (FNS) at the individual farmer level and fosters systemic change in the food system through a total of 82 Farmer Organisations in Burkina Faso, DR Congo, Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya and Rwanda. As per Agriterra’s core business, Acting Now will work with and through Farmers’ Organisations and cooperatives to build resilient food systems and to make a sustainable change in the lives of smallholder farmers and their communities. Key Activities Acting Now aims to boost productivity, improving incomes and sustainable land management practices through the following key activities: - Trainings and peer-to-peer activities on FNS related topics, such as Good Agricultural Practices (GAP), Regenerative Agriculture, productivity increase at specific value chains and production of compost and bio-inputs. - Establishment of demo plots to promote and train farmers on new or improved farming practices and technologies. - Offering sustainable services through a tailored approach per country that ensures access to seeds, fertilisers, planting material, agri-inputs and extension services. - Strengthening extension services by co-financing the salary of extension officers and agronomists at the FO through Agriterra’s Jobs Jobs Jobs approach - Co-financing investments and innovations to boost agricultural productivity and food security. | Placeholder text | Farmer Organisations and its member farmers

A farmers’ organization is defined as a formal or informal (registered or unregistered) membership-based collective action group serving its members, whose livelihood (partly or in full) comes from agriculture (crops, livestock, fisheries, etc.). A job created is attributable to Agriterra’s support only if Agriterra’s contribution can be demonstrated, e.g. through a financial contribution to the payment of the FTE’s salary. FNS interventions are the activities planned between Agriterra and FOs in the scope of acting Now aimed at achieving outcome indicators: increased productivity and income for member farmers, and sustainable farmland. | Hectares of farmland directly reached aimed at improvement (structural/temporary) of agro-ecological sustainability | Number of hectares of farmland on which farmers directly trained by Agriterra in Acting Now and farmers with improved access to inputs and services that promote the Acting Now FNS outcomes report intending to apply the techniques taught during the trainings. Structural agro-ecological sustainability refers to: Hectares of farmland reached in a targeted way (i.e. farmland area reached is – or can be – known) with an intervention that structurally and/or systemically contributes to improving ecologically sustainable land use (i.e. aimed at long term outcome results, as formulated in the IGG-FNS framework). This can for instance be because the intervention covers multiple aspects of sustainable land use (soil fertility, biodiversity, crop rotation) and/or there is regular follow-up. Examples: targeted farmer training and inputs for climate-smart agriculture (CSA), integrated soil fertility management, crop rotation, erosion protection measures, (…) Temporary agro-ecological sustainability refers to: Hectares of farmland reached in a targeted way (i.e. farmland area reached is – or can be – known) with an intervention that temporarily and/or partially improves ecological sustainability. In other words, the intervention in itself cannot be assumed to lead to measurable (long-term) outcome results. Examples: providing access to digital weather forecast for specific farmers; onetime (group) training on land degradation, (…)

title: Adaptation at Altitude – Taking Action in the Mountains
description: The overall objective of the Adaptation at Altitude programme is to increase knowledge on climate change and appropriate adaptation solutions in mountains and feed it into science-policy platforms for informed decision-making in national, regional and global policy processes, in order to increase the resilience of both mountain communities and ecosystems to climate change. Given the unprecedented speed and magnitude of climate change in mountains, adaptation strategies have to be developed and practical solutions implemented urgently. However, to be effective, climate change adaptation (CCA) strategies must respond to other change processes as well. In this holistic perspective, CCA strategies and solutions in mountains should be understood as technologies, processes or approaches to adjust natural or human systems to actual or expected climate impacts, while addressing interlinked environmental and socio-economic opportunities and constraints at the same time. Adaptation and development are inextricably linked and reciprocal: good adaptation can deliver good development outcomes, and securing good development requires effective adaptation action. Therefore, CCA strategies and solutions in mountains should help mountain communities to conserve, restore and sustainably manage the key ecosystem goods and services on which their livelihoods depend.

title: Protecting the Marine Environment from Land-Based Pollution through Coordinated and Strengthened Global Action
description:
The overall objective of this project is to strengthen responses to land-based pollution of the marine environment and address related issues of concern identified by governments. This also includes strengthening of co-operation around the prevention of land-based pollution by fostering action targeting the sources of marine litter, nutrients and wastewater pollution. 

Land-based pollution has been widely recognized to impact the health of aquatic ecosystems, including coastal and marine ones. Over time, population growth has led to the increasing demand for water, food and consumable goods, and the rising number of anthropogenic activities has resulted in augmented pollution from point and non-point sources. Also, extreme weather events and climate change pose additional stress on natural resources, with major consequences on human health, ecosystems, and infrastructures. 

UN Environment, as the Secretariat of the Global Programme of Action for the Protection of the Marine Environment from Land-Based Activities (GPA), plays a crucial role in identifying and acting on the challenge of land-based pollution. The GPA is the only intergovernmental mechanism that provides governments with conceptual and practical guidance on preventing, reducing, controlling and eliminating marine degradation resulting from land-based activities. The GPA activities serve to help achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) contained in the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, specifically SDG 6 and 14, and contribute to the implementation of UN Environment Assembly’s (UNEA) resolutions on “Addressing water pollution to protect and restore water-related ecosystems” (UNEP/EA.3/L.27) and “Marine litter and microplastics” (UNEP/EA.3/L.20). The goal of this project is in line with the GPA Programme of Work (PoW) for the period 2018-2022 as well as with the objective of UN Environment’s Chemicals, Waste and Air Quality sub-programme. UN Environment will implement the project in close co-operation with key partners and stakeholders, including the Regional Seas Programme, and through the three multi-stakeholder partnerships: the Global Partnership on Marine Litter (GPML), the Global Partnership on Nutrient Management (GPNM), and the Global Wastewater Initiative (GW²I).

title: Multi-Sectoral Humanitarian Assistance to Drought-Affected Displaced Communities in Marsabit and Isiolo in Kenya
description:
Compounded by climate change, communities in the dry region of Kenya are driven to migrate in search of essential assistance and resources. The vulnerable population displaced by prolonged droughts face significant challenges in accessing basic needs such as food, water, hygiene, health, education, and infrastructure.

title: Kenya: Enhancing Peace through the Prevention of Natural Resource-based Conflicts in Northwestern Kenya
description: This funding will support the Government of Kenya (GoK) and target communities in Turkana, West Pokot, and Baringo Counties in preventing resource-based conflict in the framework of building sustainable peace and promoting social cohesion among communities. Extreme climatic conditions in Northwestern Kenya have had devastating effects on the environment and the livelihoods of communities, shifting traditional migration patterns and pushing groups into conflict over scarce resources. These resource-based conflicts, exacerbated by climate change, have led to insecurity, undermining socio-economic development. Still, little is understood about the details of the climate change - migration - conflict nexus, and there is significant space to reduce the issues through community mediation mechanisms, if their capacities to do so are strengthened.To ensure that the GoK strengthens its conflict preventative measures, the hot spots, root causes, existing peace structures and possible solutions for insecurity caused by climate change will be mapped out and consolidated into a framework which will be further mainstreamed into existing peace structures in each target county (Outcome 1). After, to improve resilience to natural resource-based conflict, the programme aims to train key community leaders (women and men) on the issues of natural resource-based conflict and mediation skills so they can contribute to developing and leading community events to promote peace at the community level (Outcome 2). Finally, socio-economic stability in target communities will be enhanced through assistance to diversify livelihood opportunities to prevent over-reliance on limited resources by establishing and implementing Community Assistance Projects (CAPs) that will benefit all the communal groups, in a gender- and age-sensitive manner, to ensure not to leave anyone behind in the community (Outcome 3). Ultimately, the three-pronged approach will lead to strengthened peace mechanisms and a reduction in resource-based conflict in the communities.

title: Strengthening African Civil Society and Governments’ leadership and voices on Climate Change
description:
The decisions agreed at COP 26 made progress towards addressing the climate crisis but fell short of key expectations and asks of the vulnerable countries, including the Africa Group. The COP failed to raise the twice-promised $100bn annual climate funding to vulnerable countries, did not close the mitigation and adaptation ambition gaps in line with staying below 1.5°C. At COP29 country parties failed to agree to scale up climate finance to the requisite US$1,3trillion via the new collective quantified goal (NCQG) leaving climate-affected countries to the vices of climate catastrophe's and debt as a result of limited capacity to raise climate finance.. 
The science and message from leaders from vulnerable developing nations and organisations is unequivocal; failure to effectively implement the Paris Agreement and close the mitigation, adaptation, and financial gaps in this decade will mean that the opportunity to make the world safe for the present and future generations will be lost.
COP27, 28 and 29 held in Egypt, UAE and Azerbaijan respectively, provided opportunities for the continent to ensure that fair and ambitious outcomes that meet the needs of climate vulnerable countries and communities are met. 
Africa remains the most vulnerable continent severely affected by climate change. International climate policy and processes including mobilisation around COPs present opportunities to catalyse green and resilient investments in the continent. Despite the challenges and opportunities presented by climate change, Africa is the least engaged region on climate diplomacy and there is currently minimal public debate on clean energy and climate change. This is because there are structural barriers, including capacity gaps both within national and regional African decision-making bodies, as well as within civil society and other non-state actors that could otherwise support enhanced climate leadership. 
Power Shift Africa will help facilitate informed and effective participation of Africa in the global climate change negotiations including at the UNFCCC through building capacities of government officials and CSOs, support effective media campaign and promoting ambitious and equitable positions and demands, and helping to secure a fair, robust and science-based outcomes at COP30.

title: Enhancing Climate Change Adaptation and Sustainable Energy in Kenya and Kajiado County
description: The project seeks to enhance local climate change adaptation actions and access to sustainable energy in Kenya and Kajiado County through empowering women and other marginalized groups while fostering dialogue with power holders. The project also aims at building and strengthening grassroot movements that will advocate and lobby for just energy transition, sustained climate action while holding duty bearers accountable to realize climate justice among the marginalized and most vulnerable community members. At different levels, participatory research will be undertaken to understand drivers limiting local adaptation strategies taking into consideration the on-going initiatives such as the devolved climate financing, climate smart agriculture among others. Qualitative and quantitative approaches tailoring possible remedies to inefficiencies including development of software/app that would aid in early warning and weather information translation for decision making will inform next steps. In the case of influencing power dimensions for women representation and other marginalized groups taking up positions of leadership, sundry strategies will be devised during project inception phase and will explore dialogue with local leadership at ward, sub-county, county and national assembly’s levels including budgeting committees. These will include influencing existing legislations, leveraging on policy moments and processes as well as using local voices to articulate for equality/climate change justice and equity responsive policies, action plans, legislations etc. Community mobilizations will be key to ensure strong local movements through strategies that promote collaboration and shared value among communities, private and civil society organizations. Private sector collaborations in this case will be key towards realization of intended climate responsive actions such as weather-based insurance, provision of quality renewable energy products and fostering partnerships with the local community institutions and government to create sustainability.

description:
ACRE: Accelerating Cooperation and Resilience to tackle natural resource challenges in fragile and conflict affected borderlands, using the Humanitarian-Development-Peacebuilding Nexus

title: Strengthening Climate Adaptation, Resilience, Livelihoods, and Gender Inclusion in Kisumu and Bungoma Counties_ADSW
description:
This project aims to enhance climate adaptation, resilience, and economic growth at the community level in Kisumu and Bungoma Counties by promoting inclusive and effective climate finance strategies and sustainable practices. This will be achieved through improved communication, transparency, and accountability in the distribution and management of climate funds, fostering inclusive decision-making and optimal resource utilization. By strengthening communication channels, monitoring systems, and reporting frameworks, the project will enhance public confidence and ensure that community priorities are reflected in climate action initiatives, leading to more impactful outcomes.
Additionally, this project seeks to increase access to climate finance for vulnerable and marginalized groups, particularly women. This will strengthen local resilience and facilitate more effective adaptation strategies, allowing these groups to engage fully in climate resilience efforts. Improved governance and coordination systems for climate finance will enhance management, transparency, and collaboration among stakeholders, leading to more equitable and impactful climate actions.
This project also emphasizes the need for local communities to prepare for the evolving challenges posed by climate change. Recognizing that there is no one-size-fits-all solution, it will focus on awareness-raising and capacity-building efforts tailored to the diverse ecosystems and socio-economic conditions of the regions. The project will assess various livelihood systems, profiling vulnerable groups, conduct participatory climate risk assessments, and examine the impacts of past and current climate events.
By addressing these areas, this project will promote institutional and technical capacity building within key agencies and community organizations, enabling them to deliver demand-responsive services that better equip communities to adapt to climate change effectively.

title: Energy Access Advocacy Project in Africa
description:
At the heart of transforming Africa’s energy landscape is the need for robust civil society engagement. Empowered civil society organizations (CSOs) can drive policy advocacy, foster community-led energy solutions, and hold institutions accountable, but their participation in MDB decision-making remains fragmented and under-resourced. The project targets several key challenges:
1.      Underrepresentation of CSOs and communities: Most CSOs lack the technical knowledge, access, or resources to influence MDB processes or attend key forums.
2.      Persistent fossil fuel financing: Ongoing MDB and public support for fossil projects delays clean energy transitions and exposes countries to fuel price volatility.
3.      Underinvestment in DREs: Proven technologies remain underfunded, limiting access for last-mile communities.
4.      Neglect of local innovators: Community-based enterprises face major financing and policy barriers, excluding marginalized groups from the transition.
5.      Limited transparency and accountability: MDBs rarely publish timely, disaggregated project data, reducing public oversight.
6.      Weak advocacy capacity: CSOs lack tools to track policy shifts, public sentiment, and influence outcomes.
To close Africa’s energy gap, public finance must shift toward inclusive, community-driven DRE solutions. Empowering civil society and improving transparency are essential to ensuring that energy investments align with development, equity, and climate goals.

title: 1.	Project title:	Building Climate-Resilient Livelihoods through Community-Led Adaptation in Makueni and Kitui Counties
description:
The project is set to improve the resilience of the semi-arid communities in Kitui and Makueni counties, whose livelihoods are continually being threatened by frequent drought, land degradation, and erratic rainfall patterns due to climate change. Increased access to climate information for communities, improved agroecological farming practices, strengthened local disaster risk governance, and increased adaptive capacity for local communities and institutions are the interventions through which the project will reach its vision.
Key interventions will include:
i. Training and capacity development of the County and National government stakeholders, Ward Climate Change Planning Teams and Committees,(WCCPC/Ts), Self Help Groups (SHGs),  and local farmers on climate resilient agriculture and early warning systems.
ii. Facilitating community led climate risk assessment and localized adaptation action planning. 
iii. Facilitating policy dialogue and building institutional capacity for climate governance at the ward and county levels.
iv. Promoting nature based solutions and land management at the ward level while collaborating with the ward natural resource management committees. 
 
The project will take a rights oriented and participatory strategy in making sure that it is inclusive, especially to the women, youth, and people with disabilities. Locally led innovation, knowledge exchange, and capacity building will make sure that the project contributes meaningfully to long term climate sustainability and resilience.

title: Scaling inclusive and accountable climate finance for resilient communities in Kisumu County
description:
Suswatch Kenya proposes to implement the Scaling Inclusive and Accountable Climate Finance for Resilient Communities in Kisumu County project, aimed at strengthening inclusive, transparent, and accountable climate finance governance systems that empower communities especially women, youth, and marginalized groups to actively engage in and benefit from climate action. The project builds on insights and successes from earlier implemented climate finance projects, aiming to strengthen locally led climate action by tackling ongoing challenges such as low community participation, weak institutional coordination, limited transparency and accountability in climate finance management, and inadequate public access to climate finance information in Kisumu County
Kisumu County faces increasingly severe climate-related risks such as flooding, drought, and environmental degradation, all of which are intensified by rapid urbanization, deforestation, weak infrastructure, and high poverty levels. Although Kenya’s climate finance framework such as the Financing Locally Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) program offers an opportunity to build resilience at the ward level, local communities often lack the capacity, awareness, and access needed to fully participate in these processes. Marginalized groups, including women, youth, and persons with disabilities, remain underrepresented in climate governance structures and decision-making platforms.
This project aims to close these gaps by focusing on three interconnected outcomes: (1) Enhanced transparency and accountability in climate finance governance in Kisumu County; (2) Strengthened institutional capacity and stakeholder collaboration; and (3) Increased meaningful participation of women, youth, and marginalized groups in climate governance structures and decision-making processes in policy engagement. By achieving these goals, the project will ensure that climate funds are not only allocated more effectively but are also equitably distributed based on community priorities and vulnerabilities.

title: The Imarisha Kilimo Plus Project (TIK +)
description:
The project titled  The Imarisha Kilimo Plus Project (TIK +) is a 12-month initiative aimed at building sustainable livelihoods through climate-smart agriculture, inclusive market systems, and policy advocacy. Implemented by Beacon of Hope (BOH) in partnership with Christian Aid Kenya (CAK), the project will operate in Dagoretti North and South Sub-Counties, Nairobi County, and directly benefit 150 smallholder farmers—60% women, 30% youth and 10% men. This proposal builds on the strong foundation laid during Phase 1 of The Imarisha Kilimo Project (TIK), which surpassed its target by reaching 130 smallholder farmers (108% of goal). Over 92% of participants adopted climate-smart agriculture (CSA) practices, 80% reported increased vegetable production, and 65% engaged in value addition (primarily through kale powder production). Notably, women's financial empowerment increased by 75%, and 70% of beneficiaries were linked to local markets, with 20% gaining access to formal buyers.
 
The proposed project (Phase 2) seeks to scale and deepen these outcomes by promoting indigenous, drought-resistant crops (e.g., managu, cowpeas, amaranth), enhancing local value chains through processing, branding, and packaging, and expanding access to microcredit and digital marketplaces. The project also emphasizes policy engagement to reduce structural barriers for smallholder farmers, such as lack of subsidies, high tariffs, and stringent certification processes. Key interventions include: Training 150 farmers in CSA techniques, composting, and organic pest control. Distribution of drought-resistant seed kits and irrigation tools. Establishment of six demonstration farms for peer learning. Support for Seven (7) VSLAs with training in record-keeping, savings mobilization, and credit access. Advanced training in value addition (e.g., vegetable drying, KEBS compliance) and e-commerce. Facilitation of market linkages with supermarkets, hotels, and exporters. Policy dialogues with government actors to advocate for pro-smallholder policies. The expected impact is substantial: 80% of farmers will adopt drought-resilient crops and CSA practices. 65% will participate in value-added processing. 70% will access formal and digital markets. 40% of VSLA members will secure microloans to grow their agri-businesses. At least one policy changes will be influenced at the county level. Sustainability is central to the project. BOH will guide farmer groups toward forming cooperatives and establishing a table banking initiatives from value-added sales to support future investments. Additionally, partnerships with government agencies and the private sector will be solidified through formal   agreements, ensuring continued support beyond the project’s life cycle.

title: Deepening Impacts and Learning Opportunities for Climate Resilience in Bungoma County
description:
Since 2018, Anglican Development Services Western (ADS-W), in partnership with Christian Aid, has been implementing climate change initiatives across Western Kenya counties (Kakamega, Vihiga, Bungoma, Nandi and Trans-Nzoia). The latest intervention was implemented in Bungoma County, Bumula Sub-County with a particular focus on smallholder farmers under the project title Strengthening Climate Adaptation, Resilience, Livelihoods, and Gender Inclusion in Kisumu and Bungoma Counties through Inclusive Climate Finance and Climate-Smart Practices. The collaboration has evolved into a robust platform for promoting community-level climate adaptation through inclusive climate finance, the adoption of climate-smart practices, and the strengthening of local climate governance structures. The ongoing project, Strengthening Climate Adaptation, Resilience, Livelihoods, and Gender Inclusion, aimed to improve the adaptive capacities of vulnerable communities while aligning with Kenya’s devolved climate finance frameworks and policies, such as the Bungoma County Climate Change Act (2022) and the Bungoma County Climate Change Action Plan.
Significant achievements to date include the establishment and capacity building of Ward Climate Change Planning Committees (WCCPCs)—the core local structures mandated to plan and oversee climate actions; support to 500 local farmer producers to adopt climate-smart agricultural practices, diversify their livelihoods, and implement green energy technologies; and improved access to localized climate information, enhancing community-level planning and preparedness. These gains demonstrate the potential of community-led, policy-anchored approaches in building resilience to climate change at the grassroots level.
As climate risks grow in scale and complexity, there is an increasing need to consolidate these outcomes, scale successful models, and generate actionable learning to inform adaptive management and evidence-based policy implementation. This proposed project by ADSW is aimed at strengthening the capacity of local institutions in preparing themselves for the changing situations and integrating them into various government (County and National) policy frames; Scale proven models embedded within the Bungoma County Climate Change Action Plan and Build knowledge base that supports continuous learning through innovations and advocacy.  These will help the project to promote institutional and technical capacity building within key agencies and among community associations/groups for demand-responsive services needed to better adapt and govern their existing systems. Moreover, the emerging ecosystem of supportive policies, multi-stakeholder networks, and devolved governance frameworks in Bungoma provides ground to strengthen institutional capacities, unlock climate finance flows, and mainstream resilience into sustainable development planning.

title: Fanikisha Mjane (Ensuring the Success of a Widow)
description: Fanikisha Mjane is a widow-centred agricultural empowerment project that seeks to strengthen the economic resilience and social dignity of 150 widows living in Ganze Sub-County, Kilifi County. Ganze is widely recognized as a marginalized area where poverty and Gender-Based Violence have become part of daily life, especially for widows. Many of them have been victims of economic exclusion, land disinheritance, social stigma, and sexual abuse. Many remarry out of desperation for safety and economic support, but instead find themselves in abusive relationships. Shockingly, when these widows remarry in search of safety and support, their daughters are often exposed to incestuous abuse by stepfathers, stepbrothers, or male relatives in the new household. These violations are shrouded in silence, sustained by fear, shame, and entrenched cultural norms. Because they are forced to rely on abusive remarried partners for basic survival and acceptance within their communities, these widows feel they have no voice and are compelled to remain in toxic relationships and conform to societal expectations where they have no choice but to sacrifice their dignity, their autonomy, and the safety of their children in the process. The project aims to break this cycle by economically empowering widows through climate smart cassava farming. Cassava farming is well-suited to Ganze’s dry conditions and valued both culturally and also for its high nutritional and commercial value. Widows will receive Page 3 of 14 hands-on training in sustainable cassava production, covering key areas such as land preparation, pest and disease management, organic methods, soil conservation, and post-harvest techniques. These skills will improve productivity while promoting environmentally responsible farming. To further support income generation, the project will establish two community-based cassava processing hubs where widows will engage in value addition, producing products such as flour, crisps, porridge mix, and livestock feed. They will also be trained in product development, branding, packaging, and food safety compliance to help them compete in formal markets. These skills will enhance the marketability and quality of their products, allowing them to meet the demands of institutional buyers such as local hotels, supermarkets, and other retail outlets within Kilifi County and beyond.

title: African Activists for Climate Justice
description: To amplify and unite the voices in Africa to ensure that women, youth and local and indigenous communities defend and realize their human rights and live a decent and dignified life in a healthy and sustainable environment, within the context of the climate emergency. The Project’s long-term impact is a strong and inclusive African movement that has mobilised citizens, companies and governments (local, national, regional, global) in support of climate justice.PACJA in collaboration with four other partners,  Oxfam Novib, Natural Justice, African Women Communications Network (FEMNET) and African Youth Commission (AYC), as a consortium,  believe that all people have the right to live a decent and dignified life in a healthy environment. PACJA in Ethiopia will fast track climate action that is strong, all-inclusive and gender sensitive climate justice movement that advocates for fair, accessible and equitable climate policies, including community-driven adaptation strategies, which specifically benefit disadvantaged groups (in particular women, youth and indigenous communities). PACJA in Burkina Faso will promote traditionally excludes groups in acceleration of climate cation through the organization of young and female farmers, pastoralists, people with disabilities, refugees in the Centre, Nord, Sahel, Sud-Ouest and Centre-Nord regions, and local and national authorities become aware of the challenges posed by climate change, and decide to work in synergy towards climate justice. Natural Justice in Senegal,  will promote a better-informed population to play an an active role in the debate and decisions on climate change and contributes to improved recognition of the concerns and rights of climate-affected communities and vulnerable groups and their contribution to addressing climate change. In South Africa, Natural Justice  will strengthen CSOs platforms and engage with key climate actors working with women, youth, Indigenous People and Local Communities to promote an inclusive and human rights-based approach to climate action. FEMNET in Mozambique will lead in strengthening climate resilience and Justice for rural communities with key climate actors working with marginalized groups and local communities, particularly women and youth, who are at the frontline of the climate crisis, are strengthened to claim their rights for climate justice and climate resilience. Oxfam in Nigeria will lead a climate action for sustainable and resilient and inclusive economic growth through a  grassroots driven movement – bringing together local organizations and broad constituencies  to drive  the implementation of climate policies that enable all Nigerians to thrive and live in a healthy environment. In Somalia, Oxfam will lead in building a climate justice movement in groups that are most affected by the climate crisis  including rural pastoralists and farmers, young unemployed, and disadvantaged women, understand its effect on their situation and rally together to demand investments and policy changes from governments, companies and the aid system. The Somali government in turn is able to pass environmental protection laws, make strong climate action plans and access global finance to fund them.The African Youth Commission (AYC) is an implementing partner, playing a key role in bringing more young people on board to raise awareness on climate change and  influence national governments to implement climate-related projects in a transparent manner that benefits young people. The network also sees a vital role for youth in Africa to contribute to the development of practical solutions and efforts to enhance the livelihoods of vulnerable communities. The AYC has 228 members in 46 countries on the African continent | women, youth and local communities

title: DEEPENING DEMOCRACY PROGRAMME
description: The program will enhance resilience of vulnerable households in West Pokot to climate extremes and disasters through a community-led, systems-driven approach aimed to improve public sector engagement and service delivery, increase community capacity to manage resources and prepare for disasters, and ultimately to secure resources and livelihoods. Mercy Corps believes that effective action to combat the effects of climate change will result when communities and the leaders who govern them are empowered with knowledge, systems and resources to undertake locally-driven planning processes to effectively manage natural resources, mitigate the impact of natural disasters, and manage conflict.

title: PROGRESS: Programme for Resilient Systems to build absorptive, adaptive and transformative capacity for over 530,000 vulnerable individuals in Kenya and Uganda
description: To build resilience, PROGRESS will scale approaches, practices and technologies based on six cross-cutting methodologies we have successfully employed across our East Africa resilience portfolio. Developed around empowerment and governance perspectives, the programme focuses on facilitating a process that puts communities, private sector, and governments in a position of responsibility to decide and affect their future vulnerability to shocks and stresses. This approach acknowledges that activities are not just an end but a means to achieving transformational impacts and behaviour change. All the approaches and practices embed this idea of programme as process to take impact to scale. GOAL: enhancing household wellbeing amid increasing climate extremes and disasters OBJECTIVES: - improved food security, nutrition, and livelihood opportunities for men, women, boys, and girls even in the face of droughts and climate variability, across Wajir and Karamoja - improved citizen voice in formal and informal governance which will enhance accountability and appropriate use of public resources, ultimately resulting in government investments that are more responsive to community needs and are more climate-smart

title: Financial Services Development in Africa
description: The Making Markets Work for the Poor (M4P) approach hinges on facilitation, rather than direct implementation, and as such, represents a radical shift in how donors envision and how development actors interact with financial systems. Although the theoretical frameworks for this approach are well developed, there is a comparative lack of detailed analysis regarding application in the financial sector.Significant questions remain how to apply M4P frameworks and tactics to fragile and conflict-affected states or conflict-affected regions within specific countries (i.e. Kenya and Uganda). Recognizing the large number of underserved populations and untapped potential, FSD Africa and forward-thinking donors are looking to explore the relevance and applicability of using a M4P approach for financial sector development in FCAS. Mercy Corps will provide guidance to FSDA on different approaches required between ‘fragile’ and ‘conflicted-affected’, and appropriate and realistic financial sector interventions in different stages of conflict: rapid on-set, active, latent, post-conflict and during the unpredictable casual chains between states of conflict as a crisis’s stabilizes or expands. We will also explore different strategy and tactics between conflict typologies (i.e. epidemic or climate-led, ethnic or political instability. Deliverables include a think piece and four complementary mini-studies on financial sector development work in fragile and conflict-affected states (FCAS) in Africa. | The think piece and 4 case studies will be structured around these areas of investigation: 1. Define FCAS in different Africa contexts and detail why these contexts warrant attention and donor funds. 2. Define financial sector development in FCAS to qualify the demand and need for further investment in financial sector development. 3. Detail the unique nature of FCAS and the linkages between fragility on financial sector development and how underdevelopment of the financial sector can influence fragility and conflict. 4. Set the stage for future financial sector development in African FCAS based on past and current investments and the future for potential investments. This includes strategic operational prioritization and clear principles for success and recommendations for action by government and related agencies, the private sector, and financial market development donors. This also includes engagement with the African diaspora for remittances and investments.

title: Climate Resilient Education Systems Trial (CREST)
description: Initiative will draw on best practices in the humanitarian sector toreduce the impact of climate-related crises on schools, school children and communities. CRESTwill do this by connecting community-driven, early-action approaches with parametric climateinsurance to increase the volume and speed of funding available for schools and communitiesaffected by climate-related school closures, ensure continuity of learning and prevent and disruptadverse coping mechanisms impacting children’s development and wellbeing and ensurechildren’s safe return to school. This will reduce the disruptions to school and the chances of long-term dropout and learning loss. CREST has the capacity to be scaled across multiple contexts,following an initial, successful pilot.

title: Emergency Response to Drought and Natural Disasters and Improvement of Socio-economic Conditions for Host and Refugee Communities
description:
Kalobeyei Settlement has hosted increasing refugee-host populations for more than twenty years – in the last two years, there has seen an increase of 15.6% from 38,081 to 45,122, with the settlement population rapidly expanding. The Advisory Settlement Development Plan formulated by UN-Habitat in 2017-2018 anticipates a total population of 60,000, and with rapid population increase, existing public infrastructures will struggle to cope. 
Over the last two years, Turkana has experienced dire humanitarian-climate change catastrophes such as severe droughts (27% of rainfall during Oct’21 to Mar’22) and flooding of unpredictable natures (180% of rainfall during Dec’20-May’21 at 180% and May’22 at 192%, and possibility of El Nino effect upcoming). From experience, there are high risks of flash floods emerging after extended droughts which can displace communities resulting in large loss of lives, as well as destruction of public facilities. 
These vulnerabilities are exacerbated by crop failure and water scarcity compounded by the global economic crisis from the combined impact of the Covid-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine. 
The pandemic has devastated the existing economy with many refugees and host members losing income and livelihood opportunities and has also spread health risks to refugees and hosts who have insufficient access to health and basic services, increasing overall tensions and conflicts within the region. This requires urgent interventions to ensure communities are food secure improve disaster preparedness and response, rehabilitate land for better efficient use, provide adequate infrastructures and build capacity for resilience

title: Emphasising Ecosystems, Elevating People (3EP): Planning for “Rivers and People” in the Nairobi River Life Project (RLP)
description: Emphasising Ecosystems, Elevating People (3EP) will employ a bottom-up approach to the rediscovery, regeneration, and protection of Nairobi’s natural assets throughout the river system. In turn 3EP will underpin and activate the city-wide Nairobi River Life Project (RLP): a multi-actor, interdisciplinary initiative which aims to reclaim and regenerate Nairobi’s three main rivers through public, private and civil society partnerships. Focused on Ngong River Basin, 3EP demonstrates how EbA principles incorporate scales from neighbourhood to city. Within the city-wide RLP context, 3EP catalyses and integrates basin scale visioning, co-produced settlement ‘Rivers + People’ plans, and builds tangible community-driven climate adaptations into the most challenging urban river corridors. The 3EP team comprises the convening members of RLP (UN-Habitat (UNH) and Nairobi Metropolitan Services (NMS)), as well as experts in the mainstreaming of ecological planning within municipal governance (ICLEI Cities Biodiversity Centre (CBC)).  By demonstrating replicable models for the upscaling of EbA, 3EP will also catalyse action throughout Kenya and beyond, positioning communities and local governments to more comprehensively address the growing challenges of climate risk, urbanisation, and loss of natural assets.

title: ROAF/KEN/Nairobi Rivers Basin Regeneration - Connecting the city and its people with the rivers in Nairobi: A catalyst to Inclusive Urban Regeneration through efficient multi-level stakeholder engagement
description:
The Nairobi Rivers Basin is a distinctive ecosystem consisting of several rivers including the Nairobi River, Mathare River and Ngong River, and a mix of forests and savanna grasslands, key green public spaces, a large national park, wetland areas and several significant urban forests.
However, in recent years, there has been a dramatic decrease in natural assets and green coverage by an estimated 20% across Nairobi, resulting in a decline in the larger river ecosystem. These rivers have significantly suffered from the ‘triple planetary crises' of climate change, nature and biodiversity loss, and pollution, with many of the settlements along the rivers being at risk due to their location in flood-prone areas. These intertwined challenges have cumulatively led to environmental degradation, increased loss of biodiversity, public health concerns, and a decline in the overall quality of life of the residents, coupled with significant effects from climate change. 
There is therefore a need for urgent action to regenerate these rivers. The rising interest in the regeneration of the rivers of Nairobi amongst stakeholders in the recent past provides a unique opportunity to kick start the process, leveraging on the political will and commitment, led from the highest level of Government, the President and the Deputy President, as an unparalleled chance to convene stakeholders and demonstrate inclusive participation in the rivers regeneration.
The Nairobi Rivers Commission was established by the President of the Republic of Kenya on 2nd December 2022, through a gazette notice that underscored the State’s role in protecting the environment, mitigating environmental degradation, combatting the devastating impacts of climate change, and enhancing protection of biodiversity. The commission is mandated to protect and restore the ecological integrity of Nairobi's rivers through a basin-wide approach that ensures their sustainability and improves the quality of life of the communities living along the waterways. It is key for the Commission to work with various stakeholders, including government agencies, NGOs, the private sector, development and multi-lateral partners and more significantly the river line communities, to achieve its goals and promote building consensus, collaboration, and alignment of the efforts with the needs and aspirations of the communities they serve.

title: Cool waters: Youth-Led Climate Adaptation in Nairobi River Communities
description: The "Cool Waters" project is a two-year initiative aimed at enhancing climate resilience in Nairobi's riverine communities through youth-led interventions. Focusing on informal settlements along the Nairobi Rivers Basin, where approximately 1.8 million people (40% of Nairobi's residents) live within 1km of the rivers, the project addresses critical climate challenges including projected increases in annual precipitation, temperature rise, flooding risks, and heat vulnerability. Through three main objectives, the project seeks to develop community capacity for climate adaptation, implement resilience solutions, and advocate for the mainstreaming of local adaptation strategies into government plans. Key activities include establishing a Climate Adaptation Academy, conducting participatory hazard mapping, developing community adaptation plans, and implementing nature-based solutions. The initiative emphasizes gender equality with a 50/50 participation target and special consideration for women's needs, as they are often primary caregivers and most affected by climate impacts. Aligned with SDGs 11, 13, and 17, and supporting the newly formed Nairobi Rivers Commission's mandate, the project is implemented by UN-Habitat and the Public Space Network. Serving as a catalytic initiative in the early stages of the larger Nairobi Rivers regeneration project, it has potential for additional co-funding from other donors to expand its impact on protecting and restoring the ecological integrity of Nairobi's rivers while improving community resilience to climate change.

title: Think and Do Tank in Support of Accelerating Resilience Building in the ASALs of Kenya
description:
The Resilience Think and Do Tank (RTDT) is a three-year program (2024–2027) funded by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Kenya and implemented by the Millennium Water Alliance, VNG International, and Akvo Kenya Foundation. It focuses on catalyzing investments in Kenya’s Arid and Semi-Arid Lands (ASALs), regions with untapped potential for climate-smart agri-food development. The program generates reliable data on investment opportunities across food crop, fodder, livestock, and fish value chains, and shares this knowledge through conventions, investment forums, and a digital repository and interaction platform that connects investors with viable ventures.
RTDT also works to strengthen the enabling environment for investments. This includes providing technical support to county-level institutions to enhance their capacity in investment brokerage, as well as empowering local communities through training and coaching on social accountability tools. By equipping citizens to participate in decision-making at ward, sub-county, and county levels, the program ensures that investments are inclusive, transparent, and responsive to local needs.
Expected outputs include well-developed investment opportunity profiles, high-level investor convenings, stronger county institutions, and empowered communities that can shape development priorities. The program’s ultimate goal is to accelerate agri-food investments and achieve sustainable economic development in Kenya’s ASALs.

title: Green Ambassadors in Kenya
description: The aim of this preparatory study is to advance climate change conversations. We wish to start a partnership project with Activista Kenya where we seek to support the education of youth on climate change, with a focus on co-producing knowledge and tools to empower them to use their voice on climate change, with the end game of becoming a ‘Green Ambassador’ in their local communities. The overall project will be divided into two different stages - the first stage will be conducting a training of trainers where they will get knowledge about climate change including tools for advocacy followed by the second stage of contextualised training at their local communities through fun and interactive workshops. Therefore, this preparatory study aims to situate the volunteers into the realities of what the climate impacts are in Kenya, what the norms of volunteering are in Kenya, how we can find the right volunteers to become Green Ambassadors, and to start developing our pilot project.

title: Shifting power: Voices for Climate Action
description: The Alternative Youth and Declares Kenya are conducting a preparatory study to evaluate youth awareness in West Pokot County, Kenya, about climate change and its link to natural disasters, identifying barriers to their participation in climate policies. The pilot project targets youths aged 15 to 35, focusing on climate change mitigation, resilience, and adaptation advocacy. It aims to empower young individuals with climate education and leadership skills, enhance organizational capacity through volunteer engagement, and promote gender equality by including marginalized voices in decision-making. Key activities include workshops with local and Danish volunteers, community projects, media engagement, and policy advocacy. Expected outcomes include a youth empowerment workshop format, mobilization of 25 youth volunteers, and increased youth inclusion in climate policies. This holistic approach ensures sustainable outcomes, fostering a strong volunteer culture and contributing to climate-resilient, gender-equal communities in West Pokot County in Kenya .
