title: WFP Capacity Strengthening for DRR and resilience
description:
The aim is to ensure that national and county institutions in Kenya have strengthened capacity and systems for assisting food-insecure and nutritionally vulnerable populations and that targeted food-insecure and vulnerable populations benefit from sustainable, inclusive food systems and increased resilience to climate shocks to meet food and nutrition needs. | Syftet är att se till att nationella och länsinstitutioner i Kenya har stärkt kapacitet och system för att hjälpa livsmedelsotrygga kvinnor och att säkerställa att sårbara kvinnor och män kan dra nytta av hållbara, inkluderande livsmedelssystem och därigenom får ökad motståndskraft mot klimatchocker för att möta livsmedelsbehov. | The programme is expected to strengthen capacity of National and county institutions in Kenya to assist food-insecure and nutritionally vulnerable populations. The expected programme outputs are as follows:
1. National and county government institutions develop a well-functioning institutional arrangement that is effective in inter-sectorial coordination and has enhanced sustainable financing and leadership for resilient livelihoods programming and emergency preparedness and response, anchored in relevant policy and legislation.
2. National and county government institutions develop technical capacities, know-how and experience for evidence based design and planning of resilient livelihoods and Emergency Preparedness and Response programmes.
3. National and county government institutions develop systems that improve delivery efficiency, foster greater accountability and responsiveness in implementation of resilient livelihoods and emergency preparedness and response programmes.
4. Communities vulnerable to and affected by climatic shocks have strengthened productive capacities to withstand and recover their livelihoods.
sector_names: Disaster Risk Reduction | Other Multisector
participating_orgs: Sweden / SE-0 / 1 | Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency / SE-6 / 3
results_text:
Results achieved | Uppnådda resultat | During the period, support focused on providing technical and financial assistance to strengthen the capacity of both national and county governments and communities to develop climate-resilient assets, improve access to finance and risk management tools, and establish and manage institutions charged with preparing and responding to emergencies. The targeted institutions are the Ministry of Devolution and ASALS (MoDA), State Department for Devolution (SDD), State Department of ASALS (SDDA), National Drought Management Authority NDMA and nine counties where WFP continued to invest in the capacity of technical officers and extension systems.
Disaster Risk Management (DRM) committees were established within counties to provide for institutional structure and financing for government-led programmes for preparing and responding to emergencies. In 2020, the project progressed well towards strengthening food and nutrition security programmes in nine arid counties. WFP continued investing in technical and analytical capacity that broadened the pool of county officers who undertook food and nutrition security assessments, disseminated the findings and enhanced use of the evidence for planning and resource allocation. The DRM sector was also strengthened through training that enabled them to mainstream Climate Change Adaptation (CCA) and DRM in planning and budgeting. DRM committees were also established to enhance coordination and effective preparedness for disaster response at county, sub county and ward level. For sustainability of the initiatives Tana River County established a DRM Fund (2% of the County budget). Policy development at national level was however negatively impacted due to COVID-19 where the Government directed efforts towards an Interagency Committee for Emergency Relief Response where WFPs team contributed to the development of operational plan, Standard Operating Procedures and guidelines for relief assistance that were used during COVID-19 response.Priority areas for 2021 will include piloting disaster risk financing model in two counties and use the findings to further advocate for government investments in disaster risk financing. The development of the National Relief Assistance Policy will be accelerated with the aim of getting approval. County and national level emergency contingency planning and simulation will also be prioritised in view of the projected poor season.The containment measures to the risk of the spread of the COVID-19 virus resulted in a temporary suspension of activities in adherence to Government regulations. WFP utilized a blended approach of online and face-to-face engagement where feasible to ensure programme implementation coupled with continuous communication and engagement with relevant stakeholders, partners and beneficiaries. Addressing the needs of the most vulnerable was essential, and WFP ensured that vulnerable groups, including women, children, people living with disabilities and the elderly were aware of the adjustments  made to the programme and how they could share their feedback.
As a co-lead of the United Nations Gender Working Group, WFP supported the development of policy proposals to address the gendered impacts of COVID-19.
Continuous monitoring and evaluation was crucial to ensuring robust programming. As such, WFP ensured continuous monitoring of its programmes throughout the year. Remote monitoring was carried out for areas that were inaccessible due to the COVID-19 measures. title: Somalia Crisis 2022 - NRC Humanitarian Country programmes 2021-2025
description:
NRC has applied as well to Sida for funding of 364.5 million SEK to carry out “the Humanitarian Programme for 2021” in 26 humanitarian crisis settings: Afghanistan, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Iran, Iraq, Jordan, Kenya, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Honduras, El Salvador, Mexico, Palestine, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Tanzania/Burundi, Uganda, Venezuela, Yemen. The application includes provision of 40 million SEK to replenish the Rapid Response Mechanism funding instrument and 7 individual projects for method, capacity-building and coordination.
The intervention’s tentative total budget is 4 263 200 000 Norwegian krona (NOK), that the organisation is financing with Sida’s funding in a proportion of 8% approximately. Other donors, like the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, DG ECHO, UNHCR, etc. are the largest contributors, besides a dozen of other donors in agreement with NRC. Sida provides NRC with the opportunity to allocate resources flexibly within individual country programmes (Programme-Based Approach – PBA).
NRC's catalytic support for coordination and capacity building contributes greatly to the link between humanitarian aid, development and peace. NRC's advocacy work and activities enable, at least contribute to, sustainable solutions for refugees and displaced people in a significant way in cooperation with other actors. In the long run, the NRC will reduce humanitarian needs. The NRC prioritizes self-sufficiency in its programs. The NRC's analysis capability, not least through its Internal Displacement Monitoring Center (IDMC), is an advantage for relevant programming according to the nexus orientations. Among the 26 crises in NRC's portfolio that Sida prioritizes, there are 15 where Sida implements Sweden's development strategies in synergy with humanitarian aid.
Sida’s contribution to NRC for 2022 will cover around 6.5% of NRC’s total financial requirements of the supported programmes and projects. It will provides humanitarian services to almost 9 million persons (53% female). HUM adds 50 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Ukraine benefiting 90,000 people with protection, shelter, WaSH and cash assistance. Decision 5 April. Amendment nr. 5.
HUM adds 7.5 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Cameroon from the 2022 mid-year allocation (food security, legal advice for 600 households/4200 individuals in Logone-et-Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga). Decision 9 June 2022. Contract amendment No 6.
HUM adds 10 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in South Sudan from the end-of-the-year allocation. Decision 16 November 2022 nr 2022-002341. Contract amendment No 7.
NRC targets 7.7 million unique beneficiaries in total within Sida-funded humanitarian programmes in 2023, (52% female), who will receive protection and humanitarian services from NRC: Education, WASH, Shelter and settlement, Food security and livelihoods, including multi-purpose cash assistance, Protection, Legal assistance, Humanitarian mediation (community-based peace-building). Advocacy and support to humanitarian coordination and durable solution to displacements working groups in the field are part of NRC's engagement that Sida is funding. NRC's annual budget 2023 in the settings and thematics prioritized by Sida amounts to 5620 million Norwegian crowns in total. Sida's share weighs so far 8% of it: NRC's third largest donor whose cumulated 2021-2025 grant is 80% softly earmarked (programme-based approach) and 34% multi-year.
Earlier granted multi-year funding for 2023 was disbursed in January (52 MSEK) in support to continued humanitarian operations in DR Congo, Mali and Nigeria with strong emphasis on emergency response. | Norwegian Refugee Council - Norska flyktingrådet (NRC) - har ansökt om ett förnyat partnerskap med Sida 2021-2025.

2021
NRC har dessutom ansökt om finansiering på 364,5 miljoner SEK för att genomföra humanitära insatser i 26 humanitära krisområden under 2021: Afghanistan, Kamerun, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia, Ecuador, Panama, Demokratiska Republiken Kongo, Eritrea, Etiopien, Iran, Irak, Jordanien, Kenya, Libanon, Libyen, Mali, Niger, Nigeria, Honduras, El Salvador, Mexiko, Palestina, Somalia, Sydsudan, Sudan, Tanzania / Burundi, Uganda, Venezuela och Jemen. Ansökan inkluderar även 40 miljoner kronor för den humanitära snabbmekanismen (RRM) och 20 miljoner kronor i stöd till sju projekt för metodstöd, kapacitetsuppbyggnad och samordning.

Den aktuella budgeten för NRC:s hela humanitära program 2021 uppgår till 4 263 200 000 NOK, varav Sidas del för närvarande utgör ca 8%. Sida ger NRC möjligheten att nyttja resurser flexibelt inom varje enskilt landprogram, (enligt så kallad Programme-Based Approach – PBA)

Humanitär-Utveckling-Fred Nexus
NRC bidrar i hög grad till arbetet för att sammankoppla humanitärt bistånd med freds- och utvecklingsinsatser. Organisationens strävan att effektivisera biståndet genom katalytiskt stöd till samordning och kapacitetsbyggande insatser bidrar till denna ansats. I samarbetet med andra organisationer möjliggör och bidrar NRC:s verksamhet och påverkansarbete till att stärka hållbara lösningar för flyktingar och människor som har blivit tvångsfördrivna och bidrar därmed till att på sikt minska de humanitära behoven. Även krisdrabbade människors möjligheter till självförsörjning prioriteras. NRC:s analyskapacitet är en styrka som bidrar till att programmeringen anpassas till en nexus-ansats och den analys som genomförs av NRC:s internationella center för övervakning av tvångsförflyttning (IDMC) är av stor vikt för dessa analyser. 19 av de 26 kriser i NRC:s portfölj som Sida finansierar avser länder där Sverige även bedriver utvecklingssamarbete vilket öppnar för möjligheter till synergier med humanitärt bistånd.

2022
NRC ska få totalt 455,5 miljoner kronor av Sidas humanitära finansiering, enligt följande fördelning:

- Sida kommer att stödja NRC:s humanitära program i 23 krissituationer som Sida har prioriterat genom sin behovsbaserade allokeringsmodell för 2022, med 288,5 miljoner kronor :Afghanistan, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia och
regionen (Ecuador, Panamà), Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Etiopien, Irak, Jemen,
Jordanien, Kamerun, Kenya, Libanon, Libyen, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Nigeria,
Palestina, Somalia, Sudan, Sydsudan, Syrien, Uganda, Venezuela.

- Flerårig finansiering för NRC :s humanitära program i Demokratiska
republiken Kongo, Mali och Nigeria inleds 2022 och Sida har för ändamålet att ta i anspråk 104 miljoner kronor från kommande års anslag från erhållen Bemyndiganderam förutsatt att Riksdagen anvisar tillräckliga medel.

- NRC:s akuta insatser vid plötsligt uppkomna kriser kommer att stödjas genom Sidas snabbinsatsmekanism (RRM) under 2022 med 50 miljoner kronor.

- NRC:s metod- och kapacitetsstärkande projekt för skydd, miljö och IDMC (Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre) kommer under 2022 att få 13 miljoner kronor, varav 3 miljoner kronor från Sida/Globen för IDMC.

Sidas bidrag till NRC för 2022 kommer att täcka cirka 6,5 % av NRC:s totala finansiella behov för de stödda programmen och projekten. Det kommer att tillhandahålla humanitära tjänster till nästan 9 miljoner människor (53 % kvinnor) i Afghanistan, Kamerun, Centralafrikanska republiken, Colombia och regionen, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Etiopien, Irak, Jordanien, Kenya, Libanon, Libyen, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Nigeria, Palestina, Somalia, Sydsudan, Sudan, Syrien, Uganda, Venezuela och Jemen.

HUM lägger till 50 MSEK för NRC:s landprogram 2022 i Ukraina som gynnar 90,000 människor med skydd, tak över huvudet, WaSH samt kontantbistånd. Beslut 5 April. Avtalförändring nr 5.

HUM lägger till 7,5 MSEK för NRC:s landprogram 2022 i Kamerun från halvsårsanslaget 2022 (livsmedelsförsörjning, juridik rådgivning för 600 husshållen/4200 individer i Logone-et-Chari, Mayo Sava och Mayo Tsanaga). Beslut 9 juni 2022. Avtalförändring nr 6.

HUM lägger till 10 MSEK för NRC:s landprogram 2022 i Sydsudan från slutsåranslaget. Beslut 16 november 2022, 2022-002341. Avtalförändring nr 7.

2023
NRC får totalt 659.5 miljoner kronor (2023-2025) av Sidas humanitära finansiering för att genomföra:
-  humanitära insatser i 23
krisområden under 2023: Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Burkina Faso, Centralafrikanska
republiken, Colombia, Demokratiska republiken Kongo, Etiopien, Irak, Jemen,
Jordanien, Kamerun, Kenya, Libanon, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Palestina, Sudan,
Sydsudan, Syrien, Uganda, Ukraina och Venezuela. 
NRC har dessutom ansökt om 244
miljoner kronor för att kunna fortsätta sina humanitära program i Jemen, Kamerun,
Sydsudan, Syria och Venezuela under 2024 och 2025.
- ansökan inkluderar även 50
miljoner kronor till den humanitära snabbinsatsmekanismen (RRM) 
- och 40 miljoner kronor i stöd till fyra fleråriga projekt för metodstöd och kapacitetsuppbyggnad: Miljö, Skydd, Tillträde, IDMC (18,5 under 2023, 21,5 under 2024-2025). | Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) is Norway's largest international humanitarian organisation and widely recognized as a leading field-based displacement agency within the international humanitarian community. NRC is the INGO receiving the largest contribution from Sida's Humanitarian Unit to INGOs so far, based on experience of successful partnerships, NRC's capacities to respond at scale and its coverage of crises that Sida is prioritizing through the needs-based allocation approach. NRC receives approximately 8% of Sida's humanitarian unit's annual budget appropriation.

The objectives of NRC can be summarized as follows: "To protect the rights of displaced and vulnerable people during crisis, to provide assistance meeting their immediate humanitarian needs, to prevent further displacement and to contribute to durable solutions, and to provide expertise as a strategic partner to humanitarian systems and actors."  NRCs main activity is delivery of humanitarian assistance through programme activities in the field. NRC specializes in six areas of expertise, or "core competencies": shelter and settlements; livelihoods and food security; information, counselling and legal assistance (ICLA); education; camp management; and water, sanitation and hygiene promotion (WASH). Protection is lifted up as a new core competency of NRC since 2021. NRC engages closely with the affected populations to understand their needs and capacities, ensuring it tailors its assistance accordingly and involve them in the entire programme cycle, from design through implementation to evaluation. NRC advocates for respect for the rights of displaced and vulnerable people.

In 2021, the NRC Board approved the Global Strategy 20222025. The strategy
sets out four sub-objectives for areas that NRC will continue to strengthen and further institutionalize, namely, 1. assistance to hard-to-reach populations, 2. humanitarian policy, 3. protection, and 4. durable solutions. It also points to four areas of work that will be accelerated through expanded engagement and investments: i) advocacy, ii) climate and environment, iii) collaboration with  local actors, and iv) quality programming.

NRCs work is divided into three pillars: humanitarian assistance, advocacy and expert deployment. Sida's Humanitarian Unit funding will continue prioritizing mainly the first pillar through funding of the humanitarian country programmes in line with HRPs and the RRPs and through the RRM funding. To some extent, Sida will support as well the second pillar of advocacy which is integrated in the humanitarian country programmes and implemented by NRC's method, thematic and capacity development projects supported by Sida. Sida will provide NRC with only a punctual support to the third pillar, through funding to CashCap which is deploying experts to the field for invigorating cash assistance working groups (17 in 2020 to 16 countries).

The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) has applied for a renewed strategic partnership with Sida during 2021-2025.

The interventions tentative total budget is 4 263 200 000 Norwegian krona (NOK), that the organisation is financing with Sidas funding in a proportion of 8% approximately. Other donors, like the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, DG ECHO, UNHCR, etc. are the largest contributors, besides a dozen of other donors in agreement with NRC. Sida provides NRC with the opportunity to allocate resources flexibly within individual country programmes (Programme-Based Approach  PBA).

NRC was granted funding to carry out the Humanitarian Programme for 2022 in 24 humanitarian crisis settings: Afghanistan, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Colombia, DR Congo, Ethiopia, Irak, Jordan,  Kenya, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Nigeria, Palestine, Somalia, Sudan, South Sudan, Syria, Uganda, Ukraina, Venezuela and Yemen. The grant includes provision of funding replenish the Rapid Response Mechanism funding instrument and four individual projects for method, capacity-building and coordination.


Sida's assessment on performance and results

Alike many other actors in the sector, NRC excels in reporting activities and outputs, but should be better in catching what changes and impacts its interventions have resulted to ultimately on assisted communities. The reporting of data and results does not provide necessarily an accurate and consolidated overview of what NRC has achieved. Sida has notified NRC that it should provide dis-aggregated data by age in targeting and reporting which is a norm.

It is assumed that NRC will achieve its objectives in 2023 again, but the global stress on the current resource mobilisation system supporting humanitarian action may affect NRC as well, similarly to large humanitarian actors such as the ICRC.

HUM adds 7.5 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in Cameroon from the 2022 mid-year allocation (food security, legal advice for 600 households/4200 individuals in Logone-et-Chari, Mayo Sava and Mayo Tsanaga). Decision 9 June 2022. Contract amendment No 6.
HUM adds 10 MSEK for NRC's 2022 country programme in South Sudan from the end-of-the-year allocation. Decision 16 November 2022 nr 2022-002341. Contract amendment No 7.
NRC targets 7.7 million unique beneficiaries in total within Sida-funded humanitarian programmes in 2023, (52% female), who will receive protection and humanitarian services from NRC: Education, WASH, Shelter and settlement, Food security and livelihoods, including multi-purpose cash assistance, Protection, Legal assistance, Humanitarian mediation (community-based peace-building). Advocacy and support to humanitarian coordination and durable solution to displacements working groups in the field are part of NRC's engagement that Sida is funding. NRC's annual budget 2023 in the settings and thematics prioritized by Sida amounts to 5620 million Norwegian crowns in total. Sida's share weighs so far 8% of it: NRC's third largest donor whose cumulated 2021-2025 grant is 80% softly earmarked (programme-based approach) and 34% multi-year.
Earlier granted multi-year funding for 2023 was disbursed in January (52 MSEK) in support to continued humanitarian operations in DR Congo, Mali and Nigeria with strong emphasis on emergency response. | Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) is Norway's largest international humanitarian organisation and widely recognized as a leading field-based displacement agency within the international humanitarian community. NRC is the INGO receiving the largest contribution from Sida's Humanitarian Unit to INGOs so far, based on experience of successful partnerships, NRC's capacities to respond at scale and its coverage of crises that Sida is prioritizing through the needs-based allocation approach. NRC receives approximately 8% of Sida's humanitarian unit's annual budget appropriation.

The objectives of NRC can be summarized as follows: "To protect the rights of displaced and vulnerable people during crisis, to provide assistance meeting their immediate humanitarian needs, to prevent further displacement and to contribute to durable solutions, and to provide expertise as a strategic partner to humanitarian systems and actors."  NRCs main activity is delivery of humanitarian assistance through programme activities in the field. NRC specializes in six areas of expertise, or "core competencies": shelter and settlements; livelihoods and food security; information, counselling and legal assistance (ICLA); education; camp management; and water, sanitation and hygiene promotion (WASH). Protection is lifted up as a new core competency of NRC since 2021. NRC engages closely with the affected populations to understand their needs and capacities, ensuring it tailors its assistance accordingly and involve them in the entire programme cycle, from design through implementation to evaluation. NRC advocates for respect for the rights of displaced and vulnerable people.

In 2021, the NRC Board approved the Global Strategy 20222025. The strategy
sets out four sub-objectives for areas that NRC will continue to strengthen and further institutionalize, namely, 1. assistance to hard-to-reach populations, 2. humanitarian policy, 3. protection, and 4. durable solutions. It also points to four areas of work that will be accelerated through expanded engagement and investments: i) advocacy, ii) climate and environment, iii) collaboration with  local actors, and iv) quality programming.

NRCs work is divided into three pillars: humanitarian assistance, advocacy and expert deployment. Sida's Humanitarian Unit funding will continue prioritizing mainly the first pillar through funding of the humanitarian country programmes in line with HRPs and the RRPs and through the RRM funding. To some extent, Sida will support as well the second pillar of advocacy which is integrated in the humanitarian country programmes and implemented by NRC's method, thematic and capacity development projects supported by Sida. Sida will provide NRC with only a punctual support to the third pillar, through funding to CashCap which is deploying experts to the field for invigorating cash assistance working groups (17 in 2020 to 16 countries).

The Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) has applied for a renewed strategic partnership with Sida during 2021-2025.

The interventions tentative total budget is 4 263 200 000 Norwegian krona (NOK), that the organisation is financing with Sidas funding in a proportion of 8% approximately. Other donors, like the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, DG ECHO, UNHCR, etc. are the largest contributors, besides a dozen of other donors in agreement with NRC. Sida provides NRC with the opportunity to allocate resources flexibly within individual country programmes (Programme-Based Approach  PBA).

NRC was granted funding to carry out the Humanitarian Programme for 2022 in 24 humanitarian crisis settings: Afghanistan, Cameroon, Central African Republic, Colombia, DR Congo, Ethiopia, Irak, Jordan,  Kenya, Lebanon, Libya, Mali, Moçambique, Niger, Nigeria, Palestine, Somalia, Sudan, South Sudan, Syria, Uganda, Ukraina, Venezuela and Yemen. The grant includes provision of funding replenish the Rapid Response Mechanism funding instrument and four individual projects for method, capacity-building and coordination.


Sida's assessment on performance and results

Alike many other actors in the sector, NRC excels in reporting activities and outputs, but should be better in catching what changes and impacts its interventions have resulted to ultimately on assisted communities. The reporting of data and results does not provide necessarily an accurate and consolidated overview of what NRC has achieved. Sida has notified NRC that it should provide dis-aggregated data by age in targeting and reporting which is a norm.

It is assumed that NRC will achieve its objectives in 2023 again, but the global stress on the current resource mobilisation system supporting humanitarian action may affect NRC as well, similarly to large humanitarian actors such as the ICRC.

title: DRC HUM 2022-2025
description:
Founded in 1956, Danish Refugee Council (DRC) is a well-established non-profit organisation currently operating in 40 countries.

DRC works to support refugees and displaced people, protect, and safeguard their rights and empowering them towards a better future, to realise DRC’s vision for a dignified life for all displaced. As a self-mandated protection agency, protection is at the core of DRC’s vision, mission, and operational and programmatic approach. Key commitments to a rights-based approach and adherence to the Humanitarian Principles underpin DRC’s work. DRC’s is working in five core sectors: Protection, Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM), Shelter and Settlements, Humanitarian Disarmament and Peacebuilding (HDP) and Economic Recovery. | Humanitära enheten kommer under 2022 att ge stöd till Danska flyktingkommittén (DRC). DRC grundades 1956 och är en väletablerad organisation som för närvarande arbetar i 40 länder.
DRC arbetar med flyktingar och människor som befinner sig på flykt med fokus på skydd och rättigheter. Skyddsfrågan är kärnan i DRCs vision, uppdrag och operativa verksamhet. Rättighetsperspektivet och efterlevnad av de humanitära principerna ligger till grund för DRCs arbete. DRC:s arbetar inom dessa sektorer: skydd, bosättningar, humanitär nedrustning, fredsbyggande och ekonomisk återhämtning. | This contribution aims to support DRC in selected humanitarian crisis where DRC will implement specific projects and where the organisation has a clear added value to provide humanitarian assistance and protection to crisis affected populations. In most emergencies DRC works with a combination of two or more of the following sectors:
• Protection
• Shelter and Infrastructure
• NFI distribution
• Food security
• WASH
• Camp Management and Camp Coordination (CCCM)
• Humanitarian Mine Action

Sida's humanitarian assistance to DRC 2025

Based on Sida's humanitarian needs based allocation process in late 2024, additional funds were added to DRC in 2025, which is the 4th year of the current multiyear Agreement. In October 2025, additional funds were added as part of the End of Year Allocation. 

For 2025, the following support is proposed for DRC:

- Annual Projects/Programmes in line with Humanitarian Response Plans (usually 12 months) - 139 MSEK (where support to Yemen has been deducted and Cameroon and Ethiopia has been added in comparison to DRC's contextual portfolio for 2024. In October 2025, support was added to the Gaza crisis response)

- Rapid Response Mechanism- 15 MSEK (of which 5 MSEK were added as a top-up in October 2025) 

- Method Development and Capacity Building- 4 MSEK

- End of agreement evaluation 650 000 SEK

Of note is that for 2025, the initial contribution to DRC in 2025 amounted to 492 750 000 SEK, with 146 650 000 SEK allocated in 2025.  With the addition of 12 000 000 SEK as End of Year Allocation, the total contribution to DRC in 2025 amounts now to 504 750 000 SEK and for 2025, 158 650 000 SEK subject to Parliamentary appropriations.

Geographical support:

1. Burkina Faso PBA (10 MSEK): DRC has expertise in protection responses and leads the protection component of the RRM Frontline. Burkina Faso has been one of the pilot countries for the Sida funded Improved Access of the HardtoReach. DRC will focus on Boucle du Mouhoun and Nord regions in response to identified protection risks (including GBV) in partnership with local actors.

2. Cameroon (10 MSEK): In its initial submission for 2025 DRC requested 10 MSEK to provide timely and efficient multisectoral emergency response to newly displaced households in all seven divisions of the NW region many of which face significant access challenges and are hence underserved by aid actors, leaving gaps in food, protection, and shelter/NFI assistance through equitable partnerships with local civil society organisations based on strengthening their
technical, organisational and operational capacities. DRC proposes to build the capacity of 6 selected CSOs in the NW (25 per cent of funds) and partner with up to two CSO:s to deliver emergency support for displacement response (55 per cent of funds), ensuring interventions are grounded in local knowledge and community trust. In 2024, DRC was the largest humanitarian NGO in Cameroon with 8.6 per cent of total funding.

3. Colombia (9 MSEK): DRC delivers integrated protection and emergency assistance responding to humanitarian needs of the crisis affected population in Nariño and Norte de Santander departments. DRC will provide immediate protection, legal and case management, basic needs assistance, while strengthening protective environments through community based
interventions and awareness raising activities.

4. Ethiopia PBA (13 MSEK): DRC coleads the protection cluster, and plans to deliver protection centred and integrated multisectoral humanitarian assistance to refugees, IDPs returnees, and host communities affected by climate change and conflict, particularly in hardtoreach and underserved areas in Somali, Gambella, Afar, Tigray Regions and contested areas. DRC is one of four INGOs accredited in Ethiopia to work on humanitarian mine action, a key precondition for recovery. DRC serves as the administrative channel for Sidas support to the Humanitarian International NGO Forum (HINGO), which is a critical balance to the UN led Humanitarian Country Team (HCT). HINGO reinforces coordination and advocates on behalf of the NGO collective in Ethiopia on IHL, humanitarian principles and access.

5. Kenya PBA (5 MSEK): DRC will respond to humanitarian needs in refugee and hosting communities by providing emergency life saving needs in response to flooding and drought. DRC will provide support in Dadaab and Kakuma/ Kalobeyei as well as to the emergency preparedness and response to address the food security, WASH and protection needs of refugees and vulnerable persons in Garissa, Mandera, Wajir, Marsabit and Turkana counties where DRC is the leading protection actor. DRC has a s strong programmatic emphasis on
protection in both refugee camps, marginalized and hard to reach areas, providing protection case management services in the refugee camps and working with community-based protection mechanisms to support at risk individuals and survivors of violence.

6. Myanmar (11 MSEK): DRC operations seek to improve community protection capacities, physical safety, psychosocial wellbeing and food security for conflict affected people through the delivery of multisectoral assistance. DRC operate in hardtoreach locations in Sagaing, Kachin, and Northern Shan State. The added value of DRC is its strong Protection focus in hardtoreach
areas that incorporate elements of explosive ordnance risk education.

7. Somalia PBA (30 MSEK): DRC has been in the forefront of developing the humanitarian assistance regarding for example the integrated response framework, strengthening coordination efforts, and moving to vulnerability based targeting. Sida assess DRC to be a strong actor in Somalia and thus suggest to provide DRC Somalia with programme based
funding in 2025. DRCs overall objective is to support vulnerable IDP households (HHs) and communities affected by conflict and natural disasters to meet lifesaving basic needs. Sectorial focus is put on CCCM, protection, WASH, shelter/NFI, emergency response and economic recovery. DRC works in various parts of the country, with a strong focus on areas identified as those with highest level of needs in the HNRP.

8. Sudan PBA (28 MSEK): DRC will implement its programme in Central Darfur, Khartoum, South Darfur, South Kordofan, Gedaref, White Nile, and Red Sea, states that have either been among the most conflict affected or that have been the destination of newly displaced persons. DRC has a protection centred approach and is working to ensure that people in hardtoreach areas also can
receive protection, partly through local grassroots organisations. By putting protection at the centre and by having a clear ambition to reach areas affected by conflict, DRC is a relevant partner for Sidas humanitarian allocation to Sudan.

9. Ukraine (15 MSEK): DRC has a particular focus on hardtoreach areas where they seek to address the most acute basic needs and protection gaps though locally driven responses. Through their country program DRC, together with their partners, will facilitate improved access to services through tailored shelter solutions, cash assistance, legal advice, mobile protection support, psychosocial support and mine risk education.

10. Gaza (7 MSEK): Together with local partners, DRC will provide support to people in Gaza city as well as people en route southwards and in reception areas. The work will focus on distribution of basic needs items, improving living conditions in camps, and providing protection services such as psychosocial support and explosive ordnance risk education. Already working with the Gaza crisis response, DRC has communicated a need for additional funding in order to scale up the response for the remainder of 2025. 

Rapid Response Mechanism: 
- RRM (15 MSEK): Part of the annual humanitarian budget is set aside for sudden humanitarian crises and deterioration of ongoing crises. For these situations, Sida has a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with partner organizations that makes it possible to fund lifesaving responses
worldwide within 24 hours. DRC is applying for RRM funding which has both predisaster
and postdisaster objectives. DRC has as growing experience in proactive humanitarian interventions and at the end of 2024 had nine ongoing proactive interventions ahead of conflict and climate related displacement. DRC has submitted its new Anticipatory Action (AA) Policy 20252030 and an Early Action Protocol Template.

Method and capacity building support

- Advancing Preventive and Responsive Capacity and Joint Action for Quality Protection Outcomes (4 MSEK): DRC aims to further advance and strengthen DRC's and local actors capacity to prevent and respond to protection risks that crisis affected people face, thereby strengthening protection outcomes for crisis affected people at risk of violence, coercion, and deliberate deprivation.

Evaluation

- End of agreement evaluation (650 000 SEK): as 2025 is the final year for DRC's multiyear agreement, an end of agreement evaluation will be conducted to assess the overall achievements will be carried out.

results_text:
Results achieved | Uppnådda resultat | Results in 2024 (based on DRC's narrative annual report 2024)

In 2024, DRC implemented crisis response projects in 8 countries: Burkina Faso, Colombia, Kenya, Myanmar, Somalia, Sudan, Ukraine and Yemen supported by the Sida Humanitarian Partnership Agreement. All allocations were 12 months.

The crisis response projects reached a total of 559,660 conflict affected people, the PBA country programmes supported more than 976,188 and the Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) 76,025. All in all, a total of 1,611,873 people (of which 941,027 female). If the number of conflict affected people reached with PBA funding is calculated as the percentage of Sidas contribution to the country (and in the case of Burkina Faso the Boucle du Mouhoun area) programme the total number of conflict affected people reached by the Sida project, PBA and RRM funding is 744,918 ( of which 477,617 female).

For the RRM, DRC received and used almost the total 16,5 MSEK to address severe humanitarian needs. The RRM was used to save lives, alleviate suffering, and uphold human dignity for those affected by conflict (Mali and DR Congo), natural disasters (Burundi and Bangladesh), and the mpox health crisis (Uganda, DR Congo and Burundi).  Both RRM responses in Burundi, the Bangladesh RRM response and the RRM response in Goma, DR Congo used cash as modality. The RRM allocation transferred a total of SEK 5,601,639 as cash.

The DRC core sectors covered were Protection, Economic Recovery (includes food security, financial inclusion and decent livelihoods), Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM), Shelter and Settlements (includes emergency shelter and NFIs), Humanitarian Disarmament and Peacebuilding (HDP, includes the subsectors of mine actions, weapons and ammunitions management, conflict management and security governance) and Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH). In addition, DRC Ukraine, Sudan and Burkina Faso operated with a basic needs sector category. The Somalia response and the Sudan country programme were the only responses with activities in the CCCM sector.

A country level example is the use of Sida's funding in Sudan.

When DRC designated Sudan an organizational Priority Emergency in October 2024, the flexibility in Sida's grant allowed the team to fund its core emergency activities through the PBA, while utilizing organizational funds to develop responses to structural challenges in key areas of operations. These included addressing liquidity concerns through developing voucher programs, payments systems through blockchain and supporting the development of supply lines for
local Ready to Use Supplementary Food (RUSF) substitutes. The effects of these investments will be seen most acutely in the 2025 lean season when the next peak of the famine hits in Darfur, a situation that will be exacerbated by the cuts to USAID. At this point, local payment systems and production will be critical to fill the gaps left by cuts to traditional aid. Thus, with Sida PBA funding support, 13,860 famine affected beneficiaries received cash assistance, as well as 298
households of severe acute malnutrition (SAM) referrals. Finally, 48,521 beneficiaries in DRC run sites received an integrated package of WASH, protection, and food security assistance. These adaptations towards famine mitigation, coupled with the lessons learnt, provide the foundation for DRCs 2025 Sida PBA strategy as the famine worsens. Finally, across the operation as a whole 733,858 beneficiaries (344,915 men and 388,943 women) were reached in what is the worlds largest and most severe humanitarian crisis in a generation. | Not applicable | No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published | Amended and Restated Grant Agreement between Sida and_Danish Refugee Council Hum Support 2022-2025 | 2023-000562 Beslut om ändring av insats Danish Refugee Council 2023.pdf

title: Sustainable Urban Economic Development (SUED) Programme
description: Sustainable Urban Economic Development (SUED) is a £60m, five-year programme (2018 – 2022) aiming to create climate resilient, inclusive urban economic growth in 10 fast growing municipalities in Kenya. This shall be achieved by: - Supporting municipalities to develop sustainable urban economic plans. - Providing capacity building for the municipality, county (if applicable) and the local private sector. - Improve the investment climate and business environment reforms. - Draw in investments for critical climate-resilient infrastructure and value chain projects. - Providing up to £30m in seed funding (to lower the risk of investments). Coffey's current contract value is £50m. £5m of that goes directly to Coffey, up to £30m are foreseen for seedfunding. The rest goes to subcontractors. The M&E firm and IFC hold £10m. DFID therefore refers to it as a £60m programme. The main programme objectives are to: - Create climate resilient jobs and raised incomes. - Strengthen capacity of municipalities to manage the develop projects beyond the project funding. - Support policy and legislative changes to enable greater private sector led growth. - Raise investment for critical bankable, climate-resilient infrastructure and value chain projects. - Improve rural links with larger markets that were previously difficult to access.

DRC works to support refugees and displaced people, protect, and safeguard their rights and empowering them towards a better future, to realise DRC’s vision for a dignified life for all displaced. As a self-mandated protection agency, protection is at the core of DRC’s vision, mission, and operational and programmatic approach. Key commitments to a rights-based approach and adherence to the Humanitarian Principles underpin DRC’s work. DRC’s is working in five core sectors: Protection, Camp Coordination and Camp Management (CCCM), Shelter and Settlements, Humanitarian Disarmament and Peacebuilding (HDP) and Economic Recovery. | This contribution aims to support DRC in selected humanitarian crisis where DRC will implement specific projects and where the organisation has a clear added value to provide humanitarian assistance and protection to crisis affected populations. • Protection
• Shelter and Infrastructure
• NFI distribution
• Food security
• WASH
• Camp Management and Camp Coordination (CCCM)
• Humanitarian Mine Action

Sida's humanitarian assistance to DRC 2025

Based on Sida's humanitarian needs based allocation process in late 2024, additional funds were added to DRC in 2025, which is the 4th year of the current multiyear Agreement. In October 2025, additional funds were added as part of the End of Year Allocation. 

For 2025, the following support is proposed for DRC:

- Annual Projects/Programmes in line with Humanitarian Response Plans (usually 12 months) - 139 MSEK (where support to Yemen has been deducted and Cameroon and Ethiopia has been added in comparison to DRC's contextual portfolio for 2024. In October 2025, support was added to the Gaza crisis response)

- Rapid Response Mechanism- 15 MSEK (of which 5 MSEK were added as a top-up in October 2025) 

- Method Development and Capacity Building- 4 MSEK

- End of agreement evaluation 650 000 SEK

Of note is that for 2025, the initial contribution to DRC in 2025 amounted to 492 750 000 SEK, with 146 650 000 SEK allocated in 2025.  With the addition of 12 000 000 SEK as End of Year Allocation, the total contribution to DRC in 2025 amounts now to 504 750 000 SEK and for 2025, 158 650 000 SEK subject to Parliamentary appropriations.

Geographical support:

1. Burkina Faso PBA (10 MSEK): DRC has expertise in protection responses and leads the protection component of the RRM Frontline. Burkina Faso has been one of the pilot countries for the Sida funded Improved Access of the HardtoReach. DRC will focus on Boucle du Mouhoun and Nord regions in response to identified protection risks (including GBV) in partnership with local actors.

2. Cameroon (10 MSEK): In its initial submission for 2025 DRC requested 10 MSEK to provide timely and efficient multisectoral emergency response to newly displaced households in all seven divisions of the NW region many of which face significant access challenges and are hence underserved by aid actors, leaving gaps in food, protection, and shelter/NFI assistance through equitable partnerships with local civil society organisations based on strengthening their
technical, organisational and operational capacities. DRC proposes to build the capacity of 6 selected CSOs in the NW (25 per cent of funds) and partner with up to two CSO:s to deliver emergency support for displacement response (55 per cent of funds), ensuring interventions are grounded in local knowledge and community trust. In 2024, DRC was the largest humanitarian NGO in Cameroon with 8.6 per cent of total funding.

3. Colombia (9 MSEK): DRC delivers integrated protection and emergency assistance responding to humanitarian needs of the crisis affected population in Nariño and Norte de Santander departments. DRC will provide immediate protection, legal and case management, basic needs assistance, while strengthening protective environments through community based
interventions and awareness raising activities.

4. Ethiopia PBA (13 MSEK): DRC coleads the protection cluster, and plans to deliver protection centred and integrated multisectoral humanitarian assistance to refugees, IDPs returnees, and host communities affected by climate change and conflict, particularly in hardtoreach and underserved areas in Somali, Gambella, Afar, Tigray Regions and contested areas. DRC is one of four INGOs accredited in Ethiopia to work on humanitarian mine action, a key precondition for recovery. DRC serves as the administrative channel for Sidas support to the Humanitarian International NGO Forum (HINGO), which is a critical balance to the UN led Humanitarian Country Team (HCT). HINGO reinforces coordination and advocates on behalf of the NGO collective in Ethiopia on IHL, humanitarian principles and access.

5. Kenya PBA (5 MSEK): DRC will respond to humanitarian needs in refugee and hosting communities by providing emergency life saving needs in response to flooding and drought. DRC will provide support in Dadaab and Kakuma/ Kalobeyei as well as to the emergency preparedness and response to address the food security, WASH and protection needs of refugees and vulnerable persons in Garissa, Mandera, Wajir, Marsabit and Turkana counties where DRC is the leading protection actor. DRC has a s strong programmatic emphasis on
protection in both refugee camps, marginalized and hard to reach areas, providing protection case management services in the refugee camps and working with community-based protection mechanisms to support at risk individuals and survivors of violence.

6. Myanmar (11 MSEK): DRC operations seek to improve community protection capacities, physical safety, psychosocial wellbeing and food security for conflict affected people through the delivery of multisectoral assistance. DRC operate in hardtoreach locations in Sagaing, Kachin, and Northern Shan State. The added value of DRC is its strong Protection focus in hardtoreach
areas that incorporate elements of explosive ordnance risk education.

7. Somalia PBA (30 MSEK): DRC has been in the forefront of developing the humanitarian assistance regarding for example the integrated response framework, strengthening coordination efforts, and moving to vulnerability based targeting. Sida assess DRC to be a strong actor in Somalia and thus suggest to provide DRC Somalia with programme based
funding in 2025. DRCs overall objective is to support vulnerable IDP households (HHs) and communities affected by conflict and natural disasters to meet lifesaving basic needs. Sectorial focus is put on CCCM, protection, WASH, shelter/NFI, emergency response and economic recovery. DRC works in various parts of the country, with a strong focus on areas identified as those with highest level of needs in the HNRP.

8. Sudan PBA (28 MSEK): DRC will implement its programme in Central Darfur, Khartoum, South Darfur, South Kordofan, Gedaref, White Nile, and Red Sea, states that have either been among the most conflict affected or that have been the destination of newly displaced persons. DRC has a protection centred approach and is working to ensure that people in hardtoreach areas also can
receive protection, partly through local grassroots organisations. By putting protection at the centre and by having a clear ambition to reach areas affected by conflict, DRC is a relevant partner for Sidas humanitarian allocation to Sudan.

9. Ukraine (15 MSEK): DRC has a particular focus on hardtoreach areas where they seek to address the most acute basic needs and protection gaps though locally driven responses. Through their country program DRC, together with their partners, will facilitate improved access to services through tailored shelter solutions, cash assistance, legal advice, mobile protection support, psychosocial support and mine risk education.

10. Gaza (7 MSEK): Together with local partners, DRC will provide support to people in Gaza city as well as people en route southwards and in reception areas. The work will focus on distribution of basic needs items, improving living conditions in camps, and providing protection services such as psychosocial support and explosive ordnance risk education. Already working with the Gaza crisis response, DRC has communicated a need for additional funding in order to scale up the response for the remainder of 2025. 

Rapid Response Mechanism: 
- RRM (15 MSEK): Part of the annual humanitarian budget is set aside for sudden humanitarian crises and deterioration of ongoing crises. For these situations, Sida has a Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM) with partner organizations that makes it possible to fund lifesaving responses
worldwide within 24 hours. DRC is applying for RRM funding which has both predisaster
and postdisaster objectives. DRC has as growing experience in proactive humanitarian interventions and at the end of 2024 had nine ongoing proactive interventions ahead of conflict and climate related displacement. DRC has submitted its new Anticipatory Action (AA) Policy 20252030 and an Early Action Protocol Template.

Method and capacity building support

- Advancing Preventive and Responsive Capacity and Joint Action for Quality Protection Outcomes (4 MSEK): DRC aims to further advance and strengthen DRC's and local actors capacity to prevent and respond to protection risks that crisis affected people face, thereby strengthening protection outcomes for crisis affected people at risk of violence, coercion, and deliberate deprivation.

Evaluation

- End of agreement evaluation (650 000 SEK): as 2025 is the final year for DRC's multiyear agreement, an end of agreement evaluation will be conducted to assess the overall achievements will be carried out.

title: Judiciary Support through IDLO
description:
The overall goal of the project is to contribute to the efforts of ensuring that citizens of Isiolo and Marsabit counties benefit from inclusive and participatory county governance development processes. | The projects interventions will be focused on the North Frontier counties of Isiolo and Marsabit. Despite the goodwill of the Constitution to reduce the levels of marginalisation across Kenya, the residents of Isiolo and Marsabit counties still live on the periphery of society, systemically excluded from the mainstream social, political, economic, and cultural development. They experience recurrent challenges of abject poverty, condensed economic activities limited to pastoralism, political under-representation, and limited inclusion and public participation in the counties development agenda. Both counties are Arid and Semi-Arid Land (ASAL) and are negatively affected by climate change, which is often a trigger of conflict. The latter occurs specifically among pastoralists communities belonging to different ethnic groups, who, because of extreme climatic events, are forced to look for pasture and other natural resources, often invading the boundaries of other communities and counties.

The geographical inaccessibility of many areas of especially Marsabit County but lso border areas of Isiolo county also exacerbates the marginalisation of its communities, with the majority of the State institutions unable and unwilling to penetrate these areas. Building on the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development and the principle of leaving no one behind, the project will focus its interventions in these two counties.

It is expected that at the end of the intervention, the project will contribute to the efforts of ensuring that citizens of Isiolo and Marsabit counties benefit from inclusive and participatory county governance development processes and that the county Governments of Isiolo and Marsabit, will increasingly drive transparency, and accountability actions, including on climate change and Natural resource management.  In addition, the residents will be exposed to contextualised multi-door approaches to justice, including court annexed mediation (CAM) and Alternative justice systems (AJS) platforms, which will increase their chances of effectively solving their disputes in a fairer, cheaper, and more effective manner.  It is also envisaged that there will be improved ability of women, especially young women, in Isiolo and Marsabit counties to access public information and effectively participate in county-level governance processes as well as an improved capacity of the county Governments of Isiolo and Marsabit to implement gender-responsive county-level climate change and NRM Actions for inclusive climate resilience development.
sector_names: Legal and judicial development | Government & Civil Society-general
participating_orgs: Sweden / SE-0 / 1 | Swedish International Development Cooperation Agency / SE-6 / 3
results_text:
Results achieved | Uppnådda resultat | IDLO continued to implement activities to improve the County Governments of Isiolo and Marsabits ability to drive transparency and accountability actions on climate change and NRM processes by facilitating efficient commercial justice systems that respond to key indicators of an improved business climate. The first half of the year was committed to inception interventions, including undertaking (i) a security risk assessment, which was considered necessary given the
security risks identified in Isiolo and Marsabit Counties that could negatively affect project implementation; and (ii) a baseline assessment in both Counties, which presented a comprehensive and in-depth analysis of the broader context regarding transparency and accountability initiatives, climate change, and NRM efforts.

IDLO also supported initiatives to expand the multi-door approach to justice by supporting initiatives towards the roll-out of Court Annexed Mediation (CAM) and coordinated the establishment of Alternative Justice System (AJS) centres. IDLO also focused on support for inclusive and informed public participation in developing and implementing climate change and
NRM actions through community engagements with the county governments.

Some of the successes of the project in 2023 and 2024 were:

Outcome 1
 Establishment of a Court AJS in Isiolo and Marsabit counties: IDLO engaged a consultant to support the National Steering Committee on Implementation of the Alternative Justice Policy (NaSCI-AJS) in the development of Isiolo and Marsabit County Action Plans (CAPs). The CAPs set the stage for establishing accessible and user-friendly AJS suites as a framework for administering the Court Annexed AJS programme. These refer to AJS processes used to resolve disputes outside the court by the Council of Elders under the guidance and partial involvement of the court. The suites are offices the Judiciary allocates to resolve cases through the AJS programme.

In 2024,  IDLO provided expert and convening support for the training of 65 judicial officers (F: 29; M: 36) from Marsabit and Isiolo Law Courts in Meru. The training sessions were conducted from 29 April to 2 May 2024 in Marsabit and from 15 to 17 May 2024 in Isiolo. The training sessions aimed at enhancing the capacity of judicial officers on AJS, CAM, and climate change. As a result of the training, the pre- and post-training assessments demonstrated an average 32-percentage point increase in participants knowledge on AJS, CAM, and climate change.

In September 2024, Sweden participated in the launch of the AJS Suits in Isiolo. The occassion was graced by the Chief Justice. The launch of the AJS suits in Marsabit is planned for November 2024. 

 Establishment of Court Annexed Mediation Registries: IDLO supported the Judiciarys CAM Secretariat and the Mediation Accreditation Committee (MAC) to roll out CAM and expand pathways/doors for justice to vulnerable groups in both Isiolo and Marsabit courts. IDLO delivered professional certified training on mediation for qualified citizens as per the selection
criteria prescribed by the MAC, and established a pool of 80 mediators (F: 31; M: 49). This will enhance opportunities for a successful mediation process. IDLO also delivered contextualized mediation training for judges, magistrates, registrars, and clerks on the operational framework and effective administration of CAM.

Furthermore, in 2024 IDLO supported the roll-out of CAM in Isiolo and Marsabit Law Courts to provide alternative justice solutions. During the roll-out, the CAM Secretariat inducted the registry staff, and judicial officers on the CAM operational frameworks, mediation screening processes and referral of matters, provision of spaces for mediation sessions, management and payment of mediators, and adoption of settlement agreements from mediation processes. Since the engagement of mediation clerks in April 2024, the accredited mediators, trained by IDLO in 2023, have handled 25 cases. Out of these, nine (9) cases have been fully concluded, with 16 ongoing. The majority of the cases handled include land disputes, child custody and maintenance, succession as well as civil cases such as debt. This initiative aims to enhance the capacity of the courts to resolve cases expeditiously

Outcome 2

 Launch of the Marsabit County Climate Change Action Plan (MCCCAP): IDLO supported the County Government of Marsabit to review and integrate gender-responsive action plans into the MCCCAP. The MCCCAP is a key milestone towards addressing the Countys vulnerability to climate change and identifies specific investment areas to build resilience to climate change in the County. The MCCCAP was launched on 28 November 2023. In 2024, IDLO provided expert support to the Kenya Judiciary Academy (KJA) to facilitate the development of the Climate Change and Environmental Law training curriculum. The training curriculum aims to provide judicial officers with the relevant knowledge and skills to resolve climate change justice and environmental rights matters effectively. The training curriculum is currently undergoing final validation by the KJA while pending incorporation into the KJA e-learning platform.

 Facilitating access to information to increase participation of virtually impaired persons: IDLO supported the Commission on Administration of Justice (CAJ) in translating the Simplified Booklet on the Access to Information Act and Regulations, 2016 (ATI Act) into Braille. Their translation into Braille promotes a more inclusive opportunity to enhance access to relevant
information on access to justice and facilitates effective participation in the development of climate change action plans

 Delivery of Training of Trainers (TOTs) on Access to Information: IDLO facilitated the CAJ to carry out a five-day TOT session on the ATI Act for 30 (F: 12; M: 18) county government officers in Isiolo and Marsabit Counties. The TOT sought to facilitate effective knowledge transfer on implementing the ATI Act and create effective communication structures between the county government and community members on climate change and natural resource management. The TOTs will form part of the established database by the CAJ for trainers on the administration of the ATI Act. The county government officers are now informed on how to responsibly provide access to public information to members of the public on request. They
will more easily identify the information required for effective public participation in county governance processes.

Outcome 3.

Furthermore in 2024, IDLO supported the establishment of the ELC CUC in Isiolo. The ELC CUC provides a platform
to bring together court actors and users to enhance public participation and stakeholder engagement in matters related to environment and land. It also promotes effective justice sector partnerships for a coordinated, efficient, effective and consultative approach to the administration of justice in the court. The platform aims to address land, environmental and climate justice needs of justice seekers within Isiolo County.

IDLO supported the establishment of the Marsabit GCCC through convening and expert support. The Marsabit GCCC,
comprising representatives from the Ward Planning Committee (WPC), aims to address the intersection of gender and climate change at the ward level. Its mandate, derived from the WPC's role, includes consulting with the community on inclusive and gender-responsive climate finance activities, facilitating inclusive public participation with vulnerable groups, receiving gender-responsive project proposals from the community, and monitoring the implementation of projects to ensure the integration of gender equality and inclusion of the most vulnerable groups in county climate actions.

IDLO in partnership with the Isiolo and Marsabit County Governments developed a report on the disproportionate impacts
of climate change and NRM on women and girls in the two (2) Counties. The report provides a deeper understanding of the
disproportionate impacts of climate change on women and girls including on food security, education, and access to resources in both counties; and proposes response measures to mitigate the impact. The mitigation measures against climate impact proposed include involvement of women in decision-making, enhancement of womens capacity in the climate change discourse, and ensuring that there are gender-sensitive legal and institutional frameworks at the county level.

From 21-23 February 2024, IDLO offered expert and convening support to the Marsabit County government to train members of the Marsabit County Climate Change Unit and executive officers on the intersection between climate change and gender towards more equitable and sustainable solutions to climate change. In attendance were 18 (F: 5; M: 13) participants drawn from various departments within the County government of Marsabit, which include Environment, Gender, Water and Sanitation, Economics and Planning, Disaster Management, and Agriculture. title: Judiciary Support through IDLO
description:
The overall goal of the project is to contribute to the efforts of ensuring that citizens of Isiolo and Marsabit counties benefit from inclusive and participatory county governance development processes. | The projects interventions will be focused on the North Frontier counties of Isiolo and Marsabit. Despite the goodwill of the Constitution to reduce the levels of marginalisation across Kenya, the residents of Isiolo and Marsabit counties still live on the periphery of society, systemically excluded from the mainstream social, political, economic, and cultural development. They experience recurrent challenges of abject poverty, condensed economic activities limited to pastoralism, political under-representation, and limited inclusion and public participation in the counties development agenda. Both counties are Arid and Semi-Arid Land (ASAL) and are negatively affected by climate change, which is often a trigger of conflict. The latter occurs specifically among pastoralists communities belonging to different ethnic groups, who, because of extreme climatic events, are forced to look for pasture and other natural resources, often invading the boundaries of other communities and counties.

The geographical inaccessibility of many areas of especially Marsabit County but lso border areas of Isiolo county also exacerbates the marginalisation of its communities, with the majority of the State institutions unable and unwilling to penetrate these areas. Building on the 2030 Agenda for sustainable development and the principle of leaving no one behind, the project will focus its interventions in these two counties.

It is expected that at the end of the intervention, the project will contribute to the efforts of ensuring that citizens of Isiolo and Marsabit counties benefit from inclusive and participatory county governance development processes and that the county Governments of Isiolo and Marsabit, will increasingly drive transparency, and accountability actions, including on climate change and Natural resource management.  In addition, the residents will be exposed to contextualised multi-door approaches to justice, including court annexed mediation (CAM) and Alternative justice systems (AJS) platforms, which will increase their chances of effectively solving their disputes in a fairer, cheaper, and more effective manner.  It is also envisaged that there will be improved ability of women, especially young women, in Isiolo and Marsabit counties to access public information and effectively participate in county-level governance processes as well as an improved capacity of the county Governments of Isiolo and Marsabit to implement gender-responsive county-level climate change and NRM Actions for inclusive climate resilience development.

title: Barnfonden Insamlingsstiftelse CSO strategi 2025-2027
description:
Barnfonden’s program Unite for Children, Youth and Environment is designed to support eight local civil society organizations in four countries: Kenya, Ethiopia, Bolivia and Bangladesh. The program’s overarching goal is for children and young people to realize their rights through increased knowledge and strengthened resilience, ensuring their well-being, protection, participation, and equal access to a healthy and sustainable environment. The programme aims to support a green economy through nature-based solutions, sustainable resource use, and climate-smart innovations. Examples of actions to be implemented include climate-smart agriculture, green jobs, sustainable farming, climate education, eco-clubs, safe water and sanitation, environmental awareness raising, community resilience and climate adaptation strategies. | Barnfondens program Unite for Children, Youth and Environment är avsett att stödja åtta lokala civilsamhällesorganisationer i fyra länder: Kenya, Etiopien, Bolivia och Bangladesh. 
Programmets övergripande mål är att Barn och ungdomar förverkligar sina rättigheter genom ökad kunskap och stärkt motståndskraft, vilket säkerställer deras välbefinnande, skydd, deltagande och lika tillgång till en hälsosam och hållbar miljö. Programmet syftar till att stödja en grön ekonomi genom naturbaserade lösningar, hållbar resursanvändning och klimatsmarta innovationer. Exempel på aktiviteter och mål är klimatsmart jordbruk, gröna jobb, hållbart jordbruk, klimatutbildning, ekoklubbar, säkert vatten och sanitet, ökad miljömedvetenhet, samhällets motståndskraft och strategier för klimatanpassning. | Programmets övergripande mål är följande :

Barn och unga förverkligar sina rättigheter genom ökad kunskap och stärkt motståndskraft inom sina lokalsamhällen, vilket säkerställer deras välmående, skydd, delaktighet och lika tillgång till en hälsosam och hållbar miljö (Children and young people realise their rights through increased knowledge and strengthened resilience within their communities, ensuring their well-being, protection, participation, and equal access to a healthy and sustainable environment.)

Det övergripande målet delas upp i fem Outcomes, som i sin tur består av ett antal Outputs, vilka redogörs för nedan.

Outcome 1: Civilsamhällesorganisationer får stöd för att stärka sin kunskap, sina färdigheter, system och nätverk för att effektivt engagera samhällen och bemöta aktuella och framtida klimat- och miljöutmaningar (Civil society organizations are supported to strengthen their knowledge, skills, systems, and connections to effectively engage communities and respond to current and future climate and environmental challenges.)


Output 1.1: Stärkta organisatoriska system, styrning och intern kapacitet för effektivt klimat- och miljöarbete.

Output 1.2: Ökad inkludering av lokalsamhället och deltagarbaserad planering i CSO:s klimat- och miljöprogram.

Output 1.3: Förbättrad anpassningsförmåga, lärandekultur och ansvarstagande hos CSO:er.

Outcome 2: Barn, ungdomar och samhällen (särskilt flickor, kvinnor och utsatta grupper) får och tillämpar kunskap om klimatförändringar, miljöfrågor samt rättighetsbaserade och inkluderande metoder genom utbildning och kapacitetsutveckling (Children, youth, and communities (especially girls, women, and vulnerable groups) gain and apply knowledge of climate change, environmental issues, and rights-based, inclusive approaches through education and capacity building). 

Output 2.1: Högkvalitativ klimat-, biodiversitets- och miljöutbildning ges till CSO:er, i skolor och i lokalsamhällen.

Output 2.2: Rättvis och inkluderande medverkan i klimatutbildning och ledarskapsinitiativ.

Output 2.3: Ökad tillämpning av kunskap, självförtroende och ledarskap inom klimat- och miljöarbete hos målgruppen.


Outcome 3: Barn, ungdomar och lokalsamhällen ges möjlighet och resurser att föra fram krav på klimat- och miljöåtgärder, delta i beslutsfattande forum och ställa ansvariga aktörer till svars. Genom trygga, inkluderande plattformar mobiliserar de för lokalt förankrade lösningar som skyddar deras rättigheter och möter aktuella och framtida klimatutmaningar (Children, youth, and communities are empowered and equipped to advocate for environmental and climate action, participate in decision-making spaces, and hold duty bearers accountable. Through safe, inclusive platforms, they mobilize for locally driven solutions that protect their rights and respond to current and future climate challenges). 

Output 3.1: Barn, ungdomar, lokalsamhällen och CSO:er har kunskap, färdigheter och resurser för att bedriva inkluderande, rättighetsbaserat klimat- och miljöförespråkande som främjar jämställdhet, social sammanhållning och motståndskraft.

Output 3.2: Påverkansplattformar och ungdoms- eller samhällsledda grupper är inkluderande, representativa och engagerar sig effektivt i formella beslut kring klimat, miljö och barns rättigheter på lokal, nationell och internationell nivå.

Output 3.3: Ansvariga aktörer reagerar på och agerar utifrån påverkansinsatser från barn, ungdomar, samhällen och CSO:er, vilket leder till konkreta förändringar i policy, resurser eller praxis som respekterar jämställdhet, konfliktkänslighet och barns rättigheter.


Outcome 4: Barn, ungdomar och deras samhällen utvecklar färdigheter för att förutse och anpassa sig till klimatrelaterade risker, skyddar liv, försörjning och ekosystem samt skapar möjligheter för hållbar utveckling och ansvarstagande för miljön (Children, youth, and their communities build the skills to anticipate and adapt to climate risks, protecting lives, livelihoods, and ecosystems while creating opportunities for sustainable growth and stewardship). 

Output 4.1: Stärkta system för samhällens motståndskraft och beredskap.

Output 4.2: Utökade klimatsmarta försörjningsmöjligheter och gröna färdigheter.

Output 4.3: Ökad användning av förebyggande och anpassningsåtgärder för att minska klimatrelaterade risker.


Outcome 5: Stärka CSO:ers förmåga att förutse, anpassa sig till och proaktivt bemöta inskränkningar i det civila utrymmet och klimatrelaterade risker. Det stärker system, strategier och allianser som skyddar civilsamhället och främjar miljö- och klimaträttvisa (Strengthen CSOs ability to anticipate, adapt, and proactively respond to civic space restrictions and climate-related risks. It strengthens systems, strategies, and alliances that protect civil society and advance environmental and climate justice. )

Output 5.1: Stärkt oberoende, mångfald och förmåga till framförhållning inom civilsamhället för att proaktivt kunna möta och mildra inskränkningar i det civila utrymmet och klimat- och miljöutmaningar.

Output 5.2: Förbättrade samarbets- och anpassningsmekanismer inom civilsamhället och mellan CSO:er och andra aktörer, vilket möjliggör gemensamma och framåtblickande insatser mot förändrade risker kopplade till civilt utrymme, miljö och klimat.

Output 5.3: Stärkt oberoende och ekonomisk motståndskraft hos CSO:er genom diversifierade, hållbara och riskanpassade strategier för resursmobilisering.

I dialog med Barnfonden har organisationen kommunicerat att målen för Ukraina-tillägget bidrar till de övergripande målen för den pågående insatsen . Hur de nya målen och tillägsprojektet är i linje med det ursprungliga programmet beskrivs nedan:

Outcome 1. Strenghten capacity (stärkt kapacitet)

Projektet kommer att stärka ukrainska civilsamhällesorganisationer och lokala aktörer i deras förmåga att hantera de långvariga effekterna av kriget på barns psykiska hälsa. Genom att kombinera behovsbaserat kapacitetsstöd, gemensamma nätverkande aktiviteter och riktade utbildningar inom barnskydd, traumarespons och psykosocialt stöd, bidrar projektet direkt till att utveckla CSO:s organisatoriska kompetens, deras interna system samt deras förmåga att samarbeta strategiskt med lokala myndigheter. 

Outcome 2. Inform (Informera)

Projektet ska främja barns motståndskraft och välbefinnande, centrala skyddsfaktorer som i ramverket kopplas till barns rättigheter och deras möjligheter att verka i trygga och inkluderande miljöer. Healing Forests naturbaserade metodik och strukturerade lekbaserade ritualer stärker barns förmåga att hantera stress och reglerar känslor, vilket bidrar till deras deltagande, psykosociala trygghet och långsiktiga utveckling. Detta är i linje med ramverkets ambition att öka barns och ungas kunskap, färdigheter och resiliens i relation till de risker de möter i sitt vardagsliv.

Outcome 3. Engage (Engagera)

Projektet ska synliggöra de yngsta barnens psykiska hälsa i offentligheten, skapa utrymme för civilsamhälle och lokala aktörer att tillsammans formulera prioriteringar, och genom att stärka aktörernas förmåga att föra fram barns behov till ansvarsbärare, lägger projektet grunden för mer inkluderande och evidensbaserade beslut.

Outcome 4. Prepare (förbereda)

Healing Forest ger barn verktyg för att knyta an till sin omgivning, utveckla känslomässig stabilitet och bygga coping-strategier som hjälper dem att hantera framtida stressfaktorer, vilket kompletterar ramverkets inriktning på samhällsbaserad motståndskraft.

Outcome 5. Enabling environment (möjliggörande miljö)

Projektet stödjer Outcome 5 (Enabling Environment) genom att stärka förutsättningarna för civilsamhället att verka långsiktigt under svåra och snabbt föränderliga omständigheter. Genom att utveckla yrkeskompetens, utöka nätverk, skapa strukturer för mentorskap och kvalitetskontroll samt genom att bedriva riktad advocacy om barns psykiska hälsa, förbättrar projektet både civilsamhällets organisatoriska robusthet och dess möjlighet att agera fritt, professionellt och effektivt i en krigskontext.

I dialog med Barnfonden har organisationen kommunicerat att målen för Ukraina-tillägget bidrar till de övergripande målen för den pågående insatsen . Hur de nya målen och tillägsprojektet är i linje med det ursprungliga programmet beskrivs nedan:

Outcome 1. Strenghten capacity (stärkt kapacitet)

Projektet kommer att stärka ukrainska civilsamhällesorganisationer och lokala aktörer i deras förmåga att hantera de långvariga effekterna av kriget på barns psykiska hälsa. Genom att kombinera behovsbaserat kapacitetsstöd, gemensamma nätverkande aktiviteter och riktade utbildningar inom barnskydd, traumarespons och psykosocialt stöd, bidrar projektet direkt till att utveckla CSO:s organisatoriska kompetens, deras interna system samt deras förmåga att samarbeta strategiskt med lokala myndigheter. 

Outcome 2. Inform (Informera)

Projektet ska främja barns motståndskraft och välbefinnande, centrala skyddsfaktorer som i ramverket kopplas till barns rättigheter och deras möjligheter att verka i trygga och inkluderande miljöer. Healing Forests naturbaserade metodik och strukturerade lekbaserade ritualer stärker barns förmåga att hantera stress och reglerar känslor, vilket bidrar till deras deltagande, psykosociala trygghet och långsiktiga utveckling. Detta är i linje med ramverkets ambition att öka barns och ungas kunskap, färdigheter och resiliens i relation till de risker de möter i sitt vardagsliv.

Outcome 3. Engage (Engagera)

Projektet ska synliggöra de yngsta barnens psykiska hälsa i offentligheten, skapa utrymme för civilsamhälle och lokala aktörer att tillsammans formulera prioriteringar, och genom att stärka aktörernas förmåga att föra fram barns behov till ansvarsbärare, lägger projektet grunden för mer inkluderande och evidensbaserade beslut.

Outcome 4. Prepare (förbereda)

Healing Forest ger barn verktyg för att knyta an till sin omgivning, utveckla känslomässig stabilitet och bygga coping-strategier som hjälper dem att hantera framtida stressfaktorer, vilket kompletterar ramverkets inriktning på samhällsbaserad motståndskraft.

Outcome 5. Enabling environment (möjliggörande miljö)

Projektet stödjer Outcome 5 (Enabling Environment) genom att stärka förutsättningarna för civilsamhället att verka långsiktigt under svåra och snabbt föränderliga omständigheter. Genom att utveckla yrkeskompetens, utöka nätverk, skapa strukturer för mentorskap och kvalitetskontroll samt genom att bedriva riktad advocacy om barns psykiska hälsa, förbättrar projektet både civilsamhällets organisatoriska robusthet och dess möjlighet att agera fritt, professionellt och effektivt i en krigskontext.
