title: Kenya Drought & Food Insecurity Emergency/Early Recovery Phase
description:
Caritas Kenya as a development and social services commission of the Kenya Episcopal Conference has a role to ensure that the capacities of Catholic Church-based development structures are strengthened, so as to respond to the needs of the poor more effectively. 

Kenya’s disaster profile is dominated by cyclical phenomenon including drought, famine and floods. These occurrences disrupt people’s livelihoods, destroy the infrastructure, divert planned use of resources, interrupt economic activities and retard development. Others which are recurrent include fire, terrorism, technological accidents, diseases and epidemics. Through Programmes, Caritas Kenya coordinates emergency activities while at the same time integrates long term development in a bid to build mitigation capacities for disaster prevention. The overall goal is to establish and maintain an efficient, effective and coordinated system for managing disasters in order to minimize losses and resulting disruptions and destructions of people’s life and livelihoods, infrastructure, economy and degradation of the environment.

This emergency appeal is proposing to mitigate the negative impact of drought on vulnerable households in Kenya by improving food security of drought affected vulnerable pastoral, agro-pastoral and marginal agricultural households through food and nutrition, WASH and early recovery activities in 14 Dioceses of Kenya. The project will reach a total of 182,520 beneficiaries, or 30,420 households. The targeted households will benefit from both immediate life saving assistance as well as activities that will enable their livelihoods to recover from the current drought. 

The total budget of the project is €3,959,919 Euros, the full amount of which is sought from CI members, and the duration of the project is 8 months. 

Project Rationale:
Two consecutive below-average rainy seasons have caused Eastern Africa’s most severe drought in sixty years, with an estimated 3.6 million and predicted to increase to 5 million Kenyans affected by the drought and in need of emergency assistance. The drought crisis in the Horn of Africa represents the most serious food insecurity situation in the world today, in terms of both scale and severity.  Extremely low levels of precipitation have resulted in widespread food insecurity, pushing malnutrition and mortality rates to emergency levels across the country in recent months.  Critical water and pasture shortages have caused livestock deaths and rising food prices have further limited households’ access to food. North-Eastern Kenya is the worst affected part of the country, with Global Acute Malnutrition rates in some areas exceeding 30% and steadily increasing according to Kenya Health Cluster updayte of 28th July 2011.  Other areas of Kenya that have been traditionally food secure, and a safety net for vulnerable communities, are themselves under serious threat of a full blown humanitarian disaster, with FEWSNET now ranking the majority of the country at ‘crisis’ or ‘emergency’ levels. On 30 May, the Government of Kenya declared the drought a national disaster.

In the past decade Kenya has experienced three serious droughts. As droughts occur at shorter intervals, the recovery period for communities is shorter and natural resources are unable to recover to sustainable levels. The country has experienced a succession of poor cropping seasons, with the exception of the fairly good El-Niño season of 2010. Most seasons have witnessed erratic rainfall, low volumes of rainfall and extended dry periods. Such inconsistencies during normally productive periods has led to a gross reduction in the production of food, insufficient recovery of water aquifers and the increasing spread of arid areas. The traditionally productive areas that receive rains have reported inconsistencies in precipitation, which has resulted in either total failure or widespread poor crop performance.  

Specific problems identified include:
Nutrition
Nutrition assessments by UNICEF in July 2011 showed Global Acute Malnutrition (GAM) rates exceeding the critical Emergency threshold of 15% in all of the northern districts surveyed. The following are the rates established in the areas being targeted for intervention; 
• 33% in Lodwar diocese
• 22 – 32% in Garissa diocese
• 15.7% in Isiolo diocese
• 27.1% in Marsabit diocese
• 19.8% in Maralal diocese
The other dioceses included in the proposal are all experiencing malnutrition levels above the normal range of 1-5% GAM rates. Under five crude mortality rate has reached more than the emergency threshold (2/10,000 /day) in Lodwar diocese (up to 3.24). In the same diocese the crude mortality rate (adults and children) has reached more than the emergency threshold (1/10,000 /day) at 2.42

Food Access
• With many animals dead in the Northern Dioceses as a result of the drought, and with the few remaining ones being targeted by raiders, many families have no means to feed themselves. 
• Prices of staples are 60-80 percent higher than the 5-year average in most markets and are close or higher than record prices reported in 2008.. 
• In the Northern Dioceses where many families affected by the drought are entirely dependent on animal keeping for their livelihood, there has been a total loss of livelihood.. Such families are highly dependent on food aid.
• With successive failure of rain seasons, most of the families in the Marginal agricultural and coastal dioceses have lost successive crops and have no reserves of food nor the income to acquire food from the markets.
• Communities are engaging in adverse coping mechanisms, such as  skipping meals and in some cases for the whole day, including children, expectant mothers and also other vulnerable categories. Schools are reporting net migration of families from  drought affected areas. In Wajir and Turkana districts some schools are seeing a large increase in attendance (up to as much as 50%) as families access food through existent school feeding programmes. 

Water
• Poor rainfall has led to a poor recharge of water sources – (30-60% of capacity), and many of the water sources have dried up.
• Distances to water points have increased from an average of 1-5 km to 8-20 km in the areas targeted by the project.
• In many areas, the most practical intervention is to rehabilitate the available boreholes to increase the community’s access to clean water, but with the loss of livelihoods options communities are unable to support such rehabilitation.. 

Livelihoods (livestock/crops)
• Livestock conditions have continued deteriorating due to the prolonged drought period. Goats and cattle have fared worst, with many areas reporting mortalities. The condition of camels is fair to poor. 
• Due to the high concentration of livestock in areas that received little rainfall, conflict over water and pastures is reported.
• Farmers in the coastal and southeastern marginal agricultural lowlands are faced with the third successive poor season after failure of the 2011 long rains crop in these areas. Rains started one month late during the last week of April after a substantial proportion of the crop had wilted. Less than 20 percent of normal output is anticipated in these areas. 

Incorporating relevant CAFOD interests
Caritas Kenya, in close collaboration with the in-country Caritas Partners and other humanitarian actors, has closely monitored the situation as it has been unfolding since October 2010. This has included field assessments, information gathering from the Diocesan partners, and participation in humanitarian monitoring meetings. Caritas Diocesan partners have also participated in the government’s assessment process, which has included data collection and collation.

To co-ordinate the national impact of CI MO’s in country, and to capture the combined findings from all CI MO’s in country, Caritas Kenya has held coordination meetings with the Caritas Country Forum since November 2010 when the situation began to unfold. The last Caritas Country Forum meeting was held 3rd August, with representation from Caritas Kenya, CAFOD, Trocaire, Caritas Italiana, Caritas Australia, Caritas Switzerland/Luxembourg, Cordaid, CRS, Caritas Austria and representatives from Caritas Internationalis, including CI Humanitarian director Alistair Dutton and John Coughon. Caritas Kenya has mapped out the interventions by Catholic Agencies across the country, especially in areas worst hit by the drought. This has helped establish the gaps that exist in terms of interventions within the Church based actors as well by other humanitarian actors. 

The Kenya Episcopal Conference launched a local appeal on 28th July 2011 to all Dioceses, Congregations and people of good will to support humanitarian interventions in the most affected areas of the country. By 4th August 2011 the local appeal had raised over KSh. 100,000 (€ 770).

Implementation strategies reflect best practice and lessons learned from a number of Caritas Kenya emergency responses in the past, including the 2007 flood response, the 2008 post election violence emergency response, the 2009 food insecurity emergency and  the 2009 flood response. From these responses, Caritas Kenya has gained experience in the application of Sphere standards, community mobilization, aid coordination, and in utilizing the Caritas national network to improve approaches to food security and sustainable livelihoods within participating and other dioceses in the country. Of the fourteen dioceses that have been targeted in this EA, all except one ( Kitui ) have been involved in previous Caritas Kenya led Emergency responses. 

Sustainability
The overall management of funds obtained shall be done by the Kenya Episcopal Conference - Catholic Secretariat, Finance Commission, with the added support of a Finance Officer seconded from another Caritas agency.  This has been the strategy used in previous EA’s in which the CI MOs in Kenya provided capacity support for funds management, eg  during the post election violence emergency interventions in 2008.

The Diocesan Finance departments will be responsible for local finance management including the procurement. However, if situation(s) arise where the dioceses are unable to execute some elements of implementation, Caritas Kenya may step in to assist the Dioceses. 

An external audit shall be done at completion of project. All the Dioceses participating in this appeal shall submit their accounts to Caritas Kenya for verification and internal audit through the Caritas Kenya system of Finance, to be then further subjected to audit by an external auditor.

The project has already secured an M&E Officer, who has been seconded from another Caritas agency for the first 3 months. This position will be transitioned into the recruitment of a national M&E officer, dedicated to this response for the remainder of the project and 2 months beyond its completion. This position will be dedicated to the design and implementation of a monitoring framework for the response, and will also assist with reporting. 

Specific issues for CAFOD monitoring
The project has been designed to ensure that the emergency phase will transition well into an early rehabilitation stage, as the short rains are anticipated in October.  The design of the project is based on the assumption that the rains in October will be fairly normal and with the provision of drought tolerant seeds and proper water harvesting measures, both agro-pastoralists and pastoralists will have adequate pasture and crop production. Restocking the two groups of agro-pastoralists and pastoralists with both traditional and improved breeds of goats and drought tolerant seeds will also support livelihood recovery. With improved pasture and crop production, and re-stocking of livestock, beneficiaries will be supported to re-engage in the livelihoods activities, of which local diocesan partners have been supporting communities over several years, as part of their development programs. Such long term livelihood activities aim at increasing production and hence building communities’ resilience. 

Cafod would like to intervene in specific areas in this proposal, which are Monitoring and Evaluation, Communication and Accountability mechanisms.

title: Support to Drought Affected Communities in Turkana
description:
In Turkana, consecutive drought has depleted the water sources, an essential community resource. Most riverbeds have long-since dried up, and apart from relief agency-sponsored boreholes, there is no water. April and May are usually the long rains months for Turkana. This year, the rains have been sporadic and unpredictable. For most people of the region, livestock is a ‘living bank’ - a savings account with a cash value. In some parts of Turkana the drought has wiped out 70% of the livestock. For the affected families this means losing 70 % of their savings. In this scenario, many go bankrupt and whole lives are shattered. Up to 30 % of children aged under five in Turkana County are malnourished as a result of the prolonged drought. Assessment reports indicate a general increase in malnutrition rates in drought-affected districts throughout Kenya. As the drought has worsened, child malnutrition in some districts has gone critically over the World Health Organization’s (WHO) global acute malnutrition (GAM) critical threshold of 15 per cent. This shows the GAM levels exceeded the critical threshold in all of Turkana districts: Turkana North East 37.40 %, Turkana South and East 33.5 %, Turkana North West 27.80 %, Turkana Central and Loima 24.40 %. In addition, the under five crude mortality rate has reached more than the emergency threshold (2/10,000/day) in Turkana North West and North East with respectively 3.24 and 2.12 ; The crude mortality rate (adults and children) has reached more than the emergency threshold (1/10,000 /day) in Turkana North West and North East with respectively 2.13 and 2.42. 
Due to the drought, water and grazing land have become so precious that there has been an increase in the use of small arms to settle disputes over access to natural resources. Consequently, there has been a rise in armed conflict, especially along the border regions of Uganda, South Sudan and Ethiopia. Increasingly, the Turkana are resorting to using guns in their battle to preserve their way of life. Skirmishes over scarce watering holes, pasture and livestock are a part of daily life and lives are being lost and due to the insecurity, people are not able to freely access natural resources and sources of livelihood.
The project intends to provide relief and protect livelihoods of highly insecure households in the Diocese of Lodwar.The key focus areas of the project include food security, livelihoods and water, sanitation and hygiene promotion. 

Livelihoods Inputs will assist in sustaining vulnerable households.  This component includes the provision of seeds to 500 households and destocking of animals for 250 households as well as the provision of veterinary services to support livestock in the Diocese of Lodwar. 
Water for livestock will be provided through the rehabilitation and construction of water sources in the diocese of Lodwar through the cash and food for work.Advocacy and Education through the Diocese of Lodwar radio station, Radio Akicha. title: Somali Refugee Response-by CRS
description:
This Emergency Appeal responds to the refugee crisis caused by drought and famine in Somalia. In Somalia, the drought and ongoing conflict has reached a crisis level affecting over half of the population, and resulting in more than 250,000 Somalis leaving the country in 2011 alone in search of assistance.  The resulting mass movement of rural Somalis to urban areas and across the border to Kenya and Ethiopia to seek relief in a relatively secure environment has put significant pressure on the already overcrowded refugee camps in Kenya. 
To contribute to improving the situation of refugees in these camps, Catholic Relief Services Kenya developed this two-year intervention. 
Caritas Internationalis is now launching this Appeal as a fourteen-month emergency response project (twelve months implementation, plus two months for preparation of final reports and audit), and we foresee the launch of a second Appeal for Year Two. 
The Refugee Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH) Project will help drought-affected refugees in Kambioos Camp in Dabaab, Kenya to meet their immediate sanitation, hygiene, and water needs. 

CRS Kenya will meet the needs of 12,000 newly arrived refugee households (or 48,000 people, approximately 53% of the anticipated 90,000 population) who are currently in the process of relocating into Kambioos Camp by:

-providing latrines/showers with hand-washing facilities, 

-promoting camp hygiene and sanitation with hygiene education and NFI hygiene kits for 12,000 households,

-supporting solid waste disposal management and water drainage,

-planning a contingency water supply as a back up to current plans, and

-Ensuring its activities are accountable to the people it is serving.

By implementing the above activities, CRS envisions the following results:
	
-Drought-affected refugees use sanitation facilities and services daily

-Drought-affected refugees demonstrate key hygiene behaviours for hand-washing, water handling, and latrine use

-Drought-affected refugees actively engage in the response

-Drought-affected refugees have safe and sufficient water for household use

title: MARALAL DROUGHT RESPONSE RECOVERY PHASE
description:
This recovery phase project intends to contribute towards the improvement of the livelihoods of communities severely affected by the 2011 Horn and East Africa drought. 

Samburu district in northern Kenya was severely affected by the drought. In February 2011, a Government of Kenya - led assessment teams comprising U.N. and NGO representatives recorded a global acute malnutrition rate of 18.7 per cent in Samburu District, exceeding the U.N. World Health Organization emergency threshold of 15 per cent. The Diocese of Maralal conducted an emergency project in the area which mainly centred on provision of food aid and construction of water sources. This recovery project is a direct follow on from the emergency intervention in the area. 

This project intends to build on the gains achieved during the emergency phase by enhancing the resilience 
of the drought affected communities

title: Marsabit Intergrated Drought Recovery Project
description:
Marsabit is a pastoral and agro pastoral zone located in upper Eastern Kenya bordering Isiolo to the South East and Wajir to the East. It is one of Kenya's Arid counties located in Eastern Province. The County has a population of 291,166. The main livelihood activities in Marsabit are Pastoral and agro-pastoral which account for 70% and 20% respectively. Livestock and livestock products are a predominant source of food and income to households. Most parts of the County other than Marsabit town chronically experience water scarcity and food insecurity due to frequent drought, recurrent livestock disease outbreaks, poor market and road infrastructure, insecurity from cross boarder raiding and resource based conflicts.  

In 2010 Marsabit, experienced its worst drought in many years due to failure of the long rains in April and scanty rains in preceding years. As a result both water and grazing fields for animals vanished and cattle prices reduced drastically. This led to deterioration of nutrition status particularly children requiring supplementation of protein rich food sources and the problem was exacerbated by a worldwide rise in food prices with the price of grain in affected areas being 30-80% above average. In many parts of Marsabit, up to 75 percent of the pastoralist’s herds perished.  Animal prices plummeted since the surviving ones had become very emanciated while the cost of cereals soared. Malnutrition rates stood at mean of 27 %. 
After humanitarian assessment and lobbying by UN and other humanitarian agencies working in the region followed by media attention in the draught situation at the Horn and East African region where Marsabit lies, humanitarian agencies responded to the crisis with such programmes as food distribution, water trucking, Blanket supplementary feeding, cash for work programmes etc.  Cafod responded to the crisis through the diocese of Marsabit.
The situation has so far changed since and some rains fell as early as September filling some dams (e.g Kargi in Marsabit). The greatest rains however fell in the months of October and November and the first week of December. This has provided reprieve to the surviving livestock since the grazing pastures have recovered with grass. The larger human population however still remains vulnerable since it will still take at least 6 months to produce dependable food even with the rains.  The pastoralist community also largely depends on livestock for their livelihood and food but only a few herd of livestock remained after most of it perished with the draught.  Milk and food prices are still high in Marsabit.
The interventions by the Catholic Diocese of Marsabit in its drought response included cash for work for rehabilitation and desalting of water pans with the aim of providing an income to the affected community so that they could purchase food locally and the second aim being to increase the water storage. Three of the planned water pans are now complete and already filled with water as a result of the rains. The diocese also partnered with WFP to provide a BSFP programme in the affected region mainly through the diocese medical centres.

The proposed project will build on gains made during the emergency draught response by enhancing the resilience of the communities affected by the drought through supporting livelihoods of vulnerable groups, contributing to enhancing ongoing DRR programme and nutrition intervention and education with introduction of kitchen gardens.

title: Clean Drinking Water and Hygiene with a Gender focus
description:
The project aims to bring the following outcome:
 
More women and men in arid land communities of Kitui, Maralal and Marsabi influence the policies and practices that improve sustainable access, control, management and safe use of water resources assets and access to clean water and practice safe environmental sanitation and hygiene benefiting 22,550 individuals.

CAFOD Partners, The Catholic diocese of Kitui, Isiolo, Marsabit and Mararal have in the past initiated a number of projects funded by CAFOD and other partners.  A big portion of the projects have gone into provision of water for human and livestock consumption.  Most of the water facilities are provided through boreholes, water pans and rock catchments.  Whereas rock catchments and boreholes may provide clean drinking water if hygienically maintained, the earth dams provided have no facilities to provide clean drinking water for human consumption. Some of the boreholes provided are of high salinity especially in Kargi, Marsabit and there is speculation that they contain heavy metals that can cause diseases.  Most of the project beneficiaries are pastoralists.  The coverage of latrines is very low in the community and due to open defecation; there is likelihood of contamination of the water sources.  Due to low levels of education in the community, hygiene awareness is very low.    The project aims at  increasing accessibility of sufficient potable water to the community while at the same time addressing the need for safe defecation through Community Led total Sanitation programme which aims at sensitizing the community to construct their own latrines with no material support.  The project also aims at sensitizing the community in safe hygiene through simple messages on safe water (drinking only from safe water source or home treatment), safe defecation and hand washing at critical times.  The project further aims at carrying out a gender analysis and sensitizing the community leaders on gender roles and women participation with the aim of having active women leadership in the committees.  The project therefore aims to address the following mach fund outcome indicators:
 
-number of men and women reporting access to safe drinking water, 
-number of women and men reporting access to sanitation facilities, 
-number of women and men of targeted beneficiaries demonstrating good hygiene practice,  
-number of women engaged in WASH and environmental management committees reporting increased opportunity and confidence in decisions affecting access to and safe use of household and/or community resources such as water 
-CAFOD partners showing evidence of gender analysis throughout the project cycle and using sex disaggregated data in monitoring and reporting.

title: Clean Drinking Water and Hygiene with a Gender Focus
description:
This project aims to achieve the following outcomes: more women and men in the semi arid land community of Kitui Kenya, influence the local decisions and practices that improve sustainable access, control, management and safe use of water resource assets; gain access to clean water; and practice safe environmental sanitation and hygiene behaviours. The project will benefit 9009 individuals.
CAFOD partner, the Catholic dioceses of Kitui have previously implemented projects funded by CAFOD and other donors. Most of the projects have a component of provision of water for human and livestock consumption culminating in the construction of water facilities such as water pans and sand dams. Whereas sand dams constructed are likely to provide clean drinking water if hygienically maintained, the earth dams have no facilities to provide clean drinking water for human consumption. Within the same communities the coverage of latrines is very low and due to open defecation there is a likelihood of contamination of water sources.  
This project aims at increasing accessibility of sufficient potable water to the community while at the same time addressing the need for safe defecation through Community Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) activities focusing on sensitizing the community to construct their own latrines with no external material support. Success stories especially from the Public Health Department in Kitui following the CLTS approach have informed the planning of the sanitation component of this project. 
The project further aims at sensitizing the community on safe hygiene through simple messages on safe water (drinking only from a safe water source or home treatment), safe defecation and hand washing at critical times.  The project will also utilise existing gender audits/gender analysis to review the gender roles of men and women, boys and girls in the community with the aim of ultimately sensitizing community leaders on gender roles and women/girls participation, and increase women’s leadership in WASH and environmental management committees. The sensitization will be built on existing gender activities being carried out by the partners.   
This project aims to achieve the following Match Funds outcome indicators:
 
• Number of men and women, reporting access to safe drinking water, 
• Number of women and men reporting access to sanitation facilities, 
• Number of women and men demonstrating good hygiene practices.
• Number of women engaged in WASH and environmental management committees reporting increased opportunities to participate in decisions affecting access to, and safe use of, household and/or community resources such as water. 
CAFOD’s partners will show evidence of both women’s and men’s participation throughout the project cycle and use gender disaggregated data in monitoring and reporting. Gender analysis will look at the roles of men, women, boys and girls, and how gender relations affect access and management of WASH facilities and initiatives, with a view of sensitizing the community on the participation of each gender in the project. The programme will use existing gender audits that are currently being carried out by a consultant under the CAFOD-supported Governance programme. These will also inform the work schedule and other project activities so that the distinctive needs of women and girls will be included in the programme design and activities. Examples include time of working and time of meetings to ensure women have time for their young ones and meetings are organized in such a way that it does not result in women and girls walking in the darkness.  Separate consultations with each gender will also ensure women are not dominated by men in contribution to discussions.

title: Water Resource Development and Livelihoods Support Project Maralal
description:
This is a six (6) months project designed to specifically provide targeted beneficiaries in Samburu East and Samburu North Districts with improved access to clean drinking water and diversified livelihood options by introducing new technology for food and vegetable production. A key component in this project is the building of community assets, such as access roads through Cash for Work activities; hence opening access to the region for borehole construction as well as other essential goods and services. 
To improve access to clean drinking water, the project will construct and equip a borehole at Lchakwai, Samburu East to serve an estimated 2,600 community members. The community in Lchakwai was involved in the HVCA and the
water project was identified as the community priority. However due to infrastructural challenges, it was not possible constructed the planned borehole Lack of access meant that the activity could not take place, and needed to be redesigned to take into account accessibility of the area. The repair of the Lchakwai access road and construction of a borehole will enable the community members’ access portable water and reduce the distance walked and time spent in search of water To diversify livelihood options, the project will promote green house farming technology among target communities. Three green houses will be provided to farmer groups and will result in two key changes; first the groups practicing green house farming will have an alternative source of income as they sell the produce and secondly there will be access to an improved and diversified diet as vegetables become available for household consumption. The green house farming is appropriate for women as they often have no means of earning a livelihood as men are primarily engaged with livestock. Women also go to markets and they identified a gap in the supply of vegetables, as many people do not engage in farming of vegetables.

title: Consultancy - Kitui WRM
description:
The project area is located to the west of Kitui County in Nthongoni location of Kitui Rural sub-county. The name of the project is Muvitha/Kathemboni water shed management aimed at restoration of the catchment which has been degraded over time due poor land use management. Cultivation in steep slopes is evident which would have otherwise been left undisturbed with only trees growing to intercept rainwater and allow it time for water to percolate in the soil and also build up humus. Conservation efforts have been attempted but only when the hills were productive but now signs of neglect have manifested. At the foot of the hills are farms which are still being tilled and whose conservation needs to be strengthened.
Within the catchment, there is an earth dam, named Musosya that was constructed in the year 2003 and has silted up due to poor management of land use. During the earth dam construction, there was a perennial flowing stream of water in the main gully that feeds the dam.  The situation has since changed and the stream no longer flows and the flow in the gulley’s feeding the dam is only from storm water during the rainy season. Over the years there has been widening of the gully and many more gully tributaries have emerged, gully banks are slumping, widening the stream further and sand accumulation in the main gully has started a sign of mature water course.  The silt trap pond that had been made just before the inlet to the dam has been filled with sand,  The inlet pat of the dam has also been filled with sand to almost 2m estimated from a tree that was present during the construction of the dam.  The tree has been filled by sand to the first branch level. 
The Water Shed Management project is based on a concept of Land Retention Landscape from Tamera in Portugal that advocates for total retention of storm water run off within a water shed.   Tamera consultants have been invited for technical advise with specific deliverable as outlined in the ToR

title: Empowered Marasbit Community  for Good Governance and Peaceful Co-existence
description:
Diocese of Marsabit seeks to maximise benefits of devolution for good governance and peaceful co- existence. The  project  will work  with 10  advocacy  groups  formed under  ABG1  and  create  6  additional groups.  These 16 groups will be transitioned into county  education and leadership teams through  training. Thus formation and training of County Education and Leadership Teams (CELTs) of men and women selected at ward level to ensure participation in county processes. Civic education processes through the Church Structures, media house, public forums on role of county governments. Capacity building of county authorities through training on county functions, county law making processes, development of county strategic planning and budgeting processes. Establishment of county liaison (form of county parliamentary liaison desk to link county leadership teams to county authority and national assembly. Creation of enablers of citizen participation and effectiveness of Church in promoting democratic devolution processes. Key aspect of participation entails engagement of citizens in county   budgeting and monitoring processes.  Documentation of county citizen centred social audits. These County  Education and Leadership teams will have a multiple  functions as a  community  resource group to  provide  information and facilitate  engagements, public  expenditure  monitors and  agents of peace.  Being a conflict context, interfaith council forum will be formed to promote dialogue on governance and peace issues.
DOM strengthened community advocacy structures through formation of 10 community advocacy groups to monitor service delivery in the water, education and security sector. These groups registered great success in mounting pressure on government agencies to address development needs of the communities.  This project is premised on this background and it aims to continue strengthening the existing  advocacy groups in Bubisa, Karare,Dukana, Bori, Qilita, Kargi, Korr, Loiyangalani, Dirid-Gombo Sololo parishes and will form and training six new groups in Laisamis, Ileret, North Horr and Maikona parishes
Diocese of Marsabit activities will link with national activities to be carried out by CJPC Kenya. Of essence is the civic education manual being developed by CJPC, the Diocese will adapt it as its training manual of advocacy groups (CELTS) and county government. Key advocacy issues from Marsabit County warranting national attention will be picked up and supported by Bishops advocacy committee CJPC Kenya. The county parliamentary liaison    officer will learn from and link up with parliamentary liaison officer based at CJPC national office.
This is a two year project with  budget  allocations of Year 1 £ 40,000 Year 2 £ 40,000.

title: Maralal Integrated Food Security Project.
description:
This project aims to improve food security by addressing the underlying issues that negatively affect communities’ access to food throughout the year, in Samburu Central and East, Kenya.

From a needs assessment conducted, the proposed interventions respond to identified needs, including diversified livelihood sources, improved crop and livestock production, value addition and linkage to markets for farmers. As well as access to water for livestock and human use, conflict mitigation and community driven initiatives to conserve the environment. 

To achieve the aims key strategies to be used in the project include; 

Supporting men and women to improve crop production through the provision of certified seeds. 

The implementation of conflict mitigation and Peace building initiatives 

Access to sufficient water for crop and livestock production. Mothers with children under five will be provided with access to clean drinking water, community health volunteers will be trained to promote hygiene and sanitation at community level.

In the context of county government, the project will recruit community advocacy agents among the farmer groups, who will be trained and facilitated to undertake public expenditure monitoring at county level. The project will also establish a county liaison desk to be manned by the diocesan county liaison officer.

title: MARALAL WATER AND LIVELIHOODS PROJECT
description:
This project will provide the targeted communities with an alternative source of water for both agriculture and livestock, in Kenya.

Two sand dams will be constructed along the river bed to trap water during the rainy season, and a reservoir to store the water. The project will also establish 8 demonstration plots at the project site. Groups of women and youth will be trained and provided with start-up inputs to enable them establish the demonstration plots. It is anticipated that crop farming using the available water will increase, and offer the community an alternative source of food. 

Lack of water for agriculture was identified during the Hazard Vulnerability and Capacity Assessment in the area conducted in 2012. The community took part in the exercise and the problems being addressed reflect the priorities of the community. Mass movement of animals during the dry season was also identified as a key issue affecting the more vulnerable members of the community. Children under five years, women and the elderly often lack enough food during the dry season, and this is directly attributed to lack of water for livestock during the dry season. 

Anticipated change to be achieved by this project will be:
• Availability of water for agricultural use by the Lekiji community
• Availability of water for livestock use, especially during the dry season
• Improved access to food through establishment of demonstration plots

title: CAFOD Community Based Green Energy Project (CB-GEP)
description:
The Community Based Green Energy Project (CB-GEP) is a 4 year programme which begun in 2011 and is expected to end in 2015. The  programme overall aim is to contribute towards increasing access to modern, affordable and sustainable energy services for 407,792 households through 138 schools and health centres and 69 rural community based groups in rural and peri-urban areas in Kenya. 

The programme is being implemented in three counties; Kitui, Isiolo and Kajiado County  in Kenya. Partners involved in the programme are; Dupoto-E-Maa, Catholic Dioceses of Isiolo and Kitui and Solar Works East Africa Limited which is a private Sector Company focusing on Solar Energy Technology and operating in East Africa. 

The programme has 4 key specific and closely interrelated objectives these are: 
1. To improve provision of energy services for schools and health centres in rural and peri-urban areas in target districts.

title: Emergency Drought Response - Isiolo (GEF)
description:
Isiolo County is located in the Upper Eastern region of Kenya. Livestock production is the mainstay of the predominantly pastoral and agro-pastoral communities.  Ordinarily, this is supplemented by subsistence crop production, trade and bee keeping among other economic activities.  

Isiolo County is experiencing severe drought condition in all the livelihood zones characterized by among others drying up of key water sources. This is a result of poor performance of long rains in March – May 2016.  The situation was worsened by the poor performance of seasonal rains between October- December 2016.  No Arid and Semi Arid Land (ASAL) in Kenya received rain in December 2016 and in all cases the amount was depressed and its distribution rated as poor. The National Drought Management Authority (NDMA) early warning reports reveal that the drought status in Isiolo County is alarm worsening, with some areas experiencing emergency food insecurity.   The Government declared the on-going drought a national disaster in February 2017.  

The foregoing situation calls for emergency interventions to avert a human catastrophe by saving lives as well as alleviating further suffering.  

This project will target 1,240 Households comprising of 6,200people (1,120 men , 1,370 women, 1,980 girls, 1,730 boys). It will prioritise population groups most affected by the drought situation who are: women, children and the aged.

title: River Power Pod Africa Project
description:
The River Power Pod (RPP) provides an accessible, sustainable means to produce electricity or pump water where most alternatives cannot.  RPP is a patented in-stream hydro-turbine, drawing energy from flowing water without damming, diverting or altering the natural flow of the river.  Ideally suited as a remote power solution, it is transportable, scalable and can be rapidly deployed and/or relocated. RPPs are easy to install and maintain using widely available materials and methods. Our technology and training can empower local teams of all ages and backgrounds, enabling them to manufacture, install and maintain turbines for their communities – transforming living conditions, creating employment and generating income.
This project will help to build a sustainable solution based on a small team of local young women and men trained to make, install and maintain RPPs. The team will be able to make and maintain the turbines as part of their sustainable enterprise. Supported by the local expertise, skills and track record of CAFOD and the Salesians, this enterprise will be locally owned and managed, using initial contributions of training, skills and financial support to help transform communities and schools.

title: Kenya 2017 Drought Emergency Response in Marsabit and West Pokot Counties
description:
Kenya is facing a severe drought, which is because of failed rains in MAM and OCD long and short rains, respectively. On 10 February 2017, the Government declared a national drought emergency, with 23 of 47 counties affected. The number of food insecure people more than doubled – from 1.3 million to 2.7 million and then 3.0 million people in March. Marsabit( Marsabit diocese) and West Pokot(Kitale diocese) counties are among the worst affected 

Water access and availability has been adversely affected in these areas, with populations having to go through longer walking distances to the scarce water points, since the water points are also drying up, as well as very long waiting times. In Marsabit, for example, the major sources of water for livestock currently is boreholes, which was not normal at this time of the year as the main source is usually water pans. In some places, such as Moyale, Kalacha, Dukana and Gatab shallow wells, water pans and springs were being used. The return trekking distances from grazing areas to water points is 50-70 kilometres for camels, 20-30 kilometres for cattle and 15-25 kilometres for small stock in agro pastoral and pastoral livelihood zones (KFSSG , 2017).

Humanitarian interventions by the Government of Kenya, at both the national and county-level, as well as by other development partners, across various parts of the pastoral and marginal agricultural areas, are likely mitigating the severity of acute food insecurity outcomes. However, insufficient and uncoordinated response efforts to date, in some areas, and lack of clarity on numbers of planned beneficiaries and coverage areas, make it difficult to assess the impacts of the humanitarian assistance and future. FEWSNET has projected that without adequate and sustained humanitarian assistance, more poor households could face Emergency (IPC Phase 4) outcomes between the dry period of July and September, particularly in Marsabit.
In response to the appeal by Caritas international, CAFOD will contribute £50,000 to Caritas Kenya as part of the intervention in Marsabit and West Pokot Counties.

title: Kenya Green Energy Research Case Study
description:
This research will focus specifically on the greenhouse component of the green energy project which aimed to increase the income of women through women’s groups growing horticultural produce in greenhouses (tomatoes) in Kenya. The energy component in these projects was water pumping using solar energy to the greenhouses.  Due to resource and time constraints, the research will focus on greenhouse installations in Kitui county. 
The broad objective is to better understand the model(s) used, to capture learning, and to reflect on the if/how the model could be improved. We also would like to use the CAFOD/IIED Energy Delivery Model (EDM)’ approach (see http://pubs.iied.org/16551IIED/) to help to do this analysis. These objectives can be broken down as follows:
•Understand the project design and business model(s) used for delivering increased income to women through the green houses project – including stakeholders involved, detailed understanding of the business model and value chain, & differences in the model across different sites
•Analysis of the factors that have appeared to contribute to success (including ongoing financial, social and environmental sustainability), as well as challenges faced. This to include better understanding the enabling environment for the projects as well as socio-cultural factors which influenced the design and implementation of the project and/or are currently influencing its success. 
•Reflection on if/how the model could be improved for the future
•Use the CAFOD/IIED energy delivery model approach as a reflective tool to analyse an existing energy service

title: Ethiopian Asylum Seekers Humanitarian Response Project
description:
Following the political instability in Ethiopia in the month of February 2018, civilians crossed over to Kenya in great numbers seeking asylum and triggering a humanitarian crisis.  This was occasioned by the alleged government shooting that left nine civilians dead and scores injured.  The influx of the Ethiopian asylum seekers in Kenya prompted action by the Kenya Government (both National and County), host communities and humanitarian organizations to provide basic needs and services e.g. security, shelter, food and water to the affected population. This led to the establishment of two temporary camps by the Kenyan government initially hosting 9,700 people. The established camps are Somare and Dambala Fachana located in Somare and Dambala Fachana locations respectively. Somare camp is adjacent to the Kenyan Ethiopia Border while Dambala Fachana is seventeen kilometers away from the same border. 

The political situation in Ethiopia improved after the inauguration of the new Prime Minister on April 2, 2018.  This by the willingness of some asylum seekers who went back to their country reducing the number of asylum seekers to approximately 5000 persons. CSG meeting attended by Diocese of Marsbait and CAFOD agreed on 5,000 figure.

The host community has limited resources for example water yet they are magnanimous in their hospitality to the asylum seekers and continues to bear the brunt of sharing scant resources with the Ethiopian asylum seekers.

The management and coordination of the Ethiopian Asylum Seekers’ activities are going on well through the Sub-County Steering Committee (SCSC) chaired by the Moyale Sub-County Commissioner.

title: ISIOLO INTEGRATED FOOD SECURITY PROGRAMME (IIFSP2)
description:
Isiolo County is one of the Counties in the Upper Eastern region of Kenya and covers an area of approximately 25,700 km2. It has an estimated population of 143, 294  .The county which is classified as arid and semi-arid (ASAL) is hot and dry in most months in the year with two rainy seasons: short rains in October and November; long rains in March and May. The rainfall is unreliable with an annual average of 580.2 mm. The County like other ASAL areas is grappling with numerous socio-economic challenges manifested in among other indicators food insecurity, low incomes, unemployment, environmental degradation and inter-community conflicts. In view of these, the key needs of the communities are: Food security: constitutes a key challenge facing the pastoral and Agro-Pastoral communities in Isiolo County. The County has a food poverty rate of 77%. Majority of the people depend primarily on relief food.  Over 80% of the land in the County is non-arable (22,000 km2) and is used for grazing by the pastoralists. Only 1,497 hectares are under food crops production . 
Environmental management: The scarce resources in Isiolo County lead to severe environmental degradation of land and pasture that immensely contribute to the often-experienced inter-ethnic conflicts. Charcoal burning, sand harvesting, overgrazing and overstocking in most parts of the county has been rapidly depleting vegetation leaving land exposed to soil erosion. Environmental degradation has led to decreased vegetation cover; water scarcity due to destruction of water catchments, increase of environment-related diseases such as kalaazar, eyes and respiratory problems. Conflicts: Isiolo County is prone to inter and intra community conflicts triggered by among other factors competition for scarce resources such as pasture and water, cattle rustling, negative perceptions, boundary disputes and political instigations.

title: Integrated Food Security Project, Phase II - Caritas Mombasa
description:
This is phase 2 of the Integrated Food Security Project (IFSP 2), Arch Diocese of Mombasa, in Kwale and Mombasa Counties (KENYA)
In this second phase the IFSP targets to reach people and communities in three sub counties of Mombasa and Kwale namely: Lunga lunga and Kisauni Sub county.  

A total of 1,200 direct beneficiaries (500 males and 700 (female) will be reached over three years, by 2021. 

This project aims to sustain food security interventions through an integrated approach.  The integration strategy will promote food production, livestock rearing (gala goats and poultry), and income generation for target beneficiaries.  SILC group methodology will be used as an entry point for planned activities. In addition, participating community groups will be supported sustainably to manage their natural resources responsibly and to actively engage in Community Led Total Sanitation (CLTS).

It is anticipated that this project will immensely contribute towards achieving food security for Mombasa and Kwale Counties.  Low crop and livestock productivity is mainly caused by: inadequate/erratic rainfall, Crop failure which is widespread in the mixed farming livelihood zones; and inadequate pasture in livestock farming zone. Project interventions are expected to contribute towards sustainable food security, diversified household incomes, and responsible use of natural resources amongst the communities living in Mwakirunge (Kisauni subcounty) and Lunga lunga Sub county by July 2021. 

Project Outcomes:
Outcome 1:  Households sustainably produce adequate food to meet their needs and generate surplus
Outcome 2:  Households have access to stable and diversified income (for dignified livelihoods)
Outcome 3:  Communities sustainably manage water and natural resources

Overall, Caritas Mombasa will contribute towards the overall programme goal of: Sustainable food security, Resilience and peaceful co-existence for poor and vulnerable communities in Kenya

title: Support Improved water access for 800 pastoral households in Noloroi and Tuale villages of Oldonyiro
description:
Lack of adequate access to clean water constitutes among key challenges facing the pastoral communities in Isiolo County with Noloroi and Tuale Villages in Oldonyiro Ward among the hardest hit. The livelihoods of the pastoralists without access, or with very limited access to water are vulnerable because they have difficulty in obtaining food, accumulating other assets, and recuperating after recurrent natural shocks such as drought.
The main goal of this project is to improve water access to 800 pastoral households and 4 institutions (4,000 individuals) in Noloroi and Tuale villages of Oldonyiro Ward, Isiolo County. 
Construction of sand dams and rainwater harvesting systems will increase access to water for domestic and livestock use. Moreover, the water sources will not only increase water availability in the midterm, but it will also promote the livelihood and household economy and create access to basics of life for the targeted as well as build the capacity of the pastoral communities to face shocks. 

Improved access to water will also contribute to reduced distance to water sources which will enable children to have adequate time to study and play instead of spending that time to look for water. Availability of water in schools will allow the children to have enough time for their education rather than go fetch water for the school.

Construction of sand dams and rainwater harvesting systems will provide the long-term answers to the problem of water scarcity. Sand dams are environmentally friendly and provides reliable water within reach by the local people and will also improve water access to livestock. Sand dam has low maintenance cost. Roof catchment in Noloroi and Tuale schools will offer possibilities of collecting rainwater to supplement water collected from the sand dams. Rainwater will be used for drinking and cooking.
participating_orgs: Catholic Agency For Overseas Development (CAFOD) / GB-CHC-285776 / 1 | Catholic Diocese of Isiolo / 4

title: Marsabit Drought Emergency Response Project 2021
description:
The food security situation has been on a worsening trend in the Arid and Semi-Arid (ASAL) counties in Kenya attributed mainly to the poor performance of the October -December 2020 short rains and the March - May 2021 long rains. Both seasons were characterized by late onsets, below average cumulative quantities, and poor distribution both in time and space.
Assistance will be targeted at the worst affected areas which are currently not supported by any partner. A community-based targeting approach will identify people who will receive assistance. These will include female headed households with children under 5 years; pregnant or lactating mothers with children under 5 years; female headed families with no source of income; families with severely or moderately malnourished children or child (under 5 years); households headed by persons living with disabilities with no source of income and child headed households.
 Project Goal is to alleviate suffering and save livelihoods for drought affected persons in Marsabit County
Project Outcomes: Increased food access for 180 and  access to water for 1900 drought affected households in Marsabit County

Specific Objectives
1. To enhance food access for 180 drought affected households in Marsabit County
2. To improve water access for 1900 households in Marsabit County
Activities
provide  100 target households with a half month ration of as per sphere standards for 3 months. This will translate to a food voucher worth KES 5000 per month which will be restricted to essential households’ foodstuffs.
The project will provide assorted food items Worth KES.5000 to 80 families affected by the drought and are in very remote places where there are no shops to redeem food vouchers.
Water trucking for 30days, provision of fuel subsidies and provision of fast moving spare parts to improve water access for 1900hh
participating_orgs: Catholic Agency For Overseas Development (CAFOD) / GB-CHC-285776 / 1 | Catholic Diocese of Marsabit / 4

title: Drought Emergency Response Project in Marsabit, Phase II
description:
Marsabit County is experiencing one of the most severe drought never experienced before, as a result of failure of 5 consecutive rain seasons resulting to extreme water shortage, food insecurity, migration of pastoral communities, resource based conflicts,  malnutrition etc.The situation has been excerbated by high cost of food prices making it beyond reach for many and lack of market for the weak livestock. Currently, water trucking and food assistance (through food distribution, cash transfers and food vouchers) to the most affected people and institutions are amongst some of the drought emergency interventions supported by CAFOD, the National and County Government and all partners working in the humanitarian aid relief. Unless supported through interventions such as water trucking and food donations most people and institutions currently do not have access to safe, clean drinking water and food.
In the ongoing 3rd Phase of CAFOD GEF funding & support from Caritas Australia, the project targets 7 severely drought affected villages with food distribution, food voucher and water trucking, 5 schools with school feeding programs, 40 needy students with food for fees, construction of an underground tank in Tullu Dimtu and borehole drilling in Burgabo. The project is also targeting 11 strategic diesel-run boreholes among drought-affected communities of Marsabit County with the provision of fuel subsidies and 10 boreholes with fast moving spare parts. Additional funding from CAFOD GEF will support 3 villages with food distribution, water trucking, solar relocation in Burgabo and Genset house and school feeding programme for 1 school, and food for fees for 40 students. The direct beneficiaries will include school going children, men, women, pregnant and lactating women, People Living with Disability and youths in these villages. The vulnerable section of the community such as poor, elderly, female-headed households, people living with chronic diseases.
participating_orgs: Catholic Agency For Overseas Development (CAFOD) / GB-CHC-285776 / 1 | Catholic Diocese of Marsabit / 4

title: Promoting Food Security Among Drought Stricken Households in Samburu County
description:
More than 200,000 persons in Samburu County are experiencing extreme water shortages with most of the water points drying. According to NDMA drought bulletin for the month of September 2022, vegetation greenness in Samburu County has remained below the average since the beginning of the year across the livelihood zones. The situation has exposed many families to hunger and starvation. This has been the case too for livestock which is the main source of income for the pastoralist communities in the county. The situation has worsened with a number of deaths (human) being reported from Samburu East and Samburu North sub-counties.
The most affected villages are concentrated in Samburu East and Samburu North sub-counties mostly Nachola, El barta, Ndoto, Suguta Mar Mar, Wamba East, Uaso, Baawa , Wamba North, Wamba East wards and the borders between Samburu, Marsabit, Isiolo, Turkana and Baringo counties.  
The county government, through the department of special programmes and other stakeholders including Caritas Maralal, have since employed a number of interventions especially food drives targeting the most vulnerable households, but the situation is worsening as a result of the drought and insecurity arising from the same.  The situation has forced pastoralists from the entire county to migrate with their livestock to neighbouring counties, especially Laikipia county, in search of water and pasture. The migration has consequently brought about tribal clashes with a number of people losing their lives from the clashes. 
Vulnerable groups in these communities, such as women, children, elderly and young Morans who take care of livestock and households have since been weakened due to lack of food and water among other basic services. 
The project will target the most vulnerable households (250 HHs) in Terter and Keleswa villages of Samburu North sub-county with relief food
participating_orgs: Catholic Agency For Overseas Development (CAFOD) / GB-CHC-285776 / 1 | Catholic Diocese of Maralal / 4

title: Samburu Flood Response
description:
The Kenya Meteolological department predicted  El Nino rains to come from mid October.  The, rains started at the end of october and caused heavy flooding that reached a peak on the 2nd of November. Samburu County is one of the worst effected regions in Kenya, and has been selected as we have a strong presence through local partners that will enable a timely response. In Samburu County, the most affected areas are Samburu East and North sub-counties. Phone discussions with local community leaders has provided a total of 9023 people having been affected at the villages of Lerata, Tangar, Noit, Anderi, Naisunyai and Laparaan . A spike in rainfall is projected due to the ongoing El Nino rains and Samburu county may become affected with  a further population of 9366 people being displaced in other locations that have not be badly hit at the moment. No major support has reached the community except  the rescue missions by the helicopter from the Ormalo Ranch that rescued 8 people that had been swept away in their vehicle.
The funding from Caritas Australia in addition to CAFOD funding(CGF &GEF) will come in handy in adressing the immediate needs of affected population of 6,076 people in the worst affected villages of Anderi, Laparan, Noit and Tangar in Samburu North and Lerata and  Naisunyai in Samburu East, supporting them with food, NFIs, and water treatment chemicals.
participating_orgs: Catholic Agency For Overseas Development (CAFOD) / GB-CHC-285776 / 1 | Catholic Diocese of Maralal / 4

reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: F.a: Human Rights and Forced Eviction Project
description:
Many slum dwellers are under constant threat of illegal and forced evictions and displacement. In 2004, started the Kenya Slum Upgrading Programme to improve the conditions in slums, but the slum dwellers have not been included in the program and the imple
mentation of the program involves many risks. The 1972 Public Health Act, determine the standards of living and quality of water, but authorities did not enforce the law regarding to its implementation in the slums. The draft law Eviction and Resettlement 
Bill 2012, about the forced evictions and resettlement, is approved for the Parliament processing. The bill guarantees citizens the humane treatment of such cases before the eviction, during and after it. KISORA has been involved in the preparation of the 
draft law and in its lobbing. The objective is to strengthen the community-based advocacy in the realization of ESC rights: the aim is to strengthen the capacity of slum dwellers to demand the implementation of economic and social rights, particularly the 
right to adequate housing, and lobby for the administration to run according to the requirements of the main international human rights instruments. In addition, the project aims to increase the knowledge of members of the community about the economic and 
social rights. The aim is to strengthen the cooperation in the grass-roots level and to increase the KISORAn internal capacity to take action so that it would be a strong and responsible actor. Project's direct beneficiaries are the communities living in s
lums under the threat of eviction. In addition, the project is targeted at 33 grassroots organizations in Kisumu East District. Indirect beneficiaries are the other residents in the slums of Kisumu East District. KISORA (Kisumu Social Rights Association) S
elf Help Group was established in 2007, and it is a network for human rights lobbying groups operating in grass-roots slums.http://hakijamii.wordpress.com/hakijamiis-partners/kisumu-social-rights-association-kisora
participating_orgs: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland / FI-3 / 1 | KIOS Foundation | Kansalaisjärjestöjen ihmisoikeussäätiö / 22000-299 / 3

description:
Eastlands is one of a Nairobi slums. Human rights abuses and lack of awareness of the rights and the law is common in the slum. Poorly implemented are, for example, the right to housing, to sanitation, to water, to health and to education. Just as bad is a
lso implemented in the access to justice: The legal processes are slow and too expensive for the residents , the authorities are corrupt , little educated and ignorant of the contents of the law and the police is guilty of numerous human rights violations.
 The main objective of the project is to increase Eastlands slum-dwellers's awareness of their rights and their access to justice, as well as to support human rights defenders's grassroots work.Beneficiaries of the project are th residents of 14 slums. In 
addition, the project builds capacity of Kaplet’s members on legal assistance, as well as on more efficient organizational work, eg . their information technology skills will be improved . Kaplet was founded by six legal advisers in Kamukunji in Nairobi 
in 2009 and the organization was registered in the same year . http://www.kaplet.org/

reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: F.a: Meibeki Valley Area Development Project
description:
The programme works for the improvement of rural communities’ socio-economic situation and quality of life, as well for the strengthening of community capacities and enhancing children’s rights in Meibeki Valley, Western Kenya.At the beginning of the p
rogramme, water and sanitation were inadequate and the availability of clean water was weak. This was also reflected in children's health and education. One of the main goals has been the availability of clean drinking water. At present the water supply sy
stem consists of a more than 162 km long pipeline. Clean water has permanently changed the life of more than 35 000 persons. The evaluation report shows that 89% of households have now access to clean water less than 500m from their homes during the rainy 
season and 61.7 %, respectively during the dry season . (In 2004: 1.4%)More than 7,000 children are now able to go to school and have time to do their homework, when their time is not needed for fetching water. To ensure better educational possibilities fo
r the children, educational conditions have been improved with the support of the parents. Already more than 2,500 children study in the improved classrooms. With the support of the program, two dormitories have been constructed for secondary school girls.
 The program beneficiaries are the 54,000 inhabitants living in the area, especially women and children, who used use several hours a day to fetch water. Having clean water closer to the homes has freed time for time for other things as well as brought new
 income opportunities, like vegetable farming, agriculture and caring for livestock. A change in the women's role can be seen: there are many women as village chiefs and school attendance among girls has grown considerably. Children's participation in coll
ective decision-making is encouraged through the Children's Parliament. Children and young people are represented in the village committee and the water committee.The main partner is World Vision Kenya that runs the implementation and accounts for the use 
of funding.In addition there are many partners from different ministries, regional government officials, and religious communities.
participating_orgs: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland / FI-3 / 1 | Suomen World Vision / 22000-175 / 3

reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: F.a: Mogotio Area Development Project
description:
The programme works for the improvement of rural communities’ socio-economic situation and quality of life, as well for the strengthening of community capacities and enhancing children’s in Mogotio, Western Kenya.The 2012 evaluation showed a clear impr
ovement in key areas , though still only a fifth of the population have access to clean water (2007: 8.7%). When a child is ill, health services are now used by 80 percent of the mothers ( 27% in 2007 ), and 92.7 % children are vaccinated. Children's right
s have become known in the community, 95.5 % of the population now knows what child maltreatment means. The knowledge on how HIV infections are spread and on testing and support facilities has increased within the population of Mogotio. The evaluation reco
mmends that the next period of work focus would shift more and more to strengthen local capacity. In particular, access to clean water and sanitation and malnutrition among children is still a challenge.The new five -year plan has been completed and the fi
rst year of Implementation has started. Increasing the availability of clean drinking water has been initiated through the rehabilitation of water points. In addition co-operation with the Ministry of Health has been started to diminish water related disea
ses and diarrhea and a campaign has been launched for every household and school to get a toilet. Cooperation has also been done with the Ministry of Health through training of community health workers on the care and follow-up of the health of children an
d expectant mothers. In addition emphasize has been given to birth registration. Children's participation in collective decision-making is encouraged through Children's Parliament and the situation of women and girls are supported through focus on harmful 
traditions such as female genital mutilation and early marriages, as well as acts of violence against girls. The program beneficiaries are the 23,500 persons living in the programme area. The main partner is World Vision Kenya that runs the implementation 
and accounts for the use of funding.

reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: F.a: Tinderet Area Development Programme
description:
The programme works for the improvement of rural communities’ socio-economic situation and quality of life, as well for the strengthening of community capacities and enhancing children’s in Tinderet, Western Kenya.The main objectives of the previous pe
riod have been Children's rights and child protection. The evaluation shows that the work has been fruitful; child rights violations have decreased from 92.4% in 2009 to 34.3%. Child labor has also been halved during the same period. In addition work has b
een done to decrease waterborne diseases and improve general health. Health services are now closer. 70 per cent of the population has access to health services within a distance of less than five kilometers. Every third person is currently receiving clean
 water compared to only one in eight at the beginning of the programme. Through renovations of water points and sanitation trainings diarrhea and waterborne diseases have been reduced. Within disability work positive cooperation has been continued with loc
al disability institution. HIV trainings are organized through support groups and seminars. The women’s AIDS run, providing information and testing possibilities has gathered great popularity. Community members have been trained in public responsibility 
and cooperation has been established with local actors, authorities and cooperations. Children's participation in collective decision-making is encouraged through Children's Parliaments.The program covers an area of six centers with a population of about 3
5 000 people. The main partner is World Vision Kenya that runs the implementation and accounts for the use of funding.

informal settlements of Kibera and Mukuru by means of improved management of human waste increased access to sanitation services and safe water and improved community health. The project continues to build on the ecological sanitation facilities constructe
d in Phase I (bio-center and UDDTs) thus supporting existing structures but adding a new concept of closing the sanitation circle by focusing on end-use and marketing of the final products.The objective will be achieved through:a) Research development and 
marketing of by-products i.e. bio-gas from the bio-center and urine and compost from the composting latrinesb) Construction of one bio-center with water kioskc) Developing the capacity of community-based resource persons and artisans in the design planning

ity-managed water and sanitation financing facilityThe project will directly benefit 1500 users from the new and the already existing bio-centre as well as the pupils and teachers using composting latrines primarily through access to improved sanitation fa
cilities; increase in artisan skills for 100 people increased hygiene promotion through 60 trained ToTs; and income generation from the sale of by-products and wages paid to the artisans. Equal access will be available to women men children and the disable

title: WASH project in Turkana
description:
Turkana is in many ways the most underdeveloped area in Kenya. The proposed project aims to improve the area?s wellbeing by providing assistance in water supply and sanitation sectors in the neediest villages in northern Turkana County which have been sele
cted by the Turkana community themselves.During the project efforts are made to repair and rehabilitate dysfunctional water wells in the project area. In addition ca. 10 new wells with water pans and 10-20 hygienic latrines will be built and also the commu
nities are educated in the proper ways to operate and manage the mentioned facilitie.The Turkanas haven?t needed to pay fees regarding the use of drinkable water in the past. We have learned during our preparatory mission that most of the wells built in th
e Turkana County have not been properly handed over to the consumers/villages which has led to poor understanding on the ownership and responsibility issues. During the project WaterFinns develops together with the Turkana communities a maintenance and man
agement model which will be implemented in the use of the water points and the improved hygienic environment.The perennial boreholes will contribute to people living in stationary villages near schools increase the attendance in schools and decrease the nu
mber of people affected by using unsafe drinking water. This will provide a steady and healthy environment for the children and youth to grow up in.The Project aims to achieve its purpose through three interlinked results (outputs):1: Lessons learned from 
success and failure of long-term sustainability of rural WASH services reported and benchmarks of best practices promoted.2: Strengthened capacities of selected CBOs village spokesmen and wards in their management and efforts of further improving the WASH 
services.3: Improved WASH facilities in selected communities in order to fulfill their needs and HR requirements on a sustainable basis.A key element of the proposed project is to create opportunities for the future water sector professionals to have an in
teresting and unique possibility to participate in voluntary work which focuses on long-term learning of the sustainable schemes.The proposed project partner (GWAKO) has amble experience to carry out rural water and sanitation projects and they also have e
xperience in working in the northern Turkana County. reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: FLC: Strengthening local natural resources management (NRM) institutions and empowering local communities advocate for improved governance
description:
Community-based Natural Resources Management (CBNRM) is a development approach that supports natural resource conservation. More conservation-minded people will define CBNRM as a natural resources conservation approach that brings along income and employme
nt. One could also argue that conservation of natural resources and sustainable use of these resources for the benefit of the community are two sides of the same coin. The community is more inclined to conserve natural resources if is able to realize benef

title: F.a: Family Welfare Development Programme
description:
The communities in arid rural areas of Kenya are in need of holistic development for community member's wellbeing and families’ sustainable development. While the young people are left without education possibilities and employment, many of them end up i
n the streets of big cities and fall into a lifestyle of substance abuse and crime. The culturally harmful customs and gender inequality hinders girls’ educational possibilities. Communities’ wellbeing is developed holistically; families, children and 
young people are trained in human rights and gender equality issues, and the project has a strong emphasis on psychosocial support according to needs. The child protection policy is developed and monitored in practice. The project reaches out to the young 
people in Nairobi slum, Kawangare, and offers a wholesome alternative for their lifestyle of crime and substance abuse. Environment conservation awareness is created on all levels of society; in schools, among farmers, and households, as the more efficient
 and environmentally beneficial methods of farming, water harvesting and use, and fuel are introduced. Educationally the project ensures access to school for hundreds of children, including disabled, who traditionally are culturally shunned. The project go
al is to create impact on wellbeing of children and youth, their families and the whole communities, by responding to cultural, environmental and social challenges. The project purpose is to equip families and communities with skills and resources for sust
ainable development of their own wellbeing, to provide access to quality education to vulnerable children, and to take care of their environment as a source of livelihood. The project results in children’s increased access to schools as the parents are a
ble to provide their children’s school fees. Awareness about environmental conservation, WASH, tree planting and health issues increases and the social standing of the disabled, girls and other vulnerable groups strengthens. The project benefits children
, youth, their families, farmers, and the communities as a whole through a long-term impact. The churches also benefit by gaining recognized positive social influence in their communities. Fida partners with Full Gospel Churches of Kenya (FGCK).
