results_text:
Capacity development | Development of AoA website began as part of a long-term strategy as repository for journalists and journalism students tools and resources. Staff procurement began as part of AoA internal capacity development. Preparations for the April launch of the Top Story, weekly investigative journalism serial on Kenya Broadcasting Corporation 1 were started as part of AoA commitment to accountability journalism and media literacy in Kenya. | see outcomes | Accountability: Media hold power-holders to account and are accountable to their public | Kenyan journalists regularly produce investigative journalism reportages that have positive society impacts and hold political leaders and decision-makers accountable specifically through the field of development reporting and a media literate citizenry. | 2016: Top Story (media literacy initiative) - development journalism competition for university students and media literacy TV serial continued planning and pre-production activities. Focus group of 19 University journalism students: study of youth view of media's role in democracy. Focus group of 20 University non-journalism students: study of youth view of media's role in democracy. The first competition took place in 2016. 2017: sixty journalism students from twenty Kenyan Universities compete in investigative journalism competition 'Top Story'. Teams produce reportages on vital developmental issues in Kenya. Development of audience baseline/media literacy survey in preparation for premiere of 'Top Story' on Kenyan Broadcasting Corporation (KBC). In Q2 a quantitative baseline survey to assess the current public literacy level on role of the media and investigative journalism and issues relating to accountability and good governance in Kenya was carried out. The survey had a sample size of about 1100 people who were all interviewed at their homes in all the 8 regions of the country. The aim of the survey is to inform decisions by AoA as it seeks to address the challenges faced by investigative journalists by initiating projects that help improve the quantity and quality of in-depth, researched and compelling stories on good governance, citizen empowerment, gender and development issues. 9 university teams that qualified for the next stage of the Top Story competition conducted TV interviews with Kenyan decision makers at the national level. Among those interviewed are Kenya’s Foreign Affairs Minister, Amina Mohamed and the CEO of the most successful bank in East Africa. The AoA Top Story TV reality show on Kenya Broadcasting Corporation premiered in April and airs every Sunday/Tuesday nights. It continues to be highly active on social media for its audience engagement and marketing and regularly trends in Kenya on twitter. AoA started its Kenya general election-related activities by identifying and recruiting five community radio stations that will benefit from tailored training to help them produce and broadcast public debates in which the local community will come face to face with their leaders/aspiring leaders and hold them to account. The recording of the debates begins in mid-July and will run until election time. A call for applications for the Carey Institute non-fiction mentoring program was announced with many applications from Kenya reviewed by AoA. Q3: Top Story Season 2 moved from the state-owned Kenya Broadcasting Corporation (KBC) to the leading TV news station in Kenya, KTN. At KTN the programme was given a prime slot at Thursdays 7.30pm. With KBC still running repeats of Top Story Season 1, it means that the show has been airing in two stations at the same, reaching different audiences nationwide. Top Story Season 2 is reaching a weekly audience of 800,000 – 1,000,000 viewers on KTN. Early audience feedback is positive with recognition of the value of the show in promoting professionalism in the media at a time when Kenyan media has been criticised for abandoning its watchdog role. Q4: The Top Story university journalism challenge entered the semi-final stage in this quarter, during which the competing teams were each required to identify a high-profile personality who has made a difference in Kenya and interview them for TV. This a variation of the normal format of producing development stories from the field. It has had the effect of stretching the skills of the student journalists, especially in conducting high profile interviews. In this quarter, the Top Story audience continued to grow, reaching a peak of 1.8 million homes in October. One Kenyan journalist was selected to take part in the Carey Institute non-fiction mentoring programme. With this support, she will produce a documentary on the healthcare system in Kenya. 2018: Q1 The Top Story University Investigative Journalism Competition and TV show season 2 came to an on 25th March with the announcement of winners. There were four finalists and each team of 3 students had produced their own 3-minute TV report for the judges on an issue of public concern. At a well-attended gala finale, Mount Kenya University were declared the winner for their story that investigated the cartels that work in collusion with city water authorities to create artificial shortage of water in Nairobi suburbs and make a huge profit from selling the residents water. The highlight of the event was a presentation by one of Africa’s leading investigative journalists, Anas Aremeyaw Anas from Ghana. He received a standing ovation from the audience for his thought provoking and inspiring presentation that challenged the young journalists to take up investigative journalism and tackle the big issues affecting the Kenyan society today. As a result of the huge interest that Top Story show has attracted, the number of universities applying to participate in Season three has jumped from 20 to 30. The ability of the show to reach a big national audience continues to highlight the importance of a free and independent media in holding duty bearers to account. Q2: A Top Story national impact survey was carried out in June of over 1000 Kenyan households. It also included a qualitative study. The show was watched by approximately 5 million Kenyans every week. Q3: Top Story Africa Season 2 completed its broadcast on the KTN national TV network. It was on air for 54 weeks including repeats. Top Story reporting teams produced real-time investigative reportages that reached a nationwide audience which averaged over 900,000 viewers weekly. Through a detailed national audience survey on Top Story, viewers gained insights into the importance of a free and independent media in holding duty bearers to account. Due to Top Story’s popularity, AoA director Joseph Warungu has become a regular guest on the KTN TV show that reviews news events in East Africa and includes a special focus on global best practice of journalism. Q4: Top Story began its outreach phase by launching tours into universities across Kenya. The aim is to extend the value that competitors get from the mentorship project to a wider group of students a faculty. The tour offers the Top Story experience of public lectures on topical themes such as fake news, safety of journalists and public accountability. The tour also exposes the young journalists to professional ways of working including giving them the opportunity to see and handle modern television equipment and facilities. The first tour at Technical University of Kenya 28 October focused on the theme of digital self-publishing. Industry professionals including Top Story mentors gave talks and shared best practice when using social media and other digital platforms like YouTube and video blogs to tell stories. The event, which was fully practical and interactive, was attended by over 400 students and lecturers (~230 male, ~180 female). It was filed and broadcast live on Facebook. 2019 Q1: Top Story Season 3 went into pre-production in January - March, starting with the process of recruiting the universities that will take part in the new competition. 24 universities have confirmed participation in this year’s Top Story Season 3 competition. There will be 72 students taking part, with each university selecting its best three final-year journalism students. It is mandatory for each team to ensure that there is a mix of gender. Q2: Top Story Lecturers Workshop – the one-day workshop was held on 26th April 2019 in Nairobi and was attended by 25 lecturers from the 25 different universities that will be taking part in Top Story Season 3. There were 19 male and 6 female lecturers in attendance. The aim of the workshop was to review Season 2 and to brief the lecturers about the requirements of Top Story Season 3. This included competition rules, criteria for team selection and a discussion on the themes that will be covered. The lecturers received some basic training on data journalism as well as storytelling tips that the students will be required to apply. Some of the key themes for season 3 include fake news, safety of journalists and the importance of gender-nuanced approach to sourcing stories. Season 2 Winners Media Internship/Tour to UK – The top prize for the winners of Top Story season 2 was a week’s sponsored media mentorship trip to London. The winners, Mount Kenya University, travelled to London accompanied by Joseph Warungu of AoA as well as the show’s director, Bonnie Katei who documented the entire trip on video. The trip was from 19th – 26th May 2019. The team were hosted at BBC headquarters in London, the Aljazeera London studios at the Shard and Colourful Radio at the Africa Centre where they were interviewed live on air. The winners also travelled out of London to visit the University of Central Lancashire in Preston, which collaborates with AfricaonAir in Kenya. Q3: Filming and production of Top Story Season 3 started on 4 September 2019 with the judges assessing the entry videos for each university team, which were produced by the students followed by bootcamp training in Mombasa for the 17 teams that qualified. 25 universities entered Top Story Season 3, 75 students in total started the competition. Q4: Top Story Season 4 premiered on 4th November 2019 on a new channel, NTV. It’s owned by the biggest media house in East Africa, the Nation Media Group. NTV broadcasts nationwide and is available across Africa on the Multichoice DSTV satellite channels. Top Story was given a prime evening slot of 7.30pm, which is straight after the early evening news at 7pm. Top Story won Silver award in the Global Youth and News Media prize 2019. Two Top Story season 2 finalists were in Paris in November to receive the prize, accompanied by the Top Story Executive Producer. The award presentation took place at NewsXchange, an annual meeting that gathers hundreds of news executives, journalists, bloggers and start-up entrepreneurs from around the world to share, learn and cross-pollinate ideas with an array of experts, scientists, artists and thought leaders. News of the Top Story award was broadcast on NTV News at prime time and published in the Daily Nation, Kenya’s leading newspaper as well as online. The Top Story TV show and online audience engagement remain the biggest tools of visibility for Top Story and AfricaonAir. It’s the only show in Kenya that is being broadcast on two separate national TV channels at the same time. A repeat of the entire Season 2 is on air every Saturday evening on the state-owned Kenya Broadcasting Corporation TV, while Season 3 is broadcast on Monday evening on the rival NTV station. 2020 Q1: Top Story Season 3 entered the semi-final stage in February with six universities competing for a slot in the finals, which will feature only four universities. The semi-finals involved 18 contestants. They all attended a training workshop an East Africa Correspondent for the South African Broadcasting Corporation (SABC) based in Nairobi. The training was aimed at equipping the students with relevant skills to produce a quality TV feature story. The stories the teams tackled were: 1. Mental health and young people in Kenya. 2. How universal free education disadvantages pupils in rural schools in Kenya. 3. The impact of climate change on Lake Naivasha, one of Kenya’s largest fresh water lakes. 4. How art is being used to capture and retell Kenya’s history 5. Upcoming Kenyan athletes’ battles for world fame 6. The rising cases of medical negligence in Kenya These stories took the contestants to different parts of Kenya, including Eldoret in the west, Naivasha in the Rift Valley and Kajiado in the south. Each team was provided with a professional film crew, but the students had to direct the filming and editing of the material for their TV feature story. The biggest threat to Top Story Season 3 and AoA’s activities in general has been the outbreak of Covid19. The closure of hotels and meeting places has hampered the filming of the finalists’ stories. Q2: Top Story SN3 concluded its semi-final stage in May and took a break due to the Corona virus situation in Kenya. The imposition of travel restrictions between Nairobi and the rest of the country in mid-March made it impossible for the final stage of the competition to take place. The broadcast of the programmes on the national NTV channel was therefore put on hold until the final stages of the competition are filmed. However, on 6th July the president lifted the ban on travel to and from Nairobi to other regions of the country. They are therefore beginning to plan for the resumption of filming. As of May 2020, a total of 23 episodes of Top Story Season 3 have been broadcast at prime time each Monday night on the national NTV channel. The Monday night show and the repeat on Saturday late afternoon helped AoA reach a combined audience of about 1.4 million people in Kenya. Nation Media Group offered promotion for the Top Story show on TV and the Daily Nation newspaper.
Q3: The programme is back on prime time every Monday evening at 7.30pm. They will have produced a total of 30 episodes for Top Story season 3 by the time the season ends. | Gender and Inclusiveness: Media content is increasingly gender-sensitive and reflects social and cultural diversity and participation | AfricaonAir embeds reporting on issues of gender and diversity in their training materials and resources. | Q1: Sixty Kenyan journalism students were trained at the 'Top Story' bootcamp on reporting on gender and diversity, how to look for stories on gender issues and reach out to sources of information on these themes (Limuru, 20-21 February 2017). Development of distance learning module in cooperation with Foreign Policy Interrupted as part of their international gender fellowship programme. Two female journalists were selected to take part in the upcoming four-week programme. Q2: Four-week gender fellowship distance learning module completed with feature story and op-eds produced by Kenyan female journalists led by Foreign Policy Interrupted. Planning steps taken to establish Kenya-based media gender communication advocacy tools for team of female journalists. Reportages related to gender issues continue to be investigated as part of Top Story university journalism competitions. Q3: AfricaonAir and EJC have been collaborating with Foreign Policy Interrupted, on the first FPI Genders Fellows programme designed specifically for Kenya. AoA nominated two Kenyan journalists who underwent distance-learning sessions and individual reportage mentoring by FPI. The FPI rep later traveled to Nairobi for a workshop to finalise feature story outputs for publication on women's issues. The two Gender Fellows will create their own monthly version of FPI’s weekly newsletter, carefully curating and showcasing Kenyan female journalism talent, disseminating to stakeholders and media outlets across the country. The overall aim is to increase women's overall voice and visibility in the media in Kenya. Q4: Top Story journalism challenge is the flagship project and it routinely integrates gender. University teams taking part in the competition are required, as a rule to observe gender equity. The big following for the show has also seen Top Story begin to receive ideas and suggestions from the general public on development stories that they would like to see featured, including the fight against female genital mutilation (FGM). The Kenyan monthly version of FPI’s weekly newsletter was published twice. Kenya Interrupted is produced by two Gender Fellows who curate and showcase Kenyan female journalism talent. Using its big database and wide network, AfricaonAir helps distribute the newsletter to stakeholders and media outlets across the country. The main objective is to increase women's overall voice and visibility in the media in Kenya. This is the first initiative of its kind in Kenya that amplifies women’s voice and it reaches many influential people. The AoA team itself is constructed on the principle of gender equality. 2018: Q1 AfricaonAir has now fully adopted a policy of integrating gender in its initiatives. All universities taking part in the Top Story competition are required to ensure that their teams have gender balance and this includes the production teams that work on the TV show. Based on strategy meeting in Nairobi in March Meeting, Kenya Interrupted will be expanded to East Africa (in cooperation with Tanzanian Media Foundation), more frequent newsletter and preparation for social media presence. Q2: Kenya Interrupted (KI) continues to be distributed through AfricaonAir’s growing mailing list and now that the AoA website has been revamped, the newsletter will also be made available on the site. At a meeting (organised in Dar es Salaam on 8 June) led by the KI curators and Kenyan strategist several issues were discussed, that included the addition of Tanzanian female journalist produced content, social media presence, collaborative visibility events and continued expansion of content from additional countries in East Africa. AoA continues to receive and analyse feedback from the monthly newsletter. Q3: Preparations for an Interrupted Africa meeting in Dar es Salaam on 31 Oct-02 November about expanding the initiative (incl. more countries). Q4: Interrupttr Africa meeting, was held on 31 Oct-2 November in Dar es Salaam. A monthly newsletter by women journalists/experts on important issues in Africa will be published. Three experts from Kenya are part of the team. 2019 Q1: AoA has integrated gender in its activities. It is a condition of the Top Story Season 3 competition that all university teams taking part must have a mix of gender in their teams. In addition, AoA has instituted a requirement that the film crews involved in the competition must have mixed gender. The same principle is being observed in the recruitment of judges and mentors for the competition. AoA through its director published an informative article on the obstacles that stand in the way of gender equality at the decision-making level in Kenya and proposed ways to push forward a bill tabled in parliament to ensure gender equality in leadership. The article was published by BBC Online: https://www.bbc.com/news/world-africa-46507685. As a result of this article, AoA was approached by Women Deliver, a global organisation that champions gender equality about the possibilities of providing training to Kenyan journalists on gender equality in late 2019. Q3: AoA policy of requiring student teams must be of mixed gender was successful. In Season One of TS the teams were hugely male-dominated but now the gap is closing. 43% of the student participants were female and 57% were male. Q4: AoA has a firm commitment to gender equality at AfricaonAir and are continuously looking for opportunities to further integrate gender in operations and projects. Top Story relies on a filming crew of freelancers, but unfortunately in Kenya the number of women working in certain areas of production such as camera and sound operators is still very low. In Season 3 of Top Story we managed to promote one of the film personnel to become a senior director and head of content. 2020 Q2: AoA continues to work in accordance with its gender polices which aim to achieve a 50/50 gender balance in all its activities. The Top Story competition rules ensure that no one gender occupies more than two thirds of the slots in competing teams. | DD Indicators | DD1: # of laws, policies and norms, implemented for sustainable and inclusive development | DD2: # of laws, policies and norms/attitudes, blocked, adopted, improved for sustainable and inclusive development | DD3 # of times that CSOs succeed in creating space for CSO demands and positions through agenda setting, influencing the debate and/or creating space to engage | DD4: # of advocacy initiatives carried out by CSOs, for, by or with their membership/constituency | DD5: # of CSOs with increased L&A capacities | DD6: # of CSOs included in Strategic Partnership programmes | Sustainability development: Media increasingly operate as efficient and self-sustaining organisations. | AoA has a sustainable strategic business plan and is a hub for continuing education and journalism training in Kenya. | 2016: An office manager and a research/social media assistant have been hired to improve audience and stakeholder engagement as well as keep track of media developments in Kenya and the East Africa region; AfricaonAir website is upgraded for fund-raising visibility purposes, new partnerships inc IREX International and co-funding donor strategy. Long term sustainability strategy has led to production of job profiles including Office and Programme Manager, Multimedia Producer, Research Assistant. Development of AoA and Top Story websites and branding, continued upgrading of visibility strategy. 2017: new staff was hired as part of AoA's long term sustainability strategy: Multimedia Producer , Social Media/Websites Administrator, Office Assistant and Production Runner. AoA and 'Top Story' launched new websites and greatly expanded their social media presence. AoA and Top Story continue to be highly active on social media for its audience engagement and marketing and regularly trends in Kenya on twitter #TopStorySn2. 2018: Q1 Top Story has a successful digital media component that has helped it to build and interact with a growing number of followers online. Top Story trends regularly on social media through the efforts of its dedicated digital team of former contestants. Q2: The Top Story national impact survey was carried out in June by an independent research organisation which included a qualitative study. According to the survey the Top Story Show, launched in 2016 and aired twice a week on KTN TV (previously on KBC), is currently known across the country by more than a third of the population (approximately 36%) and has been watched by 25% of the population. The weekly reach/viewership number for the programme has grown from 6% since launch to a current 10%. This translates to 5 million Kenyans who watch the programme every week.  Top story show largely appeals to young people; more than 50% of its audience are the youth i.e. those below 30 years, both in rural and urban areas. The show’s appeal across gender is uniform but skewed towards educated audience. Q3: AoA has been actively seeking new partnerships with donors and commercial organisations and CSOs to make its activities sustainable. Many of the student participants have secured jobs in the media industry after taking part in Top Story Africa: the show has both raised the capacity and skills of young journalists to be employed and raised the visibility of their personal abilities. Q4: AfricaonAir continues to increase and diversify their sources of income through the prep work around the launch of a training school – the Top Story Academy – and the construction of a studio that will be used for in-house productions but also available for commercial use. AfricaonAir began the process to develop a new business plan with the goal to become self-sustaining over the next three years. 2019 Q1: Work to establish the Top Story Journalism School has started. The school will comprise a Radio and TV studio for practical work and a newsroom for the trainees. Architectural plans for the studio have been finalised and submitted for planning permission to the Nairobi City Council. A firm of broadcast studio consultants has been contracted and the preliminary work on the site has started. AoA has 20 applicants waiting to join the first group of trainees when the school opens in September 2019. AoA has contracted Research Group Africa to design and carry out a series of short surveys throughout the length of the Top Story Season 3 competition. This will create a continuous feedback loop that will help track and measure the impact of Top Story and also attitudes to investigative/in-depth journalism in Kenya. Q2: Work is still ongoing to establish the Top Story Academy, a journalism finishing school that is part of AoA’s sustainability initiative. The refurbishment work is scheduled to be completed in Q3. AoA has carried out surveys in preparation of Top Story Season 3. Lecturers gave their feedback during their training day and contestants are currently completing their survey. The data will be compiled into a report and recommendations that will inform the design of Top Story Season 3, which is currently in pre-production phase. AoA’s sustainability strategy is mainly pegged on its journalism finishing school, which continues its development path. The idea is to offer short refresher courses to new and serving journalists at a fee. Once completed, the radio/TV recording studio will also be available for commercial hire. In addition, AoA has applied to be officially registered as a filming agent. This licence will allow AoA to act as an agent for overseas film crews planning to work in Kenya, thus expanding our revenue streams. Q3: Training curriculum for the school is currently being developed with support from academic experts. The refurbishment work was delayed by planning permission hitches, but this has now been resolved. The first intake of trainees will be in Q1 of 2020. In TS SN3 AoA has established a quality monitoring system. At each level of the competition, students and lecturers are asked to give feedback on the quality of the training, mentors and other processes with a view to make improvements. AoA now keeps a detailed database of the student’ progress during and after the competition. This helps to keep track of the impact that Top Story is having on them and their work and assists AoA in taking a long-term approach to sustainability of the programme. Through AoA director’s new consulting role with East Africa’s biggest media house (Nation Media Group), AoA is receives heightened visibility and recognition. It also gives AoA a close view of how the industry works, which then feeds back to the design and delivery of its projects including Top Story so that they are further aligned with the needs of the industry. Q4: Sustainability is going to be one of the main areas of focus in 2020. They exploring a number of options starting from launch of the journalism school to partnering with relevant organisations regarding Top Story. The aim is to ensure production of Season 4 of Top Story by raising supplementary funding from other sources. 2020 Q1: AoA’s main strategy for sustainability is finding corporate organisations to partner with, including hotel chains, airlines, campaign groups whose issues resonate with AoA’s interests. We also aim to lean on our close relationships with the 25 universities that take part in the competition and come up with an appropriate cost-share model for running the competition. In Season 3, AoA partnered with the government-owned Kenya Railways Corporation to provide subsidised transport for students, lecturers and film crew attending the bootcamp in Mombasa. Q2: In Top Story Season 3, AoA entered into partnerships with different organisations to help in various aspects of training and production. BBC donated a fake news and verification trainer from its Factfinder programme. The Kenya Railways Corporation supported AoA through discounted train tickets to and from Mombasa, while PrideIn Hotel in Mombasa offered subsidised rates. The Kenya Cultural Centre in Nairobi also supported the production through discounted rates for the hire of a venue to film the judges’ sessions. | Capacity Development in Lobby & Advocacy: Media developed the skills to work as change catalysts in Lobby and Advocacy. | Journalists work professionally/ethically and safely through capacity building at post-graduate level and on specialised reporting topics. Challenges are increasing security, legal and physical threats to independent media actors. | 2016: Implementation of Security Training for Journalists in cooperation with IREX International and the National Centre for Counter Terrorism (September, 11 participants). Implementation of Food Security workshop for 14 Kenyan journalists in cooperation with food security CSO reps (December 2016, 14 participants). 2017: Sixty Kenyan journalism students were trained on the following topics: Video production, Editorial guidelines, Safety/Security, TV presenting and Reporting, Digital management, Ethics, Interviewing/Investigative techniques and Gender reporting in preparation of 'Top Story' Investigative Journalism Competition (20-24 February 2017). Sixty Kenyan journalism students receive in-the-field practical journalism training as they produce investigative reportages. Students are continuously mentored and critiqued by AoA and Top Story journalist staff. Q3: AoA conducted a series of training sessions before the general election in August to support community radio stations hold local leaders to account, through public debates. AoA chose to focus on marginalised regions or places at risk of political violence, such as the Mt Elgon area in Western Kenya. The debates involved a studio audience drawn from the local community, who interacted directly and question their elected and potential leaders directly. Over 150 people took part in the debates, which were broadcast to large audiences. The topics tackled included the role of the local County Assembly; accountability and funding the right development priorities at the local level. Youth and women were the majority in the audience. AoA will publish a localised version of a handbook developed by EJC on ‘Reporting on Development’. Safety has now become one of AoA’s most important priorities. At the start of each Top Story competition, all competitors now must undergo a mandatory intensive digital safety training session conducted by one of Kenya’s leading experts. In addition, AoA has put in place physical safety measures for crew and competitors when travelling to different places for fieldwork. This includes a ban on night driving, inspection of locations and means of transport in advance to ensure they meet safety requirements and the presence of police/security guards at all filming locations. In addition, a group personal accident insurance policy is always in place at all stages of the competition. AfricaonAir is very safety-conscious. We follow international standards of safety adopted from BBC when planning filming/public events. This includes doing a safety audit on venues and hotels before booking. AoA finalised the publication of a localised version of the EJC Reporting Development Handbook. There is a lot interest for it and it will be distributed soon, including during the awards ceremony for Top Story winners. Q4: AfricaonAir Director was a key speaker and panellist at a media event in Nairobi in December. It was to launch a report on how Kenyan media covered the general election in Kenya. The overall assessment was that media did not do a great job of covering the election. A combination of intimidation of the media and self-censorship resulted in the lack of critical reporting during the election. 2018: Q1 The Reporting Development Handbook, produced in collaboration with EJC has been published and is now available for distribution. There will be a formal launch in June. AoA completed a first print run of the EJC Reporting Development Handbook distributed to participants at Top Story Finale. Q2: The handbook on Reporting Development was published in March and was distributed to the 20 universities participating in the Top Story competition. It continues to be distributed and has been well received among the media and journalism community. Copies have also been sent to media stakeholders, including journalism trainers. AfricaonAir featured prominently in the inaugural Symposium on the Future of African Journalism organised in Nairobi (26-27 June) by the University of Central Lancashire and its partner universities in Kenya. The winners of the Top Story Season 2 competition (Mount Kenya University) were invited as panellists to one of the key discussions of the day. In addition, the winning stories from Top Story were screened at the event. Q3: AoA continues to find opportunities for distributing the development reporting handbook, especially events that bring together key media institutions and practitioners. AfricaonAir supported the Kenya Media Week, which was organised on 12-14 September, by Media Focus Africa, a Kenyan NGO that supports improvement of standards in media through public events and dialogue. A number of high profile media personalities attended the event and shared their experience. AoA was among the media organisations that took part in the exhibition during Kenya Media Week. Q4: AoA continues to find opportunities for distributing the ‘Reporting Development, A guide for African Journalists’ handbook and raise the visibility of AfricanOnAir in the region. The guide was utililsed by AoA trainers in Zambia and was a key component of a a training workshop on reporting energy. The 20 journalists from different media houses in Zambia who took part each received a copy of the handbook for use in their newsroom. 2019 Q1: Top Story Season 3 preparation includes development of intensive capacity building sessions on investigative journalism reporting techniques, ethics, digital/physical safety, for journalism student participants that will take place at the Top Story bootcamp in May. Q2: The safety of journalists will be a key theme in Top Story Season 3. There will be specialist training for contestants and lecturers focusing on both physical and digital safety. AoA will also be vigilant in ensuring the safety of contestants carrying out sensitive investigations during the competition. Q3: Safety is an integral part of AoA organisation and activities. Before any filming activity takes place or any event involving members of the public or done in public places, a security appraisal is conducted. Additionally, AoA advocates for safety (physical/cyber) to be mainstreamed across all journalism curricula of participating universities. 2020 Q2: AoA’s production and filming activities are conducted in accordance with the high standards of safety in place in international media organisations such as the BBC and Aljazeera. A thorough recce and audit of safety at proposed filming locations is carried out in advance and the teams travelling to film in such locations are always accompanied by a security specialist. In addition, competing teams undergo digital safety training at the initial bootcamp that is run at the start of each season of Top Story. | Capacity Development in strategic engagement: Media and CSOs are capable to relate strategically to achieve common goals in Lobby and Advocacy. | Media serve the interests of the public and act as a watchdog on their behalf | AfricaonAir strengthens and institutionalise relationships with local CSOs advocating on matters of national developmental interest, safety and security. Media professionals routinely source and interact with CSOs as credible sources of information on reportages of public interest. | 2016: Workshop for journalists on food security included inputs and expertise from CSOs active in the field (Nairobi, 14-16 December 2016). 2017: Introductory steps taken by AoA toward communication training with Human Rights Watch. Preparatory work taken with Media Council of Kenya and Article 19 to collaborate on delivery of election reporting and safety training for Kenyan journalists. Top Story competition journalism teams regularly work with local CSOs in production of their investigative reportages on vital development issues including health, education and the environment. Q4: AoA has a good working relationship with CSOs. That’s how they managed to attract high profile people including a Minister and CEOs to take part in Top Story. Through the nine personalities who were interviewed, AfricaonAir has expanded and strengthened its network to include leading banks, civil society organisations such as the Kenya Red Cross Society, the Kenya Film Classification Board and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. 2018: Q1 Due to the nature of work that AfricaonAir is involved in, safety considerations are paramount. AoA has security consultants who advise on its physical and digital initiatives, including deployment of personnel and work involving members of the public. Q3: AoA briefed the Netherlands Embassy in September regarding its operation. The embassy connected AoA to a number of other Dutch-funded CSOs where there’s potential for collaboration around development reportage production and sources of information for Top Story Africa participants. 2019 Q1: AoA has a good working relationship with media in Kenya, CSOs, the government as well as the private sector. The government-owned Kenya Broadcasting Corporation is about to start rebroadcasting Top Story Season 2. Participants of Top Story are required to work with local CSOs as sources of stories and of information in reportage production. AoA continues to be actively involved in the journalism ecosystem in Kenya and Africa generally. Its director is a regular analyst on TV discussions regarding media. He has now been tasked with the job of helping to develop a governance framework for a new association of African journalists who work for international media in different countries across the continent. Q2: AoA now has a direct link to the media industry in Kenya and will benefit from the deep insights it will get regarding the media environment. The appointment of its director to consult for the Nation Media Group also puts AoA in a great position to develop innovative ways of telling stories and reaching audiences as well as a chance to influence the growth of media in Kenya. The reality journalism feature on Al Jazeera’s Listening Post programme in May gave AoA a huge boost. https://www.aljazeera.com/programmes/listeningpost/2019/05/mix-journalism-reality-tv-190504104518880.html The network received numerous messages from people who did not know about Top Story. It also raised interest among the university community in Kenya. AoA Director also regularly appears on TV and radio discussions about media in Kenya and Africa. One of the shows analysing the media and politics of East Africa had one million viewers. Q3: AoA has an excellent relationship with the media industry in Kenya. It is often called upon to provide training or recommend potential employees from its experience of working closely with over 25 universities in Kenya. Participants of Top Story Season 3 are again required to work with local CSOs as sources of stories and of information in reportage production. Q4: AoA continues to enjoy a very good working relationship with the media industry in Kenya. As a result, AoA is often called upon to provide training or recommend potential employees from its experience of working closely with over 25 universities in Kenya.

description: Kenya is an important partner country of VLIR-UOS, situated in the midrange of the VLIR-UOS financial envelope. The Kenya country strategy focuses on partnerships with the following 7 established public institutions with a strong research culture that are able to take up a coordinating/ mentoring role in networking modalities with newer universities: University of Nairobi, Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology, Moi University, Egerton University, Maseno University, Kenyatta University and Kenya Marine and Fisheries Research Institute. Other accredited higher education institutions and other public (non-profit) research institutes can also be involved but preferably in partnership with one or more of the above mentioned established public institutions. VLIR-UOS supports interventions that strengthen higher education, research and extension in the following strategic domains: health, natural resource management and development, and food security. 'ICT development' and 'statistics' have been identified as crosscutting themes that are relevant for all VLIR-UOS activities in Kenya. VLIR-UOS supports projects (TEAM, SI) at departmental level and long term programmes (IUC) at institutional level. Two IUC programmes are already ongoing: one with Moi University (with different projects in the field of engineering, agriculture, health, textile, institutional development) and one with Jomo Kenyatta University of Agriculture and Technology (with different projects in the field of legumes research). One departmental TEAM project in the field of aquaculture education has started in 2017. A number of new projects for Kenya will still be selected in the 2017-2021 period.

title: Credit and Financial Services: Programme for Rural Outreach of Financial Innovations and Technologies
description: The programme''s overall goal is to contribute to the reduction of poverty in rural Kenya.  It will specifically seek to increase incomes of the target group as a result of improved production and productivity in the agriculture, livestock, fisheries and rural enterprise sectors.Key programme objectivesThe programme development objective is increased incomes of the target group as a result of improved production and productivity in the rural smallholder farm and off-farm sectors. The principal outcomes expected from the programme are that (i) poor rural households have enhanced access to a broad range of cost-effective financial services; (ii) systemic changes are made in the financial sector for a sustainable flow of funds to agricultural and rural areas; and (iii) the target group effectively manages its assets, markets its produce and increases its employment. reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: F.a: Safeguarding Biocultural Rights of the Hunter Gatherer communities in Kenya
description:
Hunter-gatherer communities in Kenya have constantly and gradually continued to lose their habitat to logging and clearing for agriculture, and development of extractive industries and have been evicted in the name of conservation. In addition, indigenous 
lands have been taken over by outside communities on the basis of their own needs. For this project, these mentioned challenges face both the Ogiek of the Mau forest, the Yiakus of the Mukogodo forest and the Sengwers of the Embobut forest. These communiti
es have joined forces and are working to advance the rights of hunter-gatherers locally, nationally and internationally.   The proposed project seeks to restore the communities' land tenure rights and the protection of biodiversity through development of C
ommunity Biocultural Protocols (BCPs). These protocols establish cultural structures, management systems and practices based on the communities' traditional knowledge, territories and natural resources, and assess the related challenges they face. Dialogue
s will be organized with the government representatives to highlight the activities of the project and to seek recognition of the land tenure rights of the communities and to promote the protection of biodiversity also as a basis for the sustainable liveli
hood of the communities. The aim is also to engage young people in restoration of lost biodiversity through tree planting.   In the case of Yiaku and Sengwer, these are their first biocultural protocols, and in the case of Ogiek, this would be an update to
 the protocol from five years back in the light of changed context and new needs. Biocultural protocols will be produced in written form and printed for each community for use by them and other relevant stakeholders.   The project is estimated to have abou
t 10,000 direct beneficiaries (Ogieks, Sengwers and Yiakus), about half of whom are women.   The legal holder of the project would be OPDP (Ogiek Peoples ?Development Program). Two other organizations acting on behalf of Kenya's hunter-gatherer communities
 are also central to this project: the Yiaku Laikipia Trust (YLT) and the Sengwer Indigenous People Program (SIPP). Information on their activities can be found e.g. from here:  www.ogiekpeoples.org, https://www.yiakulaikipiaktrust.org/, https://www.cbd.in
t/traditional/presentations/africa-sengwer-2016.pdf + https://www.survivalinternational.org/news/11911

title: FACT4BUDGET PROGRAMME
description:
Addition 2015

The federation, with support from Agriterra has been implementing the FACT4Budget project in 5 counties, where the federation has been building the capacity of the farmers to participate in budgetary allocation process at the county level. The methodology used is the Farmers Advocacy Consultation Tool (FACT) approach, which is a tool used by Farmer organizations to enhance their capacities to effectively participate in lobby processes. KENAFF would like to amplify the good lessons learned from the piloted counties on the FACT approach to cover twenty more counties as well as out scale the same to ten youth farmer organizations.

2014
Kenya National Federation of Agricultural Producers (KENFAP) is the apex farmers’ organization in Kenya. Its objective is to articulate issues affecting farmers by defending the interests of its members and the general farming community through focused lobby and advocacy to the relevant entities. The federation’s stronghold encompasses 2 million farm families drawn from the farming community structured into 10,000 farmer groups. The membership is spread over 42 out of the 47 counties in Kenya. 

The Kenya Constitution 2010 creates a county government structure which enables the national government to have considerable authority over the policy issues, regulation, capacity building, finance and technical assistance among others. On the other hand, county governments will be responsible for priority setting, financial management, agricultural production and related extension services in their respective areas of operation. This will allow a better alignment of the government actions and projects to the objectives and priorities of the national development agenda.

By using the FACT approach Kenfap want to sustain the lobby and advocacy capacities of its members and to increase their participation in policy formulation processes and their representation in relevant stakeholder platforms. title: F.a: Creative Industry: Enhanced Digital Skills for Livelihood Opportunities in the Creative Economy
description:
1.	Project: 12274 Creative Industry: Enhanced Digital Skills for Livelihood Opportunities in the Creative Economy 2.	Project area and Country: Nairobi, Kenya 3.	Project justification:  Kenya?s population is dominated by young people with those below the age of 15 making up 39% of the population. The COVID-19 pandemic has had a very large impact on the labor market with longer-term implications, nearly 2 million people are estimated to have fallen into poverty, and nearly 900,000 lost their jobs. Workers lost jobs and moved into agriculture to survive.  The growth in digital technology would enable some service sub-sectors to replicate features of the manufacturing sector that enable scale, innovation, and spillovers that are important for long-term development and job creation. The more dynamic services sector is gaining ground, such as film, tv and video, music, publishing, and video games, driven by digital innovation. Ensuring that creative industries continue to grow and expand is a way of increasing opportunities and diversity, leading to inclusive growth while adapting to new economic shifts.  The government of Kenya believes the industry is now worth more and has the potential to become a key catalyst to the country?s economic growth. For this reason, the creative economy in Kenya is growing, in particular, with regard to the employment opportunities the sector potentially offers to Kenya?s youth in the cities and counties. A resilient recovery from the pandemic and restarting economic transformation should support a thriving private sector and further enable the ?3 Ts?: trade, technology, and training.   4.	The main objective and the expected results: The main objective of the Creative Industries program is to equip the youth in the target areas with digital skills to enable them to create jobs for themselves and earn a livelihood. The expected results include a strengthened ecosystem for creative industry education with positive visibility for the creative sector as a potential source of jobs and an increased number of training opportunities in the creative sector, as well as an increase in entrepreneurial attitude and awareness among the youths. 5. Kenian väestöstä 39% on alle 15-vuotiaita. Covid-19 -pandemia on vaikuttanut työmarkkinoihin laajasti, lähes 2 miljoonan henkilön on arvioitu pudonneen köyhyysrajan alapuolelle ja lähes 900,000 on menettänyt työnsä. Monet ovat siirtyneet töihin maatalouden pariin selvitäkseen. 
Digitaalisen teknologian kasvu mahdollistaisi joidenkin palvelualojen pitkäaikaisen kehityksen ja työpaikkojen lisääntymisen. reporting_org_name: Ministry for Foreign Affairs of Finland
title: F.a: Strengthening and realization of indigenous peoples? biocultural rights with community protocols in Kenya
description:
The indigenous communities in Kenya have continuously been losing their living areas for activities like forestry, agriculture and mining, or expansion of conservation areas. In addition, outside communities have taken over lands belonging to indigenous peoples. Through these processes, the communities' cultural tradition and natural resource base have been eroded. In this project, the Ogiek, Sengwer, Endorois and Elmolo communities have joined forces in an effort to strengthen their biocultural continuity and push for the rights of indigenous peoples locally, nationally and internationally ? utilizing among other things the international conventions and treaties supporting the rights of the indigenous peoples.  This project strengthens the communities' land rights and the protection of biodiversity with the help of community biocultural protocols. They document the cultural structures, management systems and procedures based on the communities' traditional knowledge, their territories and natural resources, assess the challenges facing these, and outline legal and political instruments to strengthen the protection of the community interests. During the implementation of the project and on the basis of its outputs, the understanding of the legal rights of the communities in question and their cultural characteristics will also be increased among key stakeholders (such as the government authorities, the research community and civil society actors). The Ogiek and Sengwer are traditionally hunter-gatherer communities, the Endorois nomads and the Elmolo fishermen. The project presentation is partly a continuation of a project previously supported by Siemenpuu in 2020-21. In this project, for the Ogiek and Sengwer, the aim is to utilize the biocultural protocols prepared in the previous project in the rights related advocacy work. The protocol of the Sengwers is also updated based on the current situation of the community. The biocultural protocol of the Endorois community drawn up in 2019 will be updated. Regarding the Elmolo community, a community protocol will be prepared for them. The project will be implemented in Nakuru, Narok, Baringo, Uasin Gishu, Kericho, Nandi, Trans Nzoia, Elgeyo Marakwet and Marsabit counties. The project is estimated to have approx. 6,000 direct beneficiaries, half of whom are women. The project is implemented by Ogiek Peoples? Development Program (OPDP); https://ogiekpeoples.org/. | Alkuperäiskansayhteisöt Keniassa ovat jatkuvasti menettäneet elinalueitaan mm. metsä-, maatalous- ja kaivostoiminnalle sekä joutuneet häädetyiksi luonnonsuojelualueita perustettaessa tai laajennettaessa. Lisäksi ulkopuoliset yhteisöt ovat vallanneet alkuperäiskansoille kuuluvia maita. Näiden prosessien kautta yhteisöjen kulttuurinen perinne ja luonnonvaraperusta on heikentynyt.
Tässä hankkeessa ogiek-, sengwer-, endorois- ja elmolo-yhteisöt ovat yhdistäneet voimansa pyrkien vahvistamaan kulttuurista jatkuvuuttaan ja ajamaan alkuperäiskansojen oikeuksia paikallisesti, kansallisesti sekä kansainvälisesti – hyödyntäen mm. Kenian alkuperäiskansojen oikeustyötä tukevia ylikansallisia linjauksia.
Hankkeessa vahvistetaan yhteisöjen maaoikeuksia ja elonkirjon suojelua yhteisöjen biokulttuuristen pöytäkirjojen eli protokollien avulla. Näissä pöytäkirjoissa dokumentoidaan yhteisöjen perinteiseen tietoon, alueisiin ja luonnonvaroihin pohjautuvia kulttuurisia rakenteita, hallintajärjestelmiä ja toimintatapoja, arvioidaan näihin kohdistuvia haasteita sekä hahmotellaan juridisia ja poliittisia välineitä edunvalvonnan vahvistamiseksi. Hankkeen toteutuksen aikana ja sen tuotosten pohjalta lisätään myös keskeisten viiteryhmien (kuten asianomaiset viranomaiset, tutkimusyhteisö ja kansalaisyhteiskunnan toimijat) ymmärrystä kyseisten yhteisöjen laillisista oikeuksista ja niiden kulttuurisista ominaispiirteistä.
Ogiekit ja sengwerit ovat perinteisesti metsästäjä-keräilijäyhteisöjä, endoroisit paimentolaisia ja elmolot kalastajia.
Hanke on osittain jatkoa Siemenpuun aiemmin 2020-21 tukemalle hankkeelle; nyt edellisessä hankkeessa laadittuja ogiekien ja sengwerien biokulttuuripöytäkirjoja pyritään hyödyntämään yhteisöjen edunvalvonnassa. Sengwerien pöytäkirjaa myös päivitetään yhteisön ajankohtaisen tilanteen pohjalta. Endorois-yhteisön vuonna 2019 laadittu biokulttuuripöytäkirja saatetaan ajantasalle. Elmolo-yhteisön osalta laaditaan heitä koskeva yhteisöpöytäkirja. Hanke toteutetaan Nakurun, Narokin, Baringon, Uasingishun, Kerichon, Nandin, Trans Nzoian, Elgeyo Marakwetin ja Marsabitin piirikuntien alueella. Hankkeella arvioidaan olevan n. 6000 suoraa hyödynsaajaa, joista puolet naisia.
Hankkeen toteuttajajärjestö on Ogiek Peoples’ Development Program (OPDP): https://ogiekpeoples.org/.

title: Help Self Help Center (HSHC) - Improving Employability of Post TVET Graduates in Nyeri and Laikipia Counties
description:
The project is informed by the many challenges facing the Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) systems in Kenya, the failure to provide transferable life skills to TVET graduates is one of the challenges related to quality and relevance of TVET education.. Many employers prefer to hire youth who, in addition to possessing required technical skills, also possess such ?skills? like: positive attitudes, honesty, initiative, ambition, communication, respect, ability to follow instructions and work in teams, etc. The failure to provide transferable life skills results in TVET graduates who, even when they have the requisite technical skills, are not able to succeed at work or in developing their own business and lack the resilience to recover from inevitable setbacks. 

 The project is an extension of ?improving employability of TVET graduates? funded by the Embassy (2021/22). The project had had the following results;  531 TVET graduates were trained on soft skills, of which 26 got employed in formal & informal sectors, 291 TVET graduates got registered with service provision platform while 32 graduates started own enterprise, in farming, metal work, electronic repair. Six (6) awards given to innovative/creative business ideas in the various sectors- agriculture (2), ICT (2), energy (1), transport (1).  The proposal is a follow-up with an aim to extend the success of the first project through further training of additional post TVET graduates (PTVET) in soft skills, entrepreneurship and facilitating linkages to the job market. The development objective of the project is to improve employability and competitiveness of Kenyan post TVET Graduates through quality and relevant soft skills and entrepreneurship training. title: Supporting business opportunities for rural women in east and southern Africa
description:
Women in Zimbabwe, Kenya, and Uganda experience disadvantages and gender inequalities in labour and production. There is a supportive political environment in these countries for women's empowerment, however implementation is generally weak. A collaboration between the University of Zimbabwe, Advocates Coalition for Development and Environment, and the Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, this project aims to empower rural women economically through the development of business enterprises and decent job creation. 

This project seeks to investigate rural women's farming, agro-processing and other livelihood activities, and explore good practices in promoting decent employment, entrepreneurship, and empowerment. The research will identify factors and policy instruments influencing rural women’s choice of activities, explore how best to make agriculture more rewarding, and determine the types of entrepreneurship that are likely to result in economic empowerment of women. It will also build the capacity of women involved in small-scale agriculture through partnerships with the private sector, especially around marketing and quality control.

The project will examine the structural barriers that constrain women from becoming more innovative and limit their ability to take advantage of the opportunities available for business development. It will also identify and explore the opportunities that exist off farm for rural women, including activities that tend to be male-dominated and of higher value. Using quantitative and qualitative methods, this research project will provide comparisons between the three countries as well as generate new knowledge that can inform best practices and innovative interventions for other countries in sub-Saharan Africa. | Les femmes au Zimbabwe, au Kenya et en Ouganda connaissent des désavantages et des inégalités sexospécifiques dans le monde du travail et de la production. Bien que le climat politique dans ces pays soit favorable à l’autonomisation des femmes, la concrétisation est généralement faible. Issu d’une collaboration entre l’Université du Zimbabwe, la Advocates Coalition for Development and Environment, et le Collaborative Centre for Gender and Development, ce projet vise à promouvoir l’autonomie économique des femmes en milieu rural au moyen de la création d’entreprises et d’emplois décents. 

Ce projet vise à étudier les activités de subsistance des femmes en milieu rural en agriculture, en agroalimentaire et dans d’autres secteurs, ainsi que les pratiques exemplaires, l’entrepreneuriat et l’autonomisation. La recherche permettra de cerner les facteurs et les instruments de politique qui influent sur les activités que choisissent les femmes en milieu rural, d’étudier les meilleurs moyens de rendre l’agriculture plus gratifiante et de déterminer les types d’entrepreneuriat propices à l’autonomisation économique des femmes. Il contribuera en outre à renforcer les capacités des femmes s’investissant dans l’agriculture à petite échelle au moyen de partenariats avec le secteur privé, en particulier dans les domaines de la commercialisation et du contrôle de la qualité.

Le projet examinera les obstacles structuraux qui empêchent les femmes de devenir plus innovatrices et qui restreignent leur capacité à tirer parti des possibilités de croissance des affaires. Il permettra par ailleurs de déterminer et d’étudier les possibilités d’exploitation agricole pour les femmes en milieu rural, y compris des secteurs d’activité dominés par des hommes et plus rentables. Au moyen de méthodes quantitatives et qualitatives, ce projet de recherche produira des comparaisons entre les trois pays et de nouvelles connaissances dont d’autres pays d’Afrique subsaharienne pourront profiter comme pratiques exemplaires et interventions novatrices.

title: Privatsektorförderung in der Landwirtschaft-Kleinbewässerung Mount Kenya III
description: Dieses Vorhaben ist eine Aufstockung  des Programms Kleinbewässerung Mt. Kenya, das hiermit in seine dritte Phase kommt:Phase I ( BMZ Nr. 1999 66 466 und 2003 70 437) und Phase II (BMZ Nr. 2004 65 146 und BMZ Nr. 2006 70 224). Das Kleinbewässerungsprogramm im Mount Kenia Gebiet ist Bestandteil des deutschen EZ-Programms zur Unterstützung der Privatsektorentwicklung in der Landwirtschaft Kenias. Diese Maßnahme wird von der KfW in Kooperation mit dem DED durchgeführt.Das entwicklungspolitische Ziel ist die Verbesserung der Lebensbedingungen ländlicher Haushalte in der Programmregion um den Mount Kenia.  Das Ziel dieser FZ-Maßnahme ist die Steigerung der landwirtschaftlichen Produktion und deren Integration in die entsprechende Wertschöpfungskette durch Verbesserung der Qualität von landwirtschaftlichen Produkten. Das Vorhaben fördert die Einführung von Bewässerung, was die Effizienz, Qualität und Produktivität der kleinbäuerlichen Produktion verbessert. Das Mount Kenya Gebiet ist besonders geeignet für die Entwicklung kleiner und mittlerer Bewässerungsperimeter. Die Abläufe des Vorhabens können in einen technischen und in einen sozialen Prozess gegliedert werden. Sie reichen von der Ansprache der Bauerngruppen und der Konzeptbildung bis Inbetriebnahme der Bewässerungsperimeter und der Vermarktung landwirtschaftlicher Produkte. Im Rahmen des sozialen Prozesses werden bäuerliche Selbsthilfegruppen bei der Bildung von Genossenschaften und den notwendigen Vorbereitungen für die Investitionsmaßnahme (Beantragung von Wasserrechten und Krediten) unterstützt. Nach dem Abschluß der Baumaßnahmen werden die Bewässerungsgenossenschaften in der Unterhaltung der Perimeter geschult sowie bei der Vermarktung (DED) unterstützt. Der technische Prozeß umfaßt die Vorstudien (technische Varianten und Umweltstudie) und die notwendigen Genehmigungen (Wasserrechte), die technische Ausführungsplanung sowie die Bauarbeiten und die Inbetriebnahme der Perimeter. Die technische Planung wird von kenianischen Ingenieuren und die Bauausführung von lokal ansässigen Firmen durchgeführt. Mit den FZ Mitteln wird faktisch der gesamte Prozess gestützt. Die FZ-Mittel für die Baumaßnahmen werden über kenianische Banken (Cooperative Bank und Equity Bank) geleitet. Die teilnehmenden Genossenschaften müssen dort einen Finanzierungsantrag für ihren Perimeter einreichen. Fünfzig Prozent der den Landwirten zur Verfügung gestellten Mittel werden als Darlehen und fünfzig Prozent als Subvention zur Verfügung gestellt. Die Zurückerstattung der Kredite soll aus den Erträgen der Landwirte erfolgen. | Private sector development in agriculture-Smallholder Irrigation Programme Mount Kenya Phase III | Steigerung der landwirtschaftlichen Produktion von Kleinbauern in Distrikten östlich des Mount Kenyas.

title: Addressing Africa’s youth unemployment through skills for industries without smokestacks
description:
This project seeks to inform strategies and policies on youth employment by examining the job creation potential of industries without smokestacks, such as agriculture, the service sector, tourism, and information and communication technology-based services. 

Implemented in collaboration with the Brookings Institution, the project will fund researchers from Kenya, Senegal, South Africa, and Uganda to assess the ecosystem and employment creation potential of these industries. They will also assess the skills required, with a focus on soft skills, digital skills, and how countries can address skills mismatches.

The project is part of a cohort of IDRC-supported projects aimed at boosting decent employment for Africa’s youth. This initiative focuses on two niche areas: soft and digital skills and apprenticeship and mentorship models that work for youth. Developed as part of a collaborative effort between IDRC, the Dutch Knowledge Platform on Inclusive Development Policies (INCLUDE) and the International Labour Organization, the goal is to provide practical guidance and tools for policymakers and practitioners to help realize aspirations for large-scale positive change. | Ce projet cherche à éclairer les stratégies et les politiques sur l’emploi des jeunes en examinant le potentiel de création d’emplois des industries sans cheminée, comme l’agriculture, le secteur des services, le tourisme et les services axés sur les technologies de l’information et des communications. 

Mis en œuvre en collaboration avec la Brookings Institution, le projet financera des chercheurs du Kenya, du Sénégal, d’Afrique du Sud et d’Ouganda pour évaluer l’écosystème et le potentiel de création d’emplois de ces industries. Ces chercheurs évalueront également les compétences requises, en se concentrant sur les compétences générales, les compétences numériques et par quels moyens les pays peuvent résoudre le problème de l’inadéquation des compétences.

Le projet fait partie d’une série de projets appuyés par le CRDI visant à promouvoir les emplois décents pour la jeunesse africaine. Il se concentre sur deux créneaux : les compétences générales et numériques et les modèles d’apprentissage et de mentorat qui fonctionnent pour les jeunes. Élaboré dans le cadre d’une collaboration entre le CRDI, la plateforme de connaissances sur les politiques de développement inclusif des Pays-Bas (INCLUDE) et l’Organisation internationale du travail, l’objectif est de fournir des orientations pratiques et des outils aux décideurs et aux praticiens afin de permettre de réaliser les aspirations concernant des changements positifs à grande échelle.

title: The Effectiveness of the Metro Agri-Food Living Lab for Gender Inclusive Youth Entrepreneurship Development in Kenya
description:
The world’s urban population will surpass its rural population by 2030. In order to provide food to the growing cities, an innovative and inclusive approach for agri-food entrepreneurs will be necessary. This presents an important opportunity for youth, whose unemployment rate surpasses that of adults by 25%. 

The first phase of this project (June 2015-March 2017), implemented by the Metro Agri-Food Living Lab,  tested the effectiveness of various interventions, including training and business counselling, to actively engage Kenya’s youth in profitable agri-businesses. Three components were identified for the youth entrepreneurship model: training, mentoring, and funding. This second phase will integrate rigorous research design to test these components individually and in combination. The project seeks to answer two fundamental research questions: what works to successfully build youth-led businesses in the agriculture sector; and what is the added value of training, mentoring, and funding in building successful youth-led businesses. Other key research topics will include gender barriers and opportunities for youth entrepreneurship and the role of the external environment, including government policies. 

The project increases the number of participants from 210 to 1,200 and expands the range of agribusinesses beyond poultry and fisheries. Gender will be integrated throughout the project cycle from the selection of participants to the evaluation of outcomes. Youth participating in the program are expected to boost their sales, expand their businesses, and improve their livelihoods. This growth is expected to benefit an additional 15,000 youth as employees, suppliers, and peer mentors in the following 24 months. The financing module is also expected to catalyze private investment into early-stage enterprises.

This project is funded through the Cultivate Africa’s Future Fund (CultiAF), a joint program of IDRC and the Australian International Food Security Research Centre of the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research. CultiAF supports research to achieve long-term food security in eastern and southern Africa. | La population urbaine mondiale dépassera la population rurale d’ici 2030. Il sera nécessaire pour les entrepreneurs du secteur agroalimentaire d’appliquer une approche inclusive et novatrice afin de pouvoir offrir de la nourriture aux villes en expansion. L’occasion qui se présente est unique pour les jeunes, chez qui le taux de chômage est plus élevé de 25 % que celui trouvé chez les adultes. 

Mise en œuvre par le Metro Agri-Food Living Lab, la première phase de ce projet (juin 2015 à mars 2017) a permis de tester l’efficacité des diverses interventions, y compris la formation et les conseils aux entreprises, afin d’engager activement la jeunesse du Kenya dans des agroentreprises rentables. Trois éléments ont été identifiés dans le modèle d’entrepreneuriat chez les jeunes : la formation, le mentorat et le financement. Cette deuxième phase intégrera une conception de recherche rigoureuse pour tester ces éléments. Le projet cherche à répondre à deux questions de recherche fondamentales : déterminer ce qui fonctionne pour bâtir des entreprises dirigées par des jeunes dans le secteur agricole et établir la valeur ajoutée de la formation, du mentorat et du financement dans l’édification d’entreprises dirigées par des jeunes et qui connaissent le succès. D’autres principaux domaines de recherche incluront les obstacles sexospécifiques et les possibilités d’entrepreneuriat chez les jeunes, ainsi que le rôle de l’environnement externe, notamment les politiques gouvernementales. 

Le nombre de participants au projet augmente et passe de 210 à 1 200, et la portée des agroentreprises s’étend au-delà des secteurs de la volaille et du poisson. Les sexospécificités seront intégrées au fil du projet et les jeunes qui participent devraient augmenter leurs ventes, élargir leurs entreprises et améliorer leurs moyens de subsistance. Cette croissance devrait pouvoir profiter à 15 000 autres jeunes en tant qu’employés, fournisseurs et pairs mentors au cours des 24 prochains mois. Le module de financement devrait aussi catalyser les investissements privés dans les entreprises à un stade préliminaire.

Le projet est financé par le fonds Cultiver l’avenir de l’Afrique (CultivAf), programme conjoint du CRDI et de l’Australian International Food Security Research Centre, qui est une composante de l’Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research. CultivAf finance des travaux de recherche visant à accroître la sécurité alimentaire à long terme en Afrique de l’Est et en Afrique austral.

title: Providing strategic support to the development of Kenya’s non-communicable disease policy 2021–2025
description:
In Kenya, non-communicable diseases (NCDs) account for more than half of hospital deaths. Additionally, households of people living with NCDs in Kenya experience around a 30% decrease in household income and are thus vulnerable to catastrophic expenditures that could push them further into extreme poverty. In response to the burden of NCDs in Kenya, the Ministry of Health launched the Kenya National Strategy for the Prevention and Control of NCDs 2015–2020. The Ministry commissioned an evaluation of the Strategy with a view to informing a new Strategy for the period 2021–2025. Generally, the evaluation found that although most of the targets in the Strategy were “fully” or “partially” achieved, there were still several significant gaps and opportunities for improvement.

A significant finding of the evaluation was that the strategy was not costed, therefore hindering planning, resource allocation, and implementation. This health-led strategy also lacked coherence and synergy with relevant sectors influencing food systems, such as agriculture. The process of developing the 2021–2025 strategy began in mid-2020 and the Kenya Ministry of Health intends to cost the new strategy to facilitate more effective resource mobilization for implementation. They also seek to the strengthen the coherence of the draft strategy with the plans for other relevant national priorities such as agri-nutrition and gender equality. The goal of this project is to support the Ministry of Health in achieving these two objectives, thereby strengthening the new Strategy.

This project is funded through the Catalyzing Change for Health and Sustainable Food Systems (CCHeFS) Initiative, a co-funding partnership between IDRC and the Rockefeller Foundation. | Au Kenya, les maladies non transmissibles (MNT) sont responsables de plus de la moitié des décès dans les hôpitaux. En outre, les ménages de personnes atteintes de MNT au Kenya subissant une baisse d’environ 30 % de leurs revenus, ils sont vulnérables aux dépenses catastrophiques qui pourraient les faire sombrer davantage dans l’extrême pauvreté. En réponse au fardeau des MNT au Kenya, le ministère de la Santé a lancé la Stratégie nationale du Kenya pour la prévention et le contrôle des maladies non transmissibles 2015-2020. Le ministère a commandé une évaluation de la stratégie en vue d’en élaborer une nouvelle pour la période 2021-2025. Malgré l’atteinte « partielle » ou « totale » des objectifs de la stratégie, l’évaluation indique des lacunes importantes et des possibilités d’amélioration, ainsi que des problèmes de planification, d’affectation des ressources et de déploiement, faute de données chiffrées.

 Cette stratégie axée sur la santé manquait également de cohérence et de synergie avec des secteurs liés aux systèmes alimentaires, comme l’agriculture. Le processus d’élaboration de la stratégie 2021-2025 a débuté à la mi-2020 et le ministère de la Santé du Kenya entend chiffrer la nouvelle stratégie afin d’améliorer la mobilisation des ressources pour sa mise en oeuvre. Par ailleurs, il souhaite renforcer la cohérence de ce projet avec d’autres plans de priorités nationales telles que l’agronutrition et l’égalité des sexes. Ce projet vise à aider le ministère de la Santé à atteindre ces deux objectifs, renforçant ainsi la nouvelle stratégie.

Ce projet est financé par l’initiative Catalyzing Change for Healthy and Sustainable Food Systems (CCHeFS), un partenariat de cofinancement entre le CRDI et la Fondation Rockefeller.

title: The Effectiveness of the Metro Agri-Food Living Lab for Gender Inclusive Youth Entrepreneurship Development in Kenya
description:
The world’s urban population will surpass its rural population by 2030. In order to provide food to the growing cities, an innovative and inclusive approach for agri-food entrepreneurs will be necessary. This presents an important opportunity for youth, whose unemployment rate surpasses that of adults by 25%. 

The first phase of this project (June 2015-March 2017), implemented by the Metro Agri-Food Living Lab,  tested the effectiveness of various interventions, including training and business counselling, to actively engage Kenya’s youth in profitable agri-businesses. Three components were identified for the youth entrepreneurship model: training, mentoring, and funding. This second phase will integrate rigorous research design to test these components individually and in combination. The project seeks to answer two fundamental research questions: what works to successfully build youth-led businesses in the agriculture sector; and what is the added value of training, mentoring, and funding in building successful youth-led businesses. Other key research topics will include gender barriers and opportunities for youth entrepreneurship and the role of the external environment, including government policies. 

The project increases the number of participants from 210 to 1,200 and expands the range of agribusinesses beyond poultry and fisheries. Gender will be integrated throughout the project cycle from the selection of participants to the evaluation of outcomes. Youth participating in the program are expected to boost their sales, expand their businesses, and improve their livelihoods. This growth is expected to benefit an additional 15,000 youth as employees, suppliers, and peer mentors in the following 24 months. The financing module is also expected to catalyze private investment into early-stage enterprises.

This project is funded through the Cultivate Africa’s Future Fund (CultiAF), a joint program of IDRC and the Australian International Food Security Research Centre of the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research. CultiAF supports research to achieve long-term food security in eastern and southern Africa. | La population urbaine mondiale dépassera la population rurale d’ici 2030. Il sera nécessaire pour les entrepreneurs du secteur agroalimentaire d’appliquer une approche inclusive et novatrice afin de pouvoir offrir de la nourriture aux villes en expansion. L’occasion qui se présente est unique pour les jeunes, chez qui le taux de chômage est plus élevé de 25 % que celui trouvé chez les adultes. 

Mise en œuvre par le Metro Agri-Food Living Lab, la première phase de ce projet (juin 2015 à mars 2017) a permis de tester l’efficacité des diverses interventions, y compris la formation et les conseils aux entreprises, afin d’engager activement la jeunesse du Kenya dans des agroentreprises rentables. Trois éléments ont été identifiés dans le modèle d’entrepreneuriat chez les jeunes : la formation, le mentorat et le financement. Cette deuxième phase intégrera une conception de recherche rigoureuse pour tester ces éléments. Le projet cherche à répondre à deux questions de recherche fondamentales : déterminer ce qui fonctionne pour bâtir des entreprises dirigées par des jeunes dans le secteur agricole et établir la valeur ajoutée de la formation, du mentorat et du financement dans l’édification d’entreprises dirigées par des jeunes et qui connaissent le succès. D’autres principaux domaines de recherche incluront les obstacles sexospécifiques et les possibilités d’entrepreneuriat chez les jeunes, ainsi que le rôle de l’environnement externe, notamment les politiques gouvernementales. 

Le nombre de participants au projet augmente et passe de 210 à 1 200, et la portée des agroentreprises s’étend au-delà des secteurs de la volaille et du poisson. Les sexospécificités seront intégrées au fil du projet et les jeunes qui participent devraient augmenter leurs ventes, élargir leurs entreprises et améliorer leurs moyens de subsistance. Cette croissance devrait pouvoir profiter à 15 000 autres jeunes en tant qu’employés, fournisseurs et pairs mentors au cours des 24 prochains mois. Le module de financement devrait aussi catalyser les investissements privés dans les entreprises à un stade préliminaire.

Le projet est financé par le fonds Cultiver l’avenir de l’Afrique (CultivAf), programme conjoint du CRDI et de l’Australian International Food Security Research Centre, qui est une composante de l’Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research. CultivAf finance des travaux de recherche visant à accroître la sécurité alimentaire à long terme en Afrique de l’Est et en Afrique austral.
